items.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of painful oral erosions and flaccid blisters on her chest and abdomen that rupture easily. Physical examination reveals extensive mucosal involvement and a positive Nikolsky sign. A punch biopsy of a fresh blister is performed. Histopathologic examination shows acantholysis occurring just above the basal layer, with the basal cells remaining attached to the basement membrane zone in a characteristic linear arrangement.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Correlate suprabasal acantholysis and tombstoning with the correct blistering disorder.
items.teachingPoint: Suprabasal acantholysis with a remaining basal layer attached to the basement membrane (tombstoning) is the pathognomonic histopathologic finding for pemphigus vulgaris.
items.explanationCorrect: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is characterized by autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (and often desmoglein 1). This leads to loss of cell-cell adhesion (acantholysis) just above the basal layer. Because the basal cells are attached to the basement membrane via hemidesmosomes (which are not targeted in PV), they remain attached in a row, creating the classic 'tombstone' appearance.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Pemphigus foliaceus involves antibodies to desmoglein 1, resulting in subcorneal acantholysis. It typically lacks mucosal involvement and the blister is much higher in the epidermis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Bullous pemphigoid is a subepidermal blistering disease. Histopathology shows a full-thickness epidermal detachment from the dermis with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate, not acantholysis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is a subepidermal blistering disease caused by antibodies to type VII collagen. It does not feature suprabasal acantholysis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by subepidermal blisters with microabscesses containing neutrophils at the tips of the dermal papillae.

items.stem: A 54-year-old male with a history of chronic hepatitis C and alcohol use presents with multiple tense blisters and erosions on the dorsal aspects of his hands. He reports that these lesions appear following sun exposure and that his skin has become increasingly fragile, with easy bruising. A biopsy of a fresh blister is performed. Histopathology reveals a subepidermal blister with prominent edema of the upper dermis. The dermal papillae are markedly rounded and appear to hang or 'festoon' beneath the blister roof. There is a paucity of inflammatory cells within the blister cavity.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Correlate festooning of dermal papillae in a subepidermal blister with the appropriate porphyrin-related diagnosis.
items.teachingPoint: Festooning of the dermal papillae in a subepidermal blister is a characteristic histopathologic finding of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT), especially when associated with sun-exposed distribution and risk factors such as alcohol use or hepatitis C.
items.explanationCorrect: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria and typically presents with skin fragility and subepidermal blisters on sun-exposed areas, particularly the dorsal hands. The classic histopathologic finding is a subepidermal blister with 'festooning' of the dermal papillae, where the papillae appear as rounded, hanging loops beneath the blister roof due to the loss of the dermal-epidermal junction and associated papillary dermal edema. The clinical context of hepatitis C and alcohol use further supports this diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: B

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Bullous pemphigoid presents with subepidermal blisters, but the histology is typically characterized by a dense inflammatory infiltrate, predominantly eosinophils, which is absent in this case.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis presents with subepidermal blisters, but the histopathology usually shows a neutrophilic infiltrate, often forming microabscesses at the tips of the dermal papillae.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Porphyria variegata can cause similar cutaneous findings to PCT, but it is much rarer and often associated with systemic neurological symptoms. In the context of board examinations, the specific histopathologic description of 'festooning' in a patient with liver-related risk factors is the classic hallmark of PCT.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with multiple firm, skin-colored to reddish-brown nodules on her scalp and forehead. She notes that her father had similar lesions in the same distribution. A biopsy of a 1 cm nodule shows a well-circumscribed tumor composed of nests of basaloid cells. These nests are separated by a prominent, eosinophilic, hyaline-like basement membrane material, creating a characteristic "jigsaw puzzle" appearance. There is no evidence of peripheral palisading or retraction artifact.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Correlate an adnexal tumor pattern such as cylindroma or trichoepithelioma with the appropriate clinical diagnosis.
items.teachingPoint: Cylindroma is characterized histopathologically by a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern of basaloid islands separated by a thick, eosinophilic basement membrane. When multiple lesions occur on the scalp and face, particularly with a family history, it suggests Brooke-Spiegler syndrome (associated with CYLD mutations).
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of multiple nodules on the scalp and forehead with a family history is highly suggestive of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome. The histopathologic description of basaloid nests separated by thick, eosinophilic basement membrane material creating a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern is pathognomonic for cylindroma. Cylindromas are adnexal tumors derived from eccrine or apocrine structures.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Trichoepithelioma typically presents as small facial papules and histologically shows basaloid islands with follicular differentiation, including the presence of horn cysts, rather than a jigsaw pattern with hyaline material.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Spiradenoma consists of basaloid cells arranged in swirls or spirals. While it can be associated with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, it lacks the characteristic jigsaw architecture and thick eosinophilic basement membrane material seen here.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Poroma (e.g., eccrine poroma) typically shows a monomorphic population of basaloid cells in a trabecular or ductal pattern, often with a 'columnar' appearance, but does not exhibit the jigsaw pattern.

distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive blistering skin lesions, primarily on the trunk and proximal extremities. items.teachingPoint: The key to identifying the correct autoantigen target in immunobullous diseases lies in recognizing the distinctive clinical features of each condition, such as the type of blisters (tense vs. flaccid), their distribution, and associated findings like mucosal involvement or specific appearances like the 'string of pearls'.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is BPAG2 because the clinical presentation described, including tense bullae and the 'string of pearls' or 'cluster of jewels' appearance, is most consistent with bullous pemphigoid. items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of a pruritic rash, fever, and lymphadenopathy after starting an anticonvulsant medication 4 weeks ago. Laboratory results show eosinophilia and elevated liver enzymes.

items.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine from irritant dermatitis in a hair-dye reaction.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of an itchy, papular rash on her arms and chest after spending time outdoors. She has no history of skin conditions but has been taking hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.
items.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate polymorphous light eruption from subacute cutaneous lupus and phototoxic drug reaction
items.teachingPoint: The key to differentiating between polymorphous light eruption, subacute cutaneous lupus, and phototoxic drug reaction lies in the patient's medical history, medication use, and the characteristics of the rash. Phototoxic drug reactions are often associated with medication use and occur on sun-exposed areas, whereas polymorphous light eruption and subacute cutaneous lupus may have different underlying causes and presentations.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's symptoms are consistent with a phototoxic drug reaction, which is an adverse reaction to a medication that occurs when the skin is exposed to sunlight. The patient's recent use of hydrochlorothiazide, a known photosensitizing agent, and the appearance of the rash on sun-exposed areas support this diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: While polymorphous light eruption is a possible diagnosis, it typically occurs in individuals with a history of skin conditions and does not have a clear association with medication use.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Subacute cutaneous lupus is an autoimmune condition that can present with photosensitive rash, but it is less likely given the patient's lack of systemic symptoms and no prior history of lupus.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer as explained above.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Photoallergic contact dermatitis is a type of allergic reaction that occurs when the skin comes into contact with a substance and is then exposed to sunlight, but it is less likely in this case given the lack of contact with known allergens.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing, firm, dome-shaped nodule on his left cheek. Histopathological examination reveals a well-differentiated squamous proliferation with central crater-like necrosis and surrounding inflammatory infiltrate.
items.leadIn: What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?

items.teachingPoint: The key to distinguishing keratoacanthoma from squamous cell carcinoma lies in recognizing the clinical presentation of rapid growth and the specific histopathological features, including well-differentiated squamous proliferation and central crater-like necrosis. While both can present with squamous proliferations, the combination of clinical and histological characteristics is crucial for accurate diagnosis.

Examination reveals well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with thick, silvery scales on the extensor surfaces of her elbows and knees, and thickened, scaling plaques on her scalp. Notably, she also has lichenified papules and plaques in the antecubital and popliteal fossae, along with excoriations and mild xerosis on her lower legs. Her personal history is significant for seasonal allergies and asthma since childhood. Which clinical feature most strongly favors a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis over plaque psoriasis?
items.leadIn: Which clinical feature most strongly favors a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis over plaque psoriasis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate atopic dermatitis from plaque psoriasis in a chronic pruritic eruption by identifying the discriminating clinical clues that most strongly favor atopic dermatitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Lichenified papules and plaques in the antecubital and popliteal fossae.
items.teachingPoint: The distribution and morphology of lesions are key differentiating features between atopic dermatitis and plaque psoriasis. Flexural lichenification strongly suggests atopic dermatitis, while sharply demarcated plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces are typical of plaque psoriasis.
items.explanationCorrect: The presence of lichenified lesions in the flexural areas (antecubital and popliteal fossae) is a classic hallmark of chronic atopic dermatitis. While psoriasis can sometimes affect flexural areas (inverse psoriasis), it typically presents as smooth, erythematous patches without significant scaling or lichenification, unlike the described findings.

options.label: A
options.text: Well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with thick, silvery scales on extensor surfaces.

options.label: B
options.text: Thickened, scaling plaques on the scalp.

options.label: C
options.text: Lichenified papules and plaques in the antecubital and popliteal fossae.

options.label: D

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces are characteristic features of classic plaque psoriasis, making this finding less likely in atopic dermatitis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Scalp involvement is common in both plaque psoriasis and atopic dermatitis (seborrheic dermatitis often coexists with AD), so this feature is not discriminating.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: While a history of atopy (allergies, asthma) is strongly associated with atopic dermatitis, it does not definitively exclude psoriasis, as some patients with psoriasis also have comorbid atopic conditions. It supports AD but isn't the most specific clinical finding presented.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Intense pruritus is a prominent symptom of both atopic dermatitis and plaque psoriasis, although it is often described as more severe in atopic dermatitis. However, it is not a reliable distinguishing feature.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While a history of atopy (allergies, asthma) is strongly associated with atopic dermatitis, it does not definitively exclude psoriasis, as some patients with psoriasis also have comorbid atopic conditions. It supports AD but isn't the most specific clinical finding presented.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of intensely pruritic, erythematous, scaling plaques confined to his bilateral elbows and knees. He has a history of seasonal allergies but no asthma. His initial diagnosis was atopic dermatitis (AD), and he has failed a 4-week trial of high-potency topical corticosteroids and a 2-week trial of topical calcineurin inhibitors. The lesions are well-demarcated, with thick silvery scales, and there is minimal involvement of flexural areas. Given the chronicity, localization, morphology, and resistance to standard AD therapies, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for recalcitrant eczematous dermatitis that is labeled 'atopic dermatitis' but remains localized, treatment-resistant, or distribution-atypical.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform patch testing to evaluate for allergic contact dermatitis.
items.teachingPoint: Recalcitrant, localized, or distribution-atypical eczematous dermatitis, even when initially diagnosed as atopic dermatitis, should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses, particularly allergic contact dermatitis. Patch testing is the definitive diagnostic tool for ACD and is often the most appropriate next step in such cases before escalating systemic therapies.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation, particularly the localized distribution (extensor surfaces), morphology (well-demarcated plaques with silvery scales), and resistance to typical AD treatments, raises suspicion for an alternative diagnosis or a complicating factor. Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) can mimic chronic eczema, especially if the allergen exposure is intermittent or localized. Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing ACD and is crucial in cases of recalcitrant, localized eczematous dermatitis, even when initially diagnosed as AD.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform patch testing to evaluate for allergic contact dermatitis.

options.label: C
options.text: Obtain skin biopsies from lesional and non-lesional sites.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe a short course of oral corticosteroids.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Patch testing is indicated because the clinical picture (localized, extensor distribution, morphology, treatment resistance) is atypical for classic AD and could represent ACD mimicking or complicating AD. Ruling out ACD is essential before escalating therapy.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Skin biopsies might be considered if the diagnosis remains unclear after non-invasive investigations, but they are not typically the *next* best step in this scenario. Patch testing is less invasive and directly addresses a common cause of localized, recalcitrant eczema.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Oral corticosteroids can provide temporary relief but are associated with significant side effects and do not address the underlying cause. They are generally avoided for chronic eczematous conditions unless absolutely necessary for severe flares, and they are not the appropriate next diagnostic or management step here.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Phototherapy is a treatment option for both AD and psoriasis, but like systemic therapy, it should be considered after confirming the diagnosis or ruling out treatable causes like ACD. Patch testing is a more appropriate *next* step to clarify the etiology.

items.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of intensely pruritic, erythematous, scaling plaques confined to his bilateral elbows and knees. He has a history of seasonal allergies but no personal or family history of atopic dermatitis. Initial treatment with potent topical corticosteroids and emollients provided minimal relief. The lesions are sharply demarcated, symmetric, and lack significant excoriations despite the severe pruritus. Given the atypical distribution and resistance to standard therapy for presumed atopic dermatitis, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for recalcitrant eczematous dermatitis that is labeled 'atopic dermatitis' but remains localized, treatment-resistant, or distribution-atypical.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform patch testing to evaluate for allergic contact dermatitis.
items.teachingPoint: Localized, chronic, treatment-resistant eczematous dermatitis, particularly in atypical distributions (e.g., extensor surfaces in an adult without a clear history of AD), should prompt consideration of allergic contact dermatitis. Patch testing is the definitive diagnostic tool for ACD and should be performed before escalating to systemic therapies or assuming a diagnosis of recalcitrant atopic dermatitis.

While AD can present atypically, the lack of response to potent topical steroids and the specific location raise suspicion for an alternative diagnosis, particularly allergic contact dermatitis (ACD). Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing ACD and is indicated when ACD is suspected, especially in cases of chronic, localized, or treatment-resistant dermatitis.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of a widespread, mildly pruritic rash. It began with a single, larger oval plaque on her trunk, followed days later by numerous smaller, similar oval plaques oriented along skin lines in a 'Christmas tree' pattern on her back and abdomen. The lesions are salmon-colored with fine scale at the periphery, particularly noticeable on the upper chest and back. She reports mild fatigue but denies fever, lymphadenopathy, mucosal lesions, or recent new medications. Physical examination reveals scattered oval erythematous papules and plaques with collarette scaling on the trunk and proximal extremities. Vital signs are normal.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish pityriasis rosea from secondary syphilis and morbilliform drug eruption in a generalized papulosquamous eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Pityriasis rosea is characterized by a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption of oval, salmon-colored papules and plaques with collarette scaling, often arranged in a 'Christmas tree' pattern on the trunk. Distinguishing it from secondary syphilis (which may involve palms/soles and systemic symptoms) and drug eruptions (often more generalized and pruritic, related to medication exposure) is crucial.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for pityriasis rosea. Key features include the prodromal 'herald patch' (the initial larger plaque), followed by a generalized eruption of smaller oval, salmon-colored plaques with fine scale oriented along cleavage lines ('Christmas tree' pattern). The mild pruritus and self-limited course are also typical.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Secondary syphilis can present with a papulosquamous rash, but it often involves palms and soles, may be associated with fever, lymphadenopathy, and mucosal lesions (condyloma lata), and typically lacks the distinct herald patch and Christmas tree distribution.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: A morbilliform drug eruption is usually more generalized, intensely pruritic, and often associated with a history of recent medication initiation. While it can be papular or maculopapular, the characteristic herald patch and Christmas tree pattern are absent.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Guttate psoriasis typically presents as small, drop-like, erythematous papules with silvery scale, often triggered by a preceding streptococcal infection. It lacks the oval shape, collarette scaling, and Christmas tree distribution of pityriasis rosea.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis presents as annular lesions with central clearing and raised, erythematous, scaly borders. While it can be widespread, it does not typically present with the morphology or distribution described (oval plaques along skin lines).

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Secondary syphilis can present with a papulosquamous rash, but it often involves palms and soles, may be associated with fever, lymphadenopathy, and mucosal lesions (condyloma lata), and typically lacks the distinct herald patch and Christmas tree distribution.

The lesions are pink to salmon-colored with fine scale at the periphery, creating a 'collarette'. She reports mild fatigue and headache but denies fever, lymphadenopathy, or mucosal lesions. She started taking amoxicillin for a sinus infection 5 days prior to rash onset. A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test is negative.

Distinguishing it from secondary syphilis (often involves palms/soles, mucous membranes, systemic symptoms, positive serology) and drug eruptions (usually more uniform maculopapular rash without specific distribution or collarette scale) is crucial.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for pityriasis rosea. Key features include the prodromal herald patch, followed by a generalized eruption of oval, salmon-colored papules and plaques with peripheral scale ('collarette') arranged in a 'Christmas tree' distribution on the trunk. Mild systemic symptoms like fatigue are common. The negative RPR makes syphilis less likely.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: While secondary syphilis can present with a generalized papulosquamous eruption, it typically involves palms and soles (not mentioned here), often presents with more significant systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy), and may involve mucous membranes. The negative RPR further decreases the likelihood.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: A morbilliform drug eruption is characterized by widespread, erythematous macules and papules, often starting on the trunk and spreading centrifugally. While the timing relative to amoxicillin is suggestive, the specific morphology (oval lesions with collarette scale) and distribution ('Christmas tree' pattern) are not typical for a morbilliform reaction.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Guttate psoriasis typically presents with small, drop-like, erythematous papules with silvery scale, often triggered by streptococcal infection. The morphology described (oval lesions with collarette scale) and the 'Christmas tree' distribution are not characteristic of guttate psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis typically presents as annular lesions with central clearing and raised, scaling borders. A generalized eruption is uncommon unless it is a widespread tinea incognito or rare disseminated fungal infection; the morphology described (oval lesions in a Christmas tree pattern) is inconsistent with typical tinea corporis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: The description of oval lesions with a collarette of scale arranged in a 'Christmas tree' pattern on the trunk is highly characteristic of pityriasis rosea. While other conditions can cause generalized papulosquamous eruptions, this specific constellation of findings strongly points towards pityriasis rosea.

He also reports involvement in his axillae and groin (inverse psoriasis) and around his nose (facial psoriasis). He has been using mid-potency topical corticosteroids intermittently for the past year, but his dermatologist is concerned about potential skin atrophy, particularly on his face and in the intertriginous areas, due to prolonged use. The patient desires a long-term maintenance therapy to minimize future corticosteroid exposure. items.explanationCorrect: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs) like tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are effective for psoriasis, particularly in sensitive areas like the face and intertriginous zones (axillae, groin), where long-term corticosteroid use carries a high risk of atrophy. They do not cause skin atrophy and are considered first-line steroid-sparing agents for these locations.

distractorExplanations.text: Topical 5-fluorouracil is primarily used for actinic keratoses and superficial basal cell carcinomas, not typically for psoriasis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of worsening plaque psoriasis affecting his scalp, trunk, and lower extremities, estimated to cover 15% of his body surface area. He has failed topical therapies including high-potency corticosteroids and calcipotriene. His medical history is significant for Crohn's disease, currently well-controlled on maintenance azathioprine. He denies active joint pain or symptoms suggestive of psoriatic arthritis. Given the extent and severity of his psoriasis and his underlying Crohn's disease, which systemic therapy is the most appropriate next step?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the best systemic option for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in a patient with concomitant inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: When selecting systemic therapy for psoriasis in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), agents that are effective for both conditions or do not exacerbate the IBD should be prioritized. TNF-alpha inhibitors like adalimumab and infliximab are often preferred as they treat both psoriasis and IBD. Etanercept is contraindicated in Crohn's disease. Acitretin, methotrexate, and cyclosporine may worsen IBD.
items.explanationCorrect: Adalimumab is a TNF-alpha inhibitor approved for both moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and Crohn's disease. Its use can potentially treat both conditions simultaneously, making it an ideal choice in this patient with concomitant active inflammatory bowel disease. Studies have shown efficacy in treating psoriasis in patients with IBD.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of worsening well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale affecting his scalp, elbows, and knees. His body surface area (BSA) involvement is estimated at 15%. He reports significant pruritus and impact on his quality of life. He has a known history of Crohn's disease, currently managed with ustekinumab, which has been effective for his gastrointestinal symptoms. Topical therapies have provided minimal relief. Given his moderate-to-severe psoriasis and existing IBD management, what is the most appropriate next step in managing his skin condition?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate systemic therapy?
items.learningObjective: Select the best systemic option for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in a patient with concomitant inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: Systemic treatment of moderate-to-severe psoriasis requires careful consideration of comorbidities. While TNF-alpha inhibitors are generally avoided in Crohn's disease, IL-23 inhibitors (like guselkumab) and IL-17 inhibitors (like secukinumab) are considered safer options, although IL-17 inhibitors have been associated with IBD flares. Methotrexate and acitretin can exacerbate IBD. The choice of biologic should be made in consultation with the managing gastroenterologist.
items.explanationCorrect: Guselkumab is an IL-23 inhibitor, a class of biologics effective for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. IL-23 inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in psoriasis and generally do not exacerbate inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), unlike TNF-alpha inhibitors which can worsen Crohn's disease. Given the patient is already on ustekinumab (an IL-12/23 inhibitor) for Crohn's, adding another biologic targeting a different pathway within the IL-23 axis is a reasonable strategy.

items.stem: A 62-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic, coin-shaped lesions on his lower extremities that began during the winter months. He reports significant dry skin and notes the lesions are often weeping or crusted. He denies any history of athlete's foot or systemic symptoms. Examination reveals multiple well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with adherent scale, ranging from 1 to 5 cm in diameter, primarily on the shins and distal thighs. There is no significant edema or hyperpigmentation. KOH preparation from scrapings of one lesion is negative for fungal elements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

items.teachingPoint: Nummular eczema is characterized by intensely pruritic, well-demarcated, coin-shaped (nummular) eczematous plaques, often exacerbated by dry skin conditions like winter xerosis. Distinguishing it from tinea corporis requires a negative KOH preparation, while differentiating it from stasis dermatitis involves assessing for signs of venous insufficiency, and distinguishing it from psoriasis relies on recognizing the characteristic silvery scale and typical distribution.

items.stem: A 58-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic, violaceous papules and plaques on his shins that have been progressively worsening over 6 months. items.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressively worsening generalized erythema and scaling. He initially noticed follicular papules on his scalp and chest, which have coalesced into diffuse orange-red plaques with distinct islands of sparing. The palms and soles exhibit marked hyperkeratosis with a yellowish hue, and he reports significant pruritus. He has a history of hypertension but no other medical conditions or relevant medication use. Biopsy of a lesional plaque shows alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, acanthosis, and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, but is non-specific. Given the clinical presentation, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish pityriasis rubra pilaris from erythrodermic psoriasis and chronic eczematous dermatitis in a difficult papulosquamous case.
items.teachingPoint: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is characterized by a distinctive combination of follicular papules, orange-red plaques with islands of sparing, and palmoplantar keratoderma. Recognizing these features is crucial for differentiating it from other causes of erythroderma like psoriasis and chronic eczema.
items.explanationCorrect: The constellation of follicular papules, coalescing orange-red plaques with islands of sparing, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis (often yellowish), and a chronic course is highly characteristic of Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris (PRP). While the biopsy findings are non-specific, they do not exclude PRP.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erythrodermic psoriasis typically presents with diffuse erythema and fine scale, often preceded by plaque psoriasis. While palmoplantar involvement can occur, islands of sparing and prominent follicular papules are less common than in PRP.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Chronic eczematous dermatitis (e.g., atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis) usually presents with more lichenified plaques, intense pruritus, and often involves flexural areas. While erythroderma can occur, the specific features like islands of sparing and prominent follicular papules are not typical.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Sebopsoriasis is a combination of seborrheic dermatitis and psoriasis, typically affecting the scalp, face, and trunk with greasy scales and well-demarcated erythematous plaques. It does not typically cause generalized erythroderma with islands of sparing or significant palmoplantar hyperkeratosis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Atopic dermatitis, especially in adults, can present as chronic eczematous dermatitis. While it can become erythrodermic, the characteristic features of PRP (follicular papules, islands of sparing, specific palmoplantar changes) are usually absent.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Atopic dermatitis, especially in adults, can present as chronic eczematous dermatitis. While it can become erythrodermic, the characteristic features of PRP (follicular papules, islands of sparing, specific palmoplantar changes) are usually absent.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressively worsening generalized redness and scaling. He reports mild pruritus, primarily on his trunk and extremities. Physical examination reveals widespread, salmon-colored erythema with fine, yellowish scales covering approximately 90% of his body surface area. Notably, there are distinct islands of sparing – small, well-demarcated areas of unaffected skin – scattered across his abdomen, back, and thighs. Palmoplantar thickening is present, but nail changes are absent. Biopsy of a lesional area shows hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, alternating orthokeratosis, and acanthosis with Munro's microabscesses.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish pityriasis rubra pilaris from erythrodermic psoriasis and chronic eczematous dermatitis in a difficult papulosquamous case.
items.teachingPoint: Islands of sparing are a key clinical feature that helps differentiate Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris from other causes of erythroderma, particularly erythrodermic psoriasis and chronic eczematous dermatitis. While biopsy findings can overlap, the clinical picture, especially the presence of islands of sparing and palmoplantar thickening without significant nail changes, strongly points towards PRP.
items.explanationCorrect: The presence of 'islands of sparing' (unaffected skin within the generalized erythema) is a classic, though not pathognomonic, feature highly suggestive of PRP. The description of salmon-colored erythema with fine, yellowish scales, palmoplantar thickening, and the absence of significant nail changes also fits well with PRP. While the biopsy findings (Munro's microabscesses) can be seen in psoriasis, they are not specific and can occur in PRP.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erythrodermic psoriasis typically presents with widespread, fiery red erythema and thick, silvery scales, often associated with significant nail changes (pitting, onycholysis). Islands of sparing are uncommon.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Chronic eczematous dermatitis usually involves intense pruritus, lichenification in flexural areas, and often a personal or family history of atopy. While it can cause erythroderma, islands of sparing are not characteristic.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Sebopsoriasis is a combination of seborrheic dermatitis and psoriasis, typically affecting the scalp, face, chest, and intertriginous areas. It does not usually cause generalized erythroderma with islands of sparing.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Drug-induced erythroderma is a diagnosis of exclusion, often presenting acutely after medication initiation, and lacks the characteristic features like islands of sparing or specific palmoplantar thickening seen in PRP.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While drug-induced erythroderma is a possibility in any case of generalized redness, the presence of islands of sparing makes PRP a more likely diagnosis based on the clinical presentation described.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of itchy, erythematous, and scaling skin on her eyelids. She has been treated intermittently with topical triamcinolone 0.1% ointment for flares, which provides temporary relief but is associated with significant anxiety about potential long-term side effects like skin atrophy and glaucoma. Her condition is currently quiescent but she desires a maintenance therapy to prevent recurrence without relying solely on corticosteroids. She has no history of atopy or other autoimmune diseases. What is the most appropriate maintenance therapy?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate maintenance therapy?
items.learningObjective: Select the best maintenance therapy for chronic eyelid dermatitis when repeated topical corticosteroid exposure is undesirable.
items.correctAnswerText: Topical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or pimecrolimus) applied twice weekly
items.teachingPoint: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus and pimecrolimus) are effective steroid-sparing agents for chronic inflammatory eyelid dermatitis. For maintenance therapy in quiescent disease, intermittent application (e.g., twice weekly) is often preferred over daily use to minimize potential side effects while preventing flares.
items.explanationCorrect: Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs) approved for atopic dermatitis and are effective alternatives to topical corticosteroids for managing chronic inflammatory conditions like eyelid dermatitis. They do not carry the same risks of skin atrophy or ocular side effects as corticosteroids. For maintenance therapy in quiescent disease, applying a TCI twice weekly is a standard approach to prevent flares while minimizing potential side effects like burning or stinging, which can occur with daily use.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 10-year history of stable plaque psoriasis presents for follow-up. His disease, previously managed intermittently with topical corticosteroids, has worsened significantly over the past year, now covering approximately 25% of his body surface area and causing significant pruritus and impacting his quality of life. He has failed a trial of phototherapy. He is considering systemic therapy. His physician explains the different biologic options available, highlighting that understanding the underlying pathophysiology helps tailor treatment. Which specific inflammatory pathway, when targeted by a biologic agent, offers the most robust and consistently demonstrated efficacy specifically for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis compared to other pathways?
items.leadIn: Which pathway is the most critical target for biologic therapy in this patient's condition?
items.learningObjective: Identify the psoriasis pathogenic pathway or biologic target most tightly linked to modern plaque-psoriasis therapy selection.
items.teachingPoint: Modern psoriasis treatment prioritizes targeting key pathogenic cytokines. While TNF-α, IL-17, and JAK pathways are involved, targeting the upstream cytokine IL-23 has shown superior efficacy and often a better safety profile than TNF-α inhibitors for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, making it a primary target for biologic therapy selection.
items.explanationCorrect: Targeting the IL-23 pathway (specifically IL-23p19) has emerged as a highly effective strategy for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. IL-23 is crucial for the differentiation, survival, and function of Th17 cells, which produce IL-17 and other pro-inflammatory cytokines central to psoriasis pathogenesis. Biologics targeting IL-23 (e.g., ustekinumab, guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab) consistently demonstrate high rates of skin clearance and are often considered first-line biologic options due to their efficacy and generally favorable safety profile compared to broader TNF-α inhibitors.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: While IL-17 is a key effector cytokine in psoriasis, and targeting it (e.g., secukinumab, ixekizumab) is effective, the upstream regulator IL-23 is now considered a more fundamental target for sustained response in many patients.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: TNF-α inhibitors (e.g., etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab) are effective for psoriasis, but their efficacy is generally considered slightly less robust than IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors, and they carry a higher risk of serious infections.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: IL-13 is primarily involved in type 2 inflammation, characteristic of atopic dermatitis and asthma, not plaque psoriasis. Targeting IL-13 (e.g., dupilumab) is effective for these conditions but not psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: JAK inhibitors (e.g., tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are effective for psoriasis by inhibiting multiple cytokine signaling pathways downstream of their receptors. While efficacious, they have a broader mechanism and different safety considerations (e.g., VTE, malignancy risk) compared to pathway-specific biologics like IL-23 inhibitors.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a 10-year history of moderate plaque psoriasis, currently managed with topical corticosteroids and calcipotriene, presents with worsening disease affecting his scalp, trunk, and lower extremities. He has failed previous trials of phototherapy and methotrexate due to side effects. His PASI score is 18. He desires a systemic therapy with a favorable long-term safety profile. Considering the pathogenesis of psoriasis and the mechanisms of action of modern biologic therapies, which pathway represents the most critical target for achieving sustained clinical response in this patient?
items.leadIn: Which of the following pathways is the most critical target?
items.learningObjective: Identify the psoriasis pathogenic pathway or biologic target most tightly linked to modern plaque-psoriasis therapy selection.
items.teachingPoint: Modern biologic therapies for psoriasis target specific cytokines involved in its pathogenesis. The IL-23/Th17 axis is central to plaque psoriasis, and targeting IL-23 represents a highly effective and relatively specific strategy for achieving sustained clinical improvement with a favorable safety profile.
items.explanationCorrect: IL-23 is a key cytokine in the pathogenesis of psoriasis, primarily driving the differentiation and maintenance of Th17 cells, which produce IL-17A. Targeting IL-23 (or its receptor) is highly effective in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and is associated with durable responses and a favorable safety profile compared to some older systemic therapies. Given the patient's history and desire for long-term efficacy and safety, targeting this upstream pathway is a primary consideration.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: IL-17A is a crucial downstream effector cytokine in psoriasis, and anti-IL-17A biologics are effective. However, IL-23 is considered more upstream in the Th17 pathway, driving the production of IL-17A, making it a potentially more fundamental target for sustained response.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: TNF-α plays a role in psoriasis inflammation, and anti-TNF-α agents are used, but they are generally less specific to the core psoriatic pathway compared to IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors and may have broader immunosuppressive effects.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Anti-IL-12/23 biologics (e.g., ustekinumab) target both cytokines. While effective, they are less specific than pure IL-23 inhibitors and may have slightly lower efficacy in some studies for psoriasis compared to IL-23 targeted agents.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: The JAK/STAT pathway is involved in signaling for various cytokines implicated in psoriasis, and JAK inhibitors are effective treatments. However, they are not specific to the IL-23/Th17 axis and have a broader mechanism of action with potential side effects distinct from targeted cytokine inhibition.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: JAK/STAT pathway is involved in signaling for various cytokines implicated in psoriasis, and JAK inhibitors are effective treatments. However, they are not specific to the IL-23/Th17 axis and have a broader mechanism of action with potential side effects distinct from targeted cytokine inhibition.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intensely pruritic, tense bullae arising on erythematous and urticarial plaques, primarily affecting her flexural areas, abdomen, and thighs. Mucosal involvement is absent. She has no significant past medical history other than hypertension managed with lisinopril. A skin biopsy reveals subepidermal separation with an inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. Based on this clinical presentation and biopsy findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris in a subepidermal-versus-intraepidermal blistering presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense subepidermal blisters, intense pruritus, typically affects older adults, spares mucous membranes, and shows linear IgG/C3 deposition at the basement membrane zone on DIF. Pemphigus vulgaris, in contrast, features flaccid intraepidermal blisters (due to acantholysis), often involves mucosa, and shows intercellular IgG/C3 deposition.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's age, clinical presentation (tense bullae on erythematous/urticarial plaques, flexural distribution, intense pruritus, absence of mucosal involvement), and biopsy findings (subepidermal blister with eosinophils, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ) are classic for bullous pemphigoid. This autoimmune disease targets hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230) in the basement membrane zone, leading to subepidermal blistering.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Pemphigus vulgaris typically presents with flaccid bullae and erosions, often involving mucous membranes. Histology shows intraepidermal acantholysis (suprabasal split), and DIF shows intercellular IgG/C3 deposition within the epidermis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by intensely pruritic papules and vesicles, often symmetrically distributed on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). items.stem: A 78-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intensely pruritic, tense bullae primarily on her flexural surfaces and abdomen. She has no mucosal involvement. A skin biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings would be most consistent with the likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: The biopsy shows:
items.learningObjective: Distinguish bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris in a subepidermal-versus-intraepidermal blistering presentation.
items.correctAnswerText: Subepidermal separation with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate and eosinophils.
items.teachingPoint: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common autoimmune blistering disease, typically affecting the elderly. It is characterized by tense bullae, often on flexural surfaces, intense pruritus, and absence of mucosal involvement. Histopathology shows subepidermal separation with eosinophils and neutrophils. Pemphigus vulgaris, in contrast, presents with flaccid bullae, frequent mucosal involvement, and intraepidermal acantholysis.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of tense bullae, primarily on flexural surfaces and the abdomen, in an elderly patient without mucosal involvement is highly suggestive of bullous pemphigoid (BP). BP is characterized by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230), leading to subepidermal blister formation. Histopathology typically reveals a subepidermal split with an inflammatory infiltrate rich in neutrophils and eosinophils.

options.label: B
options.text: Subepidermal separation with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate and eosinophils.

options.label: C
options.text: Subepidermal separation with fibrin deposition and leukocytoclasis.

options.label: D
options.text: Spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles and dermal edema.

options.label: E
options.text: A dense perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with interface dermatitis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Intraepidermal acantholysis ('tombstoning') is the characteristic histological finding of pemphigus vulgaris, which typically presents with flaccid bullae and mucosal involvement. This patient's presentation is not typical for pemphigus vulgaris.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This describes the classic histology of bullous pemphigoid, consistent with the clinical vignette.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Subepidermal separation with fibrin deposition and leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust) is characteristic of vasculitis, such as leukocytoclastic vasculitis. While vasculitis can cause bullae, the clinical picture (tense bullae, flexural distribution, intense pruritus without palpable purpura) is less typical.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Spongiosis (intercellular edema) with intraepidermal vesicles and dermal edema is characteristic of eczematous dermatitis (e.g., contact dermatitis, dyshidrotic eczema), which typically presents with smaller vesicles or papules and often has a different distribution.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: A dense perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with interface dermatitis is seen in lichen planus or lupus erythematosus, which can present with bullae (bullous lichen planus, bullous lupus) but usually have other characteristic features not described here.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of painful oral erosions, difficulty swallowing, and a new rash consisting of flaccid blisters on her trunk and extremities. She reports significant weight loss due to poor oral intake. Examination reveals extensive, crusted erosions involving the buccal mucosa, tongue, and gingiva, along with several flaccid bullae and erosions on her chest and back. Her vital signs show tachycardia (110 bpm) and mild hypotension (95/60 mmHg). Laboratory tests confirm a diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris (positive anti-desmoglein 1 and 3 antibodies). Given her severe mucosal involvement, dehydration risk, and potential for systemic complications, what is the most appropriate initial management step?
items.leadIn: What is the most appropriate initial management step?
items.learningObjective: Identify the safest immediate management approach for new pemphigus vulgaris with severe mucosal disease and dehydration risk.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate intravenous fluids and systemic corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: In severe pemphigus vulgaris with significant mucosal disease leading to dehydration or hemodynamic instability, the immediate management priorities are fluid resuscitation and initiation of high-dose systemic corticosteroids. Other therapies like IVIG or rituximab are typically reserved for later stages or specific circumstances.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with severe pemphigus vulgaris, characterized by extensive mucosal involvement, painful erosions impairing oral intake, and signs of dehydration (tachycardia, hypotension). The immediate priority is to stabilize the patient by addressing the dehydration with intravenous fluids and initiating potent immunosuppression with systemic corticosteroids to control the blistering process and prevent further mucosal damage. This combined approach addresses both the acute physiological instability and the underlying autoimmune disease.

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate high-dose topical corticosteroids to the affected skin and oral mucosa.

options.label: B
options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone taper.

options.label: C
options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) as first-line therapy.

options.label: E
options.text: Initiate intravenous fluids and systemic corticosteroids.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Topical corticosteroids alone are insufficient for severe, widespread pemphigus vulgaris, especially with significant mucosal involvement and systemic symptoms. They may be used adjunctively but are not the primary or most appropriate initial step.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While systemic corticosteroids are necessary, initiating them without first addressing the patient's dehydration and hemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension) is inappropriate. Fluid resuscitation is a critical first step.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: IVIG is a potential treatment for pemphigus vulgaris, particularly in refractory cases or when corticosteroids are contraindicated, but it is not typically the first-line *initial* therapy, especially when rapid control and stabilization are needed. Systemic corticosteroids are the standard initial approach.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Rituximab is an effective long-term therapy for pemphigus vulgaris, often used as a steroid-sparing agent or for refractory disease. However, it takes weeks to months to exert its full effect and is not suitable for immediate management of acute, severe disease with dehydration.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: This option addresses the most critical immediate needs: fluid resuscitation for dehydration and hemodynamic instability, coupled with systemic corticosteroids to rapidly control the autoimmune blistering process. This is the standard initial approach for severe pemphigus vulgaris.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of painful oral erosions, difficulty swallowing, and subsequent weight loss. She reports developing tender skin lesions on her trunk and proximal extremities over the past week. Examination reveals multiple flaccid bullae and erosions on the upper trunk and scalp, along with extensive, painful ulcerations involving the buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate. Her vital signs show tachycardia (110 bpm) and mild orthostasis. She is refusing oral intake due to pain. Given her severe mucosal involvement and risk of dehydration, what is the most appropriate initial management step?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the safest immediate management approach for new pemphigus vulgaris with severe mucosal disease and dehydration risk.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) and topical anesthetics for mucosal lesions.
items.teachingPoint: Severe pemphigus vulgaris, particularly with significant mucosal involvement impacting nutrition and hydration, requires immediate initiation of high-dose systemic corticosteroids. Delaying treatment for diagnostic procedures or supportive care alone can lead to rapid deterioration.
items.explanationCorrect: Pemphigus vulgaris with severe mucosal disease requires prompt initiation of systemic immunosuppression to control blistering and prevent further complications like infection and dehydration. High-dose systemic corticosteroids are the first-line treatment to rapidly reduce autoantibody production and inflammation. Topical anesthetics (e.g., viscous lidocaine) can provide symptomatic relief for painful oral erosions, facilitating oral intake. While IV fluids may be needed, delaying immunosuppression is not appropriate given the active disease.

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) and topical anesthetics for mucosal lesions.

options.label: B
options.text: Begin intravenous pulse methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone taper.

options.label: C
options.text: Administer intravenous fluids and parenteral nutrition, deferring immunosuppression until hydration is optimized.

options.label: D
options.text: Start rituximab infusion immediately to provide long-term immunosuppression.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform a skin biopsy for definitive diagnosis before initiating any treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: While IV fluids are important, delaying immunosuppression in severe, active pemphigus vulgaris is inappropriate and risks worsening disease, infection, and dehydration. Steroids should be started promptly.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: IV pulse methylprednisolone is typically reserved for severe cutaneous involvement or refractory cases, not usually the first-line approach for initial management of mucosal-predominant disease, although high-dose oral steroids are standard. Oral prednisone is generally sufficient initially.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Rituximab is an effective treatment but is typically added as a steroid-sparing agent or for refractory disease, not usually as the immediate first step in newly diagnosed, severe pemphigus vulgaris. Steroids provide more rapid control.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: While a biopsy confirms the diagnosis, initiating treatment promptly is crucial in severe pemphigus vulgaris, especially with significant mucosal involvement and dehydration risk. Treatment should not be delayed pending biopsy results when the clinical suspicion is high.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: High-dose systemic corticosteroids are the standard first-line therapy for controlling active pemphigus vulgaris. Topical anesthetics address the painful mucosal erosions that impede oral intake. This combination provides both systemic control and symptomatic relief, which is crucial in this scenario.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic papules and vesicles symmetrically distributed on her extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). She reports a long history of similar episodes, often exacerbated by gluten ingestion. A skin biopsy is performed for direct immunofluorescence (DIF). Which finding would be most specific for confirming the diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis?
items.leadIn: The question asks for the most specific DIF finding in dermatitis herpetiformis.
items.learningObjective: Recognize the key immunopathologic finding that distinguishes dermatitis herpetiformis from other immunobullous disorders.
items.correctAnswerText: Granular deposition of IgA in the dermal papillae
items.teachingPoint: The hallmark immunopathologic finding distinguishing dermatitis herpetiformis from other autoimmune blistering diseases is the granular deposition of IgA specifically within the dermal papillae on direct immunofluorescence.
items.explanationCorrect: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is characterized by intensely pruritic vesicles and papules, often on extensor surfaces, and is strongly associated with celiac disease. The pathognomonic finding on direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of perilesional skin is granular deposition of IgA within the dermal papillae. This pattern distinguishes DH from other immunobullous diseases.

options.label: A
options.text: Linear deposition of IgG along the basement membrane zone

options.label: B
options.text: Granular deposition of IgA in the dermal papillae

options.label: C
options.text: Circumlinear deposition of C3 along the basement membrane zone

options.label: D
options.text: Focal deposition of fibrinogen in the upper dermis

options.label: E
options.text: Linear deposition of IgM along the dermoepidermal junction

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Linear IgG deposition at the basement membrane zone (BMZ) is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer, as granular IgA deposition in the dermal papillae is pathognomonic for dermatitis herpetiformis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Circumlinear C3 deposition along the BMZ is characteristic of linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD), although IgA deposition itself can be linear or granular in LABD, unlike the specific papillary pattern in DH.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Focal fibrinogen deposition in the upper dermis is seen in neutrophilic dermatoses like Sweet syndrome or erythema nodosum, not typically in immunobullous diseases like DH.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Linear IgM deposition at the dermoepidermal junction can be seen in various conditions, including some forms of lupus erythematosus or certain types of bullous pemphigoid, but it is not specific for DH.

items.teachingPoint: Localized bullous pemphigoid can often be effectively managed with topical therapy, avoiding the systemic side effects of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants, particularly in patients with significant comorbidities that increase the risk associated with systemic treatments.
items.explanationCorrect: For localized bullous pemphigoid, especially in patients with contraindications to systemic therapy, high-potency topical corticosteroids are the first-line treatment. They effectively reduce inflammation and promote healing of blisters and urticarial plaques with minimal systemic absorption, mitigating risks associated with comorbidities like diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

distractorExplanations.text: Systemic methotrexate is a potent immunosuppressant reserved for severe or refractory bullous pemphigoid, particularly when other systemic agents are contraindicated or ineffective. distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intensely pruritic urticarial plaques and tense bullae limited to her lower extremities. A skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blistering with eosinophils, and direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone. She has a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and recent myocardial infarction requiring triple therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol). Given her comorbidities and the localized nature of her disease, which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.learningObjective: Choose an evidence-aligned treatment for localized bullous pemphigoid in an older adult at high risk from systemic corticosteroids.
items.correctAnswerText: High-potency topical corticosteroids combined with potent topical antibiotics
items.teachingPoint: Localized bullous pemphigoid can often be effectively managed with high-potency topical corticosteroids, sometimes combined with topical antibiotics, avoiding the systemic risks associated with oral corticosteroids, especially in elderly patients with multiple comorbidities.
items.explanationCorrect: For localized bullous pemphigoid (BP), especially in patients with significant comorbidities precluding systemic therapy, high-potency topical corticosteroids are the first-line treatment. The addition of a potent topical antibiotic (like erythromycin or tetracycline) can enhance efficacy by inhibiting neutrophil chemotaxis and inflammatory mediators. This approach minimizes systemic side effects.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of an annular, erythematous rash on her upper chest and back, which she notes is photosensitive. A skin biopsy reveals interface dermatitis consistent with cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE). She denies systemic symptoms such as fever, joint pain, fatigue, or oral ulcers. Her physical examination is otherwise unremarkable, including no signs of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) like malar rash, discoid lesions elsewhere, or arthritis. Given the new diagnosis of CLE without overt systemic features, what is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best evaluation step when cutaneous lupus erythematosus is newly diagnosed and systemic disease has not yet been assessed.
items.teachingPoint: Patients with cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) should be evaluated for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), even in the absence of overt systemic symptoms, as CLE can be the initial manifestation of SLE. The antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is the most sensitive initial screening test for SLE.
items.explanationCorrect: The ANA is the most sensitive screening test for SLE and other connective tissue diseases. While this patient currently lacks overt systemic symptoms, CLE can be the presenting manifestation of SLE in approximately 10-20% of cases. Therefore, screening for systemic autoimmune disease is warranted. The ANA is the best initial screening test due to its high sensitivity.

options.label: B
options.text: Order a complete blood count (CBC) with differential and comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP).

options.label: C
options.text: Refer her to a rheumatologist for evaluation of potential SLE.

options.label: D
options.text: Order specific autoantibodies including anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform a urinalysis to screen for renal involvement.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: While a CBC and CMP are part of a general workup, they are not the most specific or sensitive initial tests for evaluating potential underlying SLE in a patient with newly diagnosed CLE. They may be abnormal in SLE but are not diagnostic or highly sensitive screening tools.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Referral to rheumatology is appropriate if the ANA is positive or if systemic symptoms develop, but it is premature as the first step before basic screening tests are performed. Initial evaluation can often be initiated by the dermatologist.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies are highly specific for SLE but have lower sensitivity than ANA. Ordering these specific antibodies before performing the more sensitive ANA screen is not the standard approach. They are typically ordered if the ANA is positive.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Urinalysis is important for assessing renal involvement, a potential complication of SLE. However, it is not the best initial screening test for SLE itself. It should be performed if there is clinical suspicion of renal disease or if the ANA is positive and further workup is indicated.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While CBC/CMP are part of a general workup, they lack sensitivity and specificity for detecting underlying SLE compared to an ANA. They are not the most appropriate *next* step specifically targeting the evaluation for systemic autoimmune disease in this context.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of annular, erythematous plaques with central clearing on her upper chest and back, consistent with subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE). She has no systemic symptoms, and her physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. A skin biopsy confirms the diagnosis of SCLE. Given the potential association between cutaneous lupus and systemic disease, what is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best evaluation step when cutaneous lupus erythematosus is newly diagnosed and systemic disease has not yet been assessed.
items.teachingPoint: Patients with cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE), particularly SCLE, should be evaluated for underlying systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or other connective tissue diseases. The antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is the most sensitive initial screening test for SLE and should be performed first when systemic disease is suspected or needs to be ruled out.
items.explanationCorrect: ANA testing is the most sensitive initial screening test for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and other connective tissue diseases. While SCLE can occur in isolation, it is frequently associated with SLE or Sjögren's syndrome. A positive ANA is found in >95% of patients with SLE and is therefore the best initial step to assess for underlying systemic autoimmune disease in a patient newly diagnosed with CLE.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: A CBC might show abnormalities (e.g., cytopenias) in SLE, but it is not the most sensitive initial screening test for systemic autoimmune disease. It is often performed as part of a broader workup but is less specific than ANA.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies are frequently positive in SCLE and Sjögren's syndrome, ANA testing is the more sensitive initial screening test for SLE, which encompasses a broader range of potential systemic involvement. Specific antibody testing is usually performed after a positive ANA.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Urinalysis is important for assessing renal involvement (lupus nephritis), a serious complication of SLE. However, it is typically performed as part of the workup *after* initial screening tests like ANA suggest systemic disease, or if the patient has symptoms suggestive of renal disease.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: A chest X-ray might be indicated if pulmonary symptoms are present or to screen for complications like pleural effusion or interstitial lung disease in known SLE, but it is not the primary initial step in evaluating for systemic disease in an asymptomatic patient with newly diagnosed CLE.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While a CBC is often part of the initial workup for suspected SLE, ANA testing is significantly more sensitive for detecting the presence of systemic autoimmune disease, making it the most appropriate *next* step in this specific clinical scenario.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of progressive proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and a photosensitive rash. Examination reveals violaceous papules and plaques along the knuckles (Gottron's papules), erythematous patches over the eyelids (heliotrope rash), and scaling erythematous plaques on her anterior chest in a V-neck distribution (Shawl sign). She also has mild tenderness and swelling of her metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. Laboratory tests show elevated creatine kinase and positive anti-Jo-1 antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus and allergic contact dermatitis using morphology and distribution.
items.teachingPoint: Dermatomyositis is characterized by pathognomonic skin findings (Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash) in addition to proximal muscle weakness. Recognizing these specific cutaneous manifestations and their distribution is key to differentiating it from other conditions like lupus erythematosus or contact dermatitis.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with classic features of dermatomyositis, including proximal muscle weakness, photosensitivity, Gottron's papules (violaceous papules over knuckles), heliotrope rash (erythematous patches over eyelids), and shawl sign (erythematous plaques on chest). Elevated CK and positive anti-Jo-1 antibodies further support this diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus can present with photosensitivity and erythematous plaques, but typically involves the face (malar rash) and often spares the knuckles or eyelids in this characteristic pattern. Gottron's papules and heliotrope rash are not typical features of lupus.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is characterized by pruritic, eczematous lesions in areas of contact with an allergen. While it can be erythematous and scaling, the specific distribution (Gottron's, heliotrope, shawl sign) and associated muscle weakness are not characteristic.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Bullous pemphigoid typically presents with tense bullae on erythematous or urticarial bases, often in flexural areas. While it is an autoimmune condition, the morphology described (papules, plaques) and distribution are inconsistent with bullous pemphigoid.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Vasculitis can cause various skin manifestations, including palpable purpura, ulcers, or livedo reticularis. While some forms can cause erythematous plaques, the specific combination of Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash, shawl sign, and proximal muscle weakness is not typical for vasculitis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Vasculitis can cause various skin manifestations, including palpable purpura, ulcers, or livedo reticularis. While some forms can cause erythematous plaques, the specific combination of Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash, shawl sign, and proximal muscle weakness is not typical for vasculitis.

items.learningObjective: Identify the appropriate malignancy-oriented workup step for newly diagnosed adult dermatomyositis.
items.correctAnswerText: Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening, including CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis
items.teachingPoint: Adult-onset dermatomyositis requires a thorough malignancy workup at diagnosis due to the increased risk of associated cancers. This typically involves age- and sex-appropriate screening plus comprehensive imaging, such as CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
items.explanationCorrect: Dermatomyositis in adults, especially those over 40-50 years old, carries a significantly increased risk of underlying malignancy (ovarian, lung, pancreatic, stomach, colorectal, non-Hodgkin lymphoma). A comprehensive malignancy evaluation is crucial at diagnosis. This includes age- and sex-appropriate screening (e.g., mammography, Pap smear) plus more extensive imaging like CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to screen for common associated cancers.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of progressive proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and a characteristic violaceous rash over her eyelids (heliotrope rash) and knuckles (Gottron's papules). Laboratory tests reveal elevated creatine kinase (CK) and positive anti-Jo-1 antibodies. A diagnosis of dermatomyositis is made. Given the known association between dermatomyositis and malignancy, particularly in older adults, what is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Identify the appropriate malignancy-oriented workup step for newly diagnosed adult dermatomyositis.
items.correctAnswerText: Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening including CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
items.teachingPoint: Adult-onset dermatomyositis requires a thorough malignancy evaluation due to the significant association with underlying cancer. This typically involves age- and sex-appropriate screening plus comprehensive imaging like CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
items.explanationCorrect: Dermatomyositis in adults, especially those over 40-50 years old, carries a significantly increased risk of underlying malignancy (up to 25% in some series). A comprehensive malignancy workup is crucial. This includes age- and sex-appropriate screening (e.g., mammography, colonoscopy) plus imaging such as CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to evaluate for common associated cancers (ovarian, lung, colorectal, pancreatic, etc.).

options.label: B
options.text: Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening including CT chest/abdomen/pelvis

distractorExplanations.label: B
