items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a two-week history of tender, palpable purpuric lesions on his lower extremities. He denies fever, joint pain, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination reveals multiple 3-5 mm violaceous papules and plaques, predominantly on the distal lower legs, consistent with palpable purpura. Laboratory tests show normal renal function and a negative ANA. Given the clinical presentation, which biopsy strategy and expected histopathologic finding are most appropriate for diagnosing the likely underlying condition?
items.leadIn: The patient's presentation is most suggestive of:
items.learningObjective: Correlate palpable purpura with the optimal biopsy strategy and histopathologic pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Deep incisional biopsy including dermis and subcutis; leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis.
items.teachingPoint: Palpable purpura indicates inflammation of small blood vessels in the dermis (vasculitis). Accurate diagnosis requires a deep biopsy (incisional or punch, >4mm) from an established lesion to capture vessel involvement. The hallmark histopathology is leukocytoclastic vasculitis, characterized by neutrophilic infiltrate, fibrinoid necrosis, and extravasation of red blood cells.
items.explanationCorrect: Palpable purpura strongly suggests small vessel vasculitis. The optimal biopsy technique for suspected vasculitis involves a deep incisional or punch biopsy (at least 4mm) that includes the dermis and potentially the subcutis, ideally from an established lesion (24-48 hours old) but not ulcerated. This depth is crucial to capture the involved vessels. The characteristic histopathology of leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV), the most common cause of palpable purpura, involves neutrophilic infiltration around and within small vessel walls (leukocytoclasis), endothelial cell swelling, fibrinoid necrosis, and extravasated red blood cells.

options.label: A
options.text: Shallow shave biopsy; perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

options.label: B
options.text: Deep incisional biopsy including dermis and subcutis; leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Punch biopsy of an early lesion; interface dermatitis with vacuolar alteration.

options.label: D
options.text: Suction blister; subepidermal separation with eosinophils.

options.label: E
options.text: Punch biopsy of a central, established lesion; neutrophilic infiltrate without vessel damage.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Shallow shave biopsies are inadequate for diagnosing vasculitis as they typically only sample the epidermis and superficial dermis, missing deeper vessel involvement. Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate is characteristic of various inflammatory dermatoses but not specific for LCV.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This option correctly identifies the appropriate biopsy depth and the classic histopathologic findings of leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV), which is strongly suggested by palpable purpura.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Punch biopsy is appropriate, but sampling an *early* lesion may miss the characteristic inflammatory changes. Interface dermatitis with vacuolar alteration is typical of lichen planus or lupus erythematosus, not LCV.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Suction blistering is used to diagnose subepidermal blistering diseases like bullous pemphigoid. Subepidermal separation with eosinophils is characteristic of these conditions, not vasculitis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While a punch biopsy of an established lesion is appropriate, the description of a neutrophilic infiltrate *without* vessel damage is inconsistent with LCV. Neutrophilic dermatoses (e.g., Sweet syndrome) can present with papules/plaques but typically lack palpable purpura and the specific vascular changes seen in LCV.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a one-week history of tender, palpable purpuric lesions on his lower extremities. He reports mild joint pain and fatigue but denies fever, weight loss, or recent infections. Physical examination reveals multiple erythematous papules and plaques, some exhibiting central necrosis, predominantly distributed on the distal lower legs. A skin biopsy is performed. Which of the following describes the optimal biopsy technique and expected histopathologic findings for diagnosing leukocytoclastic vasculitis in this patient?
items.leadIn: The patient's presentation is most consistent with:
items.learningObjective: Correlate palpable purpura with the optimal biopsy strategy and histopathologic pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Deep punch biopsy of an early lesion showing neutrophilic infiltrate and fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls.
items.teachingPoint: Diagnosing leukocytoclastic vasculitis requires a deep biopsy (punch or incisional) of an early (<48 hour old) palpable purpuric lesion to capture the characteristic neutrophilic infiltrate, fibrinoid necrosis, and leukocytoclasia within small dermal vessels.
items.explanationCorrect: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) is characterized by inflammation of small blood vessels, typically presenting as palpable purpura. The optimal biopsy technique involves a deep punch or incisional biopsy taken from an early lesion (ideally < 24-48 hours old) to capture the acute inflammatory process within the dermis and potentially involve the vessel wall. Histopathology classically shows neutrophilic infiltrate around and within small vessel walls, endothelial swelling, fibrinoid necrosis, extravasated red blood cells (purpura), and nuclear dust (leukocytoclasia).

options.label: A
options.text: Shallow shave biopsy showing perivascular lymphocytes and eosinophils.

options.label: B
options.text: Deep punch biopsy of an early lesion showing neutrophilic infiltrate and fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls.

options.label: C
options.text: Suction blister biopsy revealing subepidermal separation with neutrophils.

options.label: D
options.text: Incisional biopsy of a mature lesion demonstrating granulomatous inflammation surrounding vessels.

options.label: E
options.text: Full-thickness excisional biopsy of an older lesion showing epidermal atrophy and dermal sclerosis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Shallow shave biopsies are generally inadequate for diagnosing vasculitis as they typically do not include the full thickness of the dermis where the affected vessels reside. While perivascular lymphocytes and eosinophils can be seen in various inflammatory conditions, this description is not specific for LCV.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This option correctly identifies the optimal biopsy technique (deep punch) and timing (early lesion) for LCV. It also accurately describes the characteristic histopathologic features: neutrophilic infiltrate and fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Suction blister biopsy is used to diagnose subepidermal blistering diseases like bullous pemphigoid or dermatitis herpetiformis, not vasculitis. While neutrophils may be present in the blister fluid or dermis, the primary pathology is epidermal-dermal separation.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Granulomatous inflammation surrounding vessels is characteristic of granulomatous vasculitides (e.g., GPA, EGPA), not typical LCV. Biopsying a mature lesion may show resolving inflammation or scarring, potentially missing the diagnostic features.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Full-thickness excisional biopsy is often used for suspected cutaneous malignancies or extensive inflammatory processes but is usually unnecessary for LCV. Biopsying an older lesion is less likely to yield diagnostic findings as the acute inflammation may have resolved, leaving behind non-specific changes like epidermal atrophy or dermal sclerosis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer on her left lower leg that began as a pustule. She has a history of Crohn's disease diagnosed 10 years ago, currently managed with azathioprine. Examination reveals a violaceous border surrounding the ulcer, and minor trauma to her arm resulted in a similar papule developing at the site (pathergy). Biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis. Her Crohn's disease is currently quiescent based on recent colonoscopy. Given the presence of pathergy and underlying IBD, which systemic therapy is the most appropriate initial choice for her pyoderma gangrenosum?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial systemic therapy?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate initial systemic therapy for pyoderma gangrenosum with pathergy and associated inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: In patients with pyoderma gangrenosum associated with inflammatory bowel disease, TNF-alpha inhibitors like infliximab are the preferred first-line systemic therapy as they effectively treat both conditions simultaneously and offer a better long-term profile than chronic corticosteroids.
items.explanationCorrect: Infliximab, a TNF-alpha inhibitor, is the preferred first-line systemic therapy for pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). It effectively treats both the PG and the underlying IBD, particularly when the IBD is active or requires treatment itself. The presence of pathergy further supports the diagnosis of PG.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cyclosporine is a potent immunosuppressant sometimes used for severe PG refractory to other treatments, but it carries significant toxicity (nephrotoxicity, hypertension) and is generally not first-line, especially when a TNF-alpha inhibitor can address the underlying IBD.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Dapsone is effective for some neutrophilic dermatoses like dermatitis herpetiformis and linear IgA bullous dermatosis, but its efficacy in PG, particularly severe or IBD-associated PG, is limited compared to other options.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Methotrexate is used for PG, but it is generally considered second-line after TNF-alpha inhibitors or corticosteroids, especially in the context of IBD. It may also be used for Crohn's disease, but infliximab offers more targeted and often faster control of both conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic corticosteroids are highly effective for rapidly controlling PG inflammation, but long-term use is associated with significant side effects. While often used initially for rapid symptom control or in severe cases, they are typically tapered quickly if possible, and TNF-alpha inhibitors are preferred for sustained management, especially in IBD-associated PG.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic corticosteroids are highly effective for rapidly controlling PG inflammation, but long-term use is associated with significant side effects. While often used initially for rapid symptom control or in severe cases, they are typically tapered quickly if possible, and TNF-alpha inhibitors are preferred for sustained management, especially in IBD-associated PG.

Examination reveals a violaceous, undermined border surrounding purulent drainage. A biopsy confirms pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Notably, she exhibits pathergy, developing new papules and pustules at sites of minor trauma (e.g., needle sticks during blood draws). Her Crohn's disease is currently quiescent. Given the presence of pathergy and underlying IBD, what is the most appropriate initial systemic therapy?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial systemic therapy?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate initial systemic therapy for pyoderma gangrenosum with pathergy and associated inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: In patients with pyoderma gangrenosum associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly those exhibiting pathergy, anti-TNF-alpha therapy (like infliximab) is often the preferred initial systemic treatment due to its efficacy in managing both conditions simultaneously and its effectiveness in pathergic PG.
items.explanationCorrect: Infliximab is an anti-TNF-alpha agent effective for both pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Its use is particularly indicated in PG associated with IBD, especially when pathergy is present, as it targets the underlying inflammatory pathway common to both conditions. It offers a dual benefit by treating both the skin manifestations and the potential for IBD flares.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: High-dose systemic corticosteroids are often used for PG but are less effective in pathergy-positive disease and do not address the underlying IBD. Long-term use carries significant side effects.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Cyclosporine can be effective for severe PG, but it is nephrotoxic and does not treat the underlying IBD. It's generally considered a second-line option after failure of corticosteroids or biologics.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Dapsone is effective for some neutrophilic dermatoses but has limited efficacy in severe PG, especially with pathergy, and does not treat IBD.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Methotrexate is used for both PG and IBD, but its onset of action is slow, and it may not be sufficiently potent for rapidly progressive PG with pathergy. It is often considered after failure of first-line agents like corticosteroids or biologics.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: High-dose systemic corticosteroids are often used for PG but are less effective in pathergy-positive disease and do not address the underlying IBD. Long-term use carries significant side effects.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, malaise, and painful, erythematous papules and plaques on her upper extremities. She has a history of rheumatoid arthritis, currently treated with methotrexate. Physical examination reveals tender, violaceous papules and plaques, some with central pustulation, primarily on her forearms and hands. Peripheral blood work shows leukocytosis with a left shift and elevated C-reactive protein. Blood cultures are pending. A skin biopsy is performed for definitive diagnosis. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor Sweet syndrome over bacterial cellulitis?
items.leadIn: The patient's clinical presentation raises concern for both Sweet syndrome and bacterial cellulitis. Which finding best differentiates these conditions?
items.learningObjective: Identify the discriminating feature that separates Sweet syndrome from bacterial cellulitis in an acutely ill patient.
items.correctAnswerText: Skin biopsy showing a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the upper dermis without vasculitis
items.teachingPoint: Histopathology is crucial for differentiating Sweet syndrome from bacterial cellulitis when the clinical presentation is similar. The hallmark finding of Sweet syndrome is a dense neutrophilic infiltrate confined to the upper dermis without evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, unlike cellulitis which often involves deeper dermal inflammation and may show vascular changes or abscesses.
items.explanationCorrect: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) is characterized histologically by a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate in the upper dermis, often with papillary dermal edema, but notably lacking leukocytoclastic vasculitis. While cellulitis also involves neutrophils, it typically shows dermal edema and inflammation extending deeper into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, often with associated vascular changes or abscess formation. The absence of vasculitis is a key distinguishing feature on biopsy.

options.label: B
options.text: Skin biopsy showing a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the upper dermis without vasculitis

options.label: C
options.text: Positive blood cultures for Staphylococcus aureus

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Leukocytosis with neutrophilia is characteristic of both Sweet syndrome and bacterial cellulitis, reflecting an acute inflammatory response to infection or sterile inflammation. It is not a discriminating feature.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This describes the classic histopathology of Sweet syndrome. While cellulitis involves neutrophils, the pattern (dense upper dermal infiltrate without vasculitis) is specific for Sweet syndrome.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Positive blood cultures for S. aureus would strongly support bacterial cellulitis as the diagnosis, not Sweet syndrome. This finding would argue against Sweet syndrome.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Elevated C-reactive protein is a non-specific marker of inflammation and is expected in both Sweet syndrome and bacterial cellulitis. It does not help differentiate between the two.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While Sweet syndrome is often associated with underlying conditions like autoimmune diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis) or malignancy, this association is not specific enough to rule out cellulitis, which can occur in anyone. Many patients with Sweet syndrome do not have an identifiable trigger.

She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. Physical examination reveals tender, violaceous nodules and plaques, some with central pustulation, primarily on her forearms and hands. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis with a left shift, elevated C-reactive protein, and mild anemia. Blood cultures are pending. A skin biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings would most strongly suggest Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) over bacterial cellulitis?
items.leadIn: Which finding best differentiates Sweet syndrome from cellulitis?
items.learningObjective: Identify the discriminating feature that separates Sweet syndrome from bacterial cellulitis in an acutely ill patient.
items.correctAnswerText: Presence of neutrophils in the epidermis and dermis
items.teachingPoint: The key histological feature distinguishing Sweet syndrome from bacterial cellulitis is a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with marked epidermotropism (neutrophils migrating into the epidermis) and the absence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
items.explanationCorrect: Sweet syndrome is characterized histologically by a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the upper dermis, often extending into the epidermis (epidermotropism), without evidence of vasculitis. While cellulitis also involves neutrophils, the prominent epidermal involvement and lack of vasculitis are key features distinguishing Sweet syndrome. The clinical presentation of fever, malaise, and tender papules/plaques/nodules further supports this diagnosis.

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of neutrophils in the epidermis and dermis

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of organisms on Gram stain or culture of the lesion

options.label: D

distractorExplanations.text: Neutrophils are present in both conditions, but the pattern (dense dermal infiltrate with epidermotropism without vasculitis) is more characteristic of Sweet syndrome.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While absence of organisms supports Sweet syndrome, bacterial cellulitis can sometimes have negative cultures, especially if antibiotics were started. This is not the most discriminating histological feature.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Marked epidermal necrosis and ulceration are more typical of severe infections (like necrotizing fasciitis) or pyoderma gangrenosum, not typically Sweet syndrome or uncomplicated cellulitis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: A predominance of lymphocytes and histiocytes suggests a chronic inflammatory process or granulomatous disease, not acute neutrophilic dermatoses like Sweet syndrome or cellulitis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (inflammation and destruction of blood vessel walls with neutrophil debris) is characteristic of certain cutaneous small vessel vasculitides, not Sweet syndrome or typical cellulitis.

items.subtopic: Autoimmune blistering disease / CTD / vasculitis / neutrophilic dermatoses
items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of intensely pruritic, erythematous papules and vesicles primarily on his extensor surfaces, scalp, and trunk. He also reports painful oral erosions and conjunctival involvement. A skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blistering with neutrophilic infiltrate. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear deposition of C3 along the basement membrane zone. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) on salt-split skin demonstrates antibodies binding to the dermal side (floor) of the blister. Which autoantigen is most likely targeted in this patient?
items.leadIn: The clinical presentation and immunofluorescence findings are most consistent with which underlying autoimmune process?
items.learningObjective: Identify the autoantigen target most consistent with a given immunobullous disease and clinical presentation.
items.teachingPoint: The location of antibody binding on salt-split skin (epidermal roof vs. dermal floor) is critical for differentiating autoimmune blistering diseases targeting basement membrane zone components. Antibodies binding to the dermal floor typically target BP230 or Type VII Collagen, while antibodies binding to the epidermal roof typically target BP180 or Type XVII collagen (same molecule). The clinical presentation and DIF pattern help narrow the differential diagnosis.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with pruritic papules and vesicles, mucosal involvement (oral erosions), and conjunctival inflammation. DIF shows linear C3 deposition at the basement membrane zone. Crucially, IIF on salt-split skin shows antibodies binding to the dermal side (floor). This pattern is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid (BP), where autoantibodies target hemidesmosomal proteins. BP230 (BPAG1) is a cytoplasmic component of the hemidesmosome located on the dermal side of the basement membrane zone, consistent with the IIF findings. While BP180 (Collagen XVII) is also targeted in BP, it is a transmembrane protein and antibodies typically bind to the epidermal side (roof) or both sides on salt-split skin, although dermal binding can occur.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Desmoglein 1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus, which typically presents with superficial blisters and erosions, often without mucosal involvement. IIF would show intercellular staining within the epidermis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Desmoglein 3 is targeted in pemphigus vulgaris, characterized by flaccid blisters and significant mucosal involvement. IIF would show intercellular staining within the epidermis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: BP180 (Collagen XVII) is also a target antigen in bullous pemphigoid. However, antibodies typically bind to the epidermal side (roof) or both sides on salt-split skin. While dermal binding can occur, the classic BP pattern involves BP230 or both BP180 and BP230.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Type VII Collagen is the target antigen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA), which typically presents with tense blisters, often in trauma-prone areas, and may show scarring. IIF on salt-split skin shows antibodies binding to the dermal side, similar to BP, but EBA is less common and the clinical picture here is more typical for BP.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: This option is not a valid autoantigen target in this context.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intensely pruritic, erythematous papules and vesicles distributed symmetrically on her extensor surfaces, scalp, and buttocks. Mucous membranes are spared. She has no history of malignancy or other autoimmune diseases. A skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blistering with neutrophilic infiltrate and fibrin deposition in the dermal papillae. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear deposition of C3 along the basement membrane zone. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) on salt-split skin shows staining of the epidermal side ('roof'). Given this clinical presentation and immunopathology, which autoantigen is most likely targeted in this patient?
items.leadIn: Which autoantigen is most likely targeted in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Identify the autoantigen target most consistent with a given immunobullous disease and clinical presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230). The pattern of staining on salt-split skin immunofluorescence helps differentiate the targets: antibodies against BP180 stain the epidermal roof, while antibodies against BP230 or Type VII collagen stain the dermal floor.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation (pruritic vesicles/papules on extensor surfaces, sparing mucous membranes), subepidermal blistering with neutrophils, linear C3 deposition at the BMZ, and IIF showing epidermal ('roof') staining on salt-split skin are classic features of bullous pemphigoid. Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies targeting hemidesmosomal proteins, primarily BP180 (Collagen XVII) and less commonly BP230 (BPAG1). The epidermal roof staining pattern specifically points towards BP180 as the target.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Desmoglein 1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus, which typically presents with superficial blisters, erosions, and scaling, often on the face and scalp, and usually lacks the intense pruritus or neutrophilic infiltrate seen here. DIF shows intercellular IgG/C3.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Desmoglein 3 is targeted in pemphigus vulgaris, characterized by flaccid blisters and erosions involving mucous membranes and skin. DIF shows intercellular IgG/C3.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: BP230 (BPAG1) is another target in bullous pemphigoid, but antibodies against BP180 are more common and often associated with the classic clinical picture described. While possible, BP180 is the *most likely* target given the typical presentation and salt-split IIF pattern.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Type VII Collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA), which presents with subepidermal blistering, often in trauma-prone areas, and can have a variable morphology including vesicles, bullae, erosions, and scarring. DIF shows linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ, but IIF on salt-split skin typically shows dermal ('floor') staining, unlike this case.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: This option is incorrect as it is not one of the choices.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of an intensely pruritic rash on his lower legs. He initially saw his primary care physician, who diagnosed eczema and prescribed a medium-potency topical corticosteroid. However, the rash worsened, spreading to involve both lower legs and becoming less well-demarcated, with some central clearing and raised, erythematous borders. The patient reports no significant changes in soaps or detergents. On examination, there are multiple annular plaques with scaling, erythema, and papules at the advancing edge, predominantly on the shins and distal thighs. KOH preparation reveals septate hyphae.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish tinea incognito from eczematous dermatitis in a patient whose eruption worsened after empiric topical corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: Topical corticosteroids can alter the typical appearance of tinea infections, leading to tinea incognito, characterized by less distinct borders, central clearing, and often increased inflammation or pustules. A high index of suspicion and KOH preparation are crucial in cases of eczematous-appearing eruptions that worsen with steroid therapy.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of annular plaques with raised, erythematous borders and central clearing, worsening after topical corticosteroid use, is classic for tinea incognito. The KOH preparation confirming hyphae further supports a fungal etiology.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Nummular eczema typically presents as coin-shaped (nummular) plaques, often intensely pruritic and eczematous, but usually lacks the distinct annular configuration with central clearing seen here. While it can be chronic, it doesn't classically worsen in this specific manner after steroid use.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis is a fungal infection presenting as annular lesions with central clearing and raised borders. However, the history of worsening after topical corticosteroid application points specifically to tinea incognito, which is tinea corporis modified by corticosteroid treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Atopic dermatitis often presents with eczematous plaques in flexural areas, but typically not with the distinct annular morphology described. While it can be chronic and pruritic, the specific pattern and response to steroids are less characteristic.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory reaction to an external agent. While it can present with erythema and papules, the distinct annular lesions with central clearing and worsening after steroid use are not typical features. The patient also denies changes in potential contactants.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis is the underlying fungal infection, but the clinical picture described (worsening, altered morphology after topical steroid use) specifically defines tinea incognito. Therefore, tinea incognito is the more precise diagnosis given the history.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of an intensely pruritic, erythematous eruption on his lower legs. He initially self-treated with an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream, which provided transient relief but ultimately led to worsening of the rash, characterized by increased redness, scaling, and development of small pustules. He denies recent travel or exposure to new detergents or lotions. Examination reveals well-demarcated, annular plaques with central clearing and raised, erythematous borders on bilateral lower legs. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation from skin scrapings taken from the active border of a lesion shows septate hyphae.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish tinea incognito from eczematous dermatitis in a patient whose eruption worsened after empiric topical corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: Topical corticosteroids can alter the clinical presentation of tinea infections, masking classic features like central clearing and scaling while enhancing inflammation (erythema, pustules). This modified presentation is termed 'tinea incognito' and should be suspected in any inflammatory dermatosis that worsens or fails to respond appropriately to topical steroids, especially if annular or asymmetric.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with annular plaques with central clearing and raised borders, which is characteristic of tinea corporis. However, the history of worsening after topical corticosteroid use is classic for tinea incognito, where the steroids modify the typical appearance of the fungal infection, often leading to less distinct borders, increased inflammation, pustules, and a more widespread eruption. The positive KOH preparation confirms the presence of fungus.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Nummular eczema typically presents as coin-shaped (nummular) plaques, often intensely pruritic and eczematous, but usually lacks the distinct annular configuration with central clearing seen here. While it can respond poorly to steroids, the KOH would be negative.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis is the underlying fungal infection, but the term 'tinea incognito' specifically describes the altered presentation due to corticosteroid use, which is a key feature of this vignette. Therefore, tinea incognito is a more precise diagnosis given the history.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Contact dermatitis usually presents with vesicles, bullae, or diffuse erythema and scaling in areas of contact with an allergen or irritant. While it can be pruritic and influenced by steroids, the distinct annular morphology and positive KOH are not typical.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Psoriasis typically presents as well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, often on extensor surfaces. Annular lesions can occur but are less common, and the positive KOH rules out psoriasis as the primary diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Psoriasis typically presents as well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, often on extensor surfaces. Annular lesions can occur but are less common, and the positive KOH rules out psoriasis as the primary diagnosis.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a long history of severe atopic dermatitis presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, malaise, and rapidly spreading, painful vesicles superimposed on her eczematous skin, particularly in her flexural areas. She reports recent stress due to a work deadline. Physical examination reveals numerous monomorphic, umbilicated vesicles and punched-out erosions on an erythematous base, consistent with eczema herpeticum. Her vital signs are stable, but she appears acutely ill. Given the clinical suspicion for disseminated herpes simplex virus infection in the setting of atopic dermatitis, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for suspected eczema herpeticum in a patient with atopic dermatitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Start systemic antiviral therapy (e.g., oral acyclovir or valacyclovir) immediately.
items.teachingPoint: Eczema herpeticum is a dermatologic emergency requiring immediate systemic antiviral therapy. Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient to initiate treatment without delay for diagnostic testing.
items.explanationCorrect: Eczema herpeticum is a potentially life-threatening disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection occurring in individuals with underlying skin disease, most commonly atopic dermatitis. Prompt initiation of systemic antiviral therapy is crucial to prevent severe complications like sepsis and widespread cutaneous involvement. Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir are the standard treatments.

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate topical antiviral therapy (e.g., acyclovir cream) and continue her current topical corticosteroids.

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe oral antihistamines to manage pruritus and sedating antihistamines for sleep.

options.label: C
options.text: Start systemic antiviral therapy (e.g., oral acyclovir or valacyclovir) immediately.

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain viral cultures from the lesions before initiating treatment.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform a skin biopsy for histopathological examination.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Topical antivirals are ineffective for disseminated HSV infection like eczema herpeticum. While topical corticosteroids are used for atopic dermatitis, they should be used cautiously or temporarily discontinued during active viral infection as they can potentially worsen the condition.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Antihistamines may help with symptoms like pruritus but do not address the underlying viral infection and are not the primary treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Delaying antiviral therapy to obtain viral cultures is inappropriate in a clinically suspected case of eczema herpeticum, as rapid treatment is essential. Cultures can be obtained if needed, but treatment should not be delayed.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: A skin biopsy is generally not necessary for the diagnosis of eczema herpeticum when the clinical presentation is classic. It would delay initiation of crucial antiviral therapy.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While topical corticosteroids are used for atopic dermatitis, they should be used cautiously or temporarily discontinued during active viral infection as they can potentially worsen the condition.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a long history of moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, malaise, and widespread eruption of painful, monomorphic, umbilicated vesicles and punched-out erosions superimposed on her eczematous skin. She reports recent use of topical corticosteroids for a flare. Her vital signs are stable, but she appears systemically unwell. Given the clinical suspicion for eczema herpeticum, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for suspected eczema herpeticum in a patient with atopic dermatitis.
items.teachingPoint: Eczema herpeticum is a dermatologic emergency requiring immediate empiric systemic antiviral therapy (typically oral acyclovir) based on clinical suspicion, without waiting for diagnostic confirmation.
items.explanationCorrect: Eczema herpeticum is a potentially life-threatening disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in patients with underlying skin disease, most commonly atopic dermatitis. Prompt initiation of systemic antiviral therapy is crucial to prevent severe complications. Given the classic clinical presentation and potential severity, empiric treatment should not be delayed pending diagnostic confirmation.

options.label: A
options.text: Obtain viral cultures from the lesions.

options.label: C
options.text: Perform a skin biopsy for viral immunohistochemistry.

options.label: D
options.text: Apply topical antiviral ointment to the lesions.

options.label: E
options.text: Prescribe a short course of systemic corticosteroids.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Viral cultures or PCR are useful for confirming the diagnosis but take time (days) to return results. Delaying treatment while awaiting confirmation is inappropriate in suspected eczema herpeticum due to the risk of rapid progression and severe outcomes.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis, it is invasive, requires specialized processing (immunohistochemistry), and also delays initiation of critical antiviral therapy. Clinical suspicion is often sufficient to start treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Topical antivirals are ineffective for disseminated HSV infection like eczema herpeticum, which requires systemic treatment to control viral replication throughout the body.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated in active viral infections like eczema herpeticum as they can suppress the immune response and worsen the infection. They might be considered later for managing the underlying atopic dermatitis flare *after* the infection is controlled, but not as an initial step.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Viral cultures or PCR are useful for confirming the diagnosis but take time (days) to return results. Delaying treatment while awaiting confirmation is inappropriate in suspected eczema herpeticum due to the risk of rapid progression and severe outcomes.

items.stem: A 58-year-old male presents with a 2-year history of progressively worsening nail changes affecting all ten fingernails and toenails. He reports nail thickening, discoloration (yellowish-brown), subungual hyperkeratosis, and onycholysis. KOH preparation confirms the presence of hyphae. Given the extensive nature of the disease involving multiple nails and significant matrix involvement, which systemic therapy approach is generally considered the most effective first-line treatment?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic therapy approach for confirmed onychomycosis when nail disease is extensive and matrix-involving.
items.teachingPoint: For extensive dermatophyte onychomycosis, especially involving the nail matrix, oral terbinafine is the most effective first-line systemic therapy due to its superior cure rates compared to other oral antifungals and topical agents.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral terbinafine is generally considered the most effective first-line systemic agent for dermatophyte onychomycosis, particularly when extensive or involving the matrix. It achieves high concentrations in the nail plate and has demonstrated superior cure rates compared to other oral antifungals like itraconazole and fluconazole in numerous studies, especially for toenail onychomycosis. A 12-week course is standard for fingernail disease.

options.label: B
options.text: Initiate oral itraconazole pulse therapy (2 weeks on, 2 weeks off) for 3 cycles.

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate oral fluconazole daily for 6 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Initiate topical ciclopirox lacquer applied daily for 1 year.

options.label: E
options.text: Initiate topical efinaconazole solution applied daily for 48 weeks.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Oral terbinafine is the most effective first-line systemic agent for dermatophyte onychomycosis, particularly extensive or matrix-involving disease.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While oral itraconazole is an alternative, continuous therapy (not pulse) is generally preferred for efficacy, and studies often show terbinafine to be superior, especially for toenails. Pulse therapy has lower cure rates.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Oral fluconazole has lower cure rates for onychomycosis compared to terbinafine and itraconazole and is typically reserved for specific situations or non-dermatophyte molds.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Topical therapies like ciclopirox lacquer have very limited efficacy for extensive or matrix-involving onychomycosis due to poor nail penetration. They are generally only suitable for mild, distal subungual onychomycosis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Similar to ciclopirox, topical efinaconazole has limited efficacy for extensive or matrix-involving disease and is best suited for mild cases.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressively worsening nail changes affecting all ten fingernails and toenails. Given the extensive involvement of multiple nails, including matrix involvement in several digits, and the patient's otherwise good health, which systemic therapy approach is most appropriate?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic therapy approach for confirmed onychomycosis when nail disease is extensive and matrix-involving.
items.teachingPoint: For extensive dermatophyte onychomycosis involving multiple nails and the matrix, oral terbinafine is generally considered the most effective first-line systemic therapy due to its superior efficacy compared to itraconazole pulse therapy and topical agents, and better efficacy than fluconazole for dermatophyte infections.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral terbinafine is considered a first-line systemic treatment for dermatophyte onychomycosis, particularly when extensive or involving the matrix. It has demonstrated superior efficacy compared to itraconazole in head-to-head trials for toenail onychomycosis and is effective for fingernail disease. A 12-week course is standard for fingernail involvement, while toenails typically require longer treatment (up to 16 weeks). Given the extensive disease involving both fingernails and toenails with matrix involvement, oral terbinafine is the most appropriate choice.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral itraconazole pulse therapy (1 week on, 3 weeks off) for 2 cycles

options.label: C
options.text: Topical ciclopirox or efinaconazole applied daily for 6 months

options.label: E
options.text: Photodynamic therapy targeting the nail matrix

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Oral terbinafine is a first-line systemic agent for dermatophyte onychomycosis due to its high cure rates and favorable side effect profile compared to older azoles. It concentrates in the nail plate and matrix, making it effective for extensive disease.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While oral itraconazole is another first-line option, pulse therapy has shown lower efficacy than continuous daily dosing or terbinafine, especially for extensive disease. It may be used for Candida onychomycosis but is less effective for dermatophyte infections.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Photodynamic therapy is an investigational treatment for onychomycosis with limited evidence supporting its efficacy, especially for extensive disease. It is not a standard or recommended systemic therapy approach.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of severe pain followed by a rash on the left side of his face. The rash consists of erythematous papules and vesicles in a dermatomal distribution involving the forehead, upper eyelid, and side of the nose. He reports photophobia and decreased vision in his left eye. He denies any recent exposure to new cosmetics or topical medications. Examination reveals unilateral vesicular lesions respecting the midline, with some crusting. There is mild conjunctival injection and decreased corneal sensation on the left.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish herpes zoster ophthalmicus from allergic contact dermatitis and HSV in a unilateral painful facial eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve. It presents with a painful, unilateral vesicular rash in a V1 dermatomal distribution and requires urgent ophthalmologic evaluation due to potential serious ocular complications like keratitis, uveitis, and vision loss.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of a widespread, non-pruritic rash. He initially noticed a single, larger oval patch on his trunk, followed by smaller, similar lesions distributed along skin lines in a 'Christmas tree' pattern. He denies fever, malaise, or recent medication changes. Physical examination reveals multiple erythematous papules and plaques with fine scale, primarily on the trunk and proximal extremities. Notably, he has macular, coppery-red papules on the palms and soles. Serological testing for rapid plasma reagin (RPR) is positive.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate secondary syphilis from pityriasis rosea and drug eruption when palms and soles are involved.
items.teachingPoint: Palmar and plantar involvement in a generalized papulosquamous eruption is a key clinical feature strongly suggestive of secondary syphilis, differentiating it from other conditions like pityriasis rosea or drug eruptions where such involvement is uncommon.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with a rash characteristic of secondary syphilis, including the initial 'herald patch', widespread eruption in a 'Christmas tree' distribution, and crucially, involvement of the palms and soles with macular, coppery-red papules. The positive RPR further supports this diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Pityriasis rosea typically presents with a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption in a 'Christmas tree' pattern, but palm and sole involvement is rare. While the morphology can be similar, the palmar/plantar lesions strongly argue against PR.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Drug eruptions can manifest in various morphologies, but widespread papules and plaques involving palms and soles are less typical, especially without a history of recent medication initiation. The specific pattern described is more suggestive of syphilis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Guttate psoriasis typically follows a streptococcal infection and presents with small, drop-like papules, often on the trunk and extremities. Palmar/plantar involvement is uncommon, and the morphology described (oval plaques, 'Christmas tree' pattern) is not typical for guttate psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis is a fungal infection presenting as annular lesions with central clearing and raised, erythematous borders. It does not typically cause a widespread eruption in a 'Christmas tree' pattern or involve the palms and soles in this manner.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While pityriasis rosea can mimic secondary syphilis in some aspects (herald patch, distribution), the involvement of palms and soles is a classic distinguishing feature highly suggestive of secondary syphilis. The positive RPR confirms this suspicion.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of pruritic, erythematous patches in his groin and axillae. He has tried over-the-counter antifungal creams without improvement. Physical examination reveals well-demarcated, reddish-brown plaques with minimal scaling in the intertriginous areas. A Wood lamp examination is performed in the office. Which finding would most strongly suggest erythrasma as the diagnosis over tinea cruris or candidal intertrigo?
items.leadIn: The Wood lamp examination reveals:
items.learningObjective: Identify the discriminating bedside or office-based clue that separates erythrasma from tinea cruris and candidal intertrigo.
items.teachingPoint: Wood lamp examination is a useful bedside tool for diagnosing certain superficial fungal infections and bacterial conditions. Erythrasma caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum characteristically exhibits coral-red fluorescence under Wood lamp examination, distinguishing it from tinea cruris and candidal intertrigo, which typically do not fluoresce or show different patterns.
items.explanationCorrect: Erythrasma, caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, does not fluoresce under Wood lamp examination. This lack of fluorescence helps differentiate it from tinea cruris (caused by dermatophytes like Trichophyton rubrum) and candidal intertrigo (caused by Candida albicans), which typically show no fluorescence as well, but the key differentiator here is the specific fluorescence patterns of other conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Bright green fluorescence is characteristic of Microsporum species causing tinea capitis or tinea corporis, not erythrasma, tinea cruris (usually caused by Trichophyton), or candidal intertrigo.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Yellow-green fluorescence can be seen with some dermatophytes (e.g., Microsporum canis) but is not typical for erythrasma or the common causes of tinea cruris/candidal intertrigo.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Coral-red fluorescence is characteristic of erythrasma caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum when viewed under Wood lamp examination. This finding would strongly suggest erythrasma.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: No fluorescence is typical for both erythrasma and candidal intertrigo, as well as most cases of tinea cruris (caused by Trichophyton species). While lack of fluorescence doesn't rule out these conditions, the presence of coral-red fluorescence is specific for erythrasma. The question asks for the finding that *most strongly suggests* erythrasma, implying a positive finding.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Blue-white fluorescence can be seen with Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections or certain medications/cosmetics, not typically with erythrasma, tinea cruris, or candidal intertrigo.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of pruritic, erythematous patches in his groin and axillae. He has tried over-the-counter antifungal creams without improvement. Examination reveals well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with minimal scaling in the intertriginous areas. The patient reports no history of diabetes or recent antibiotic use. A Wood lamp examination is performed in the office. Which finding would most strongly suggest erythrasma over tinea cruris or candidal intertrigo?
items.leadIn: The Wood lamp examination reveals:
items.learningObjective: Identify the discriminating bedside or office-based clue that separates erythrasma from tinea cruris and candidal intertrigo.
items.teachingPoint: Wood lamp examination is a valuable bedside tool for diagnosing erythrasma. The characteristic coral-red or yellow-green fluorescence caused by porphyrins produced by *Corynebacterium minutissimum* helps differentiate it from other common causes of intertrigo like tinea cruris and candidiasis, which typically do not fluoresce.
items.explanationCorrect: Erythrasma, caused by *Corynebacterium minutissimum*, characteristically exhibits coral-red or yellow-green fluorescence under a Wood lamp due to the production of porphyrins. This is a key diagnostic feature distinguishing it from tinea cruris and candidal intertrigo, which typically do not fluoresce or may show faint fluorescence.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Bright green fluorescence is characteristic of *Microsporum* species causing tinea capitis, not erythrasma.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Yellow-green fluorescence is the classic finding in erythrasma. This is the correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Blue-white fluorescence can be seen with certain fungal infections like *Trichophyton schoenleinii* (favus) or some bacterial infections, but it is not typical for erythrasma, tinea cruris, or candidal intertrigo.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Lack of fluorescence is common in many dermatoses, including tinea cruris and candidal intertrigo, but it does not specifically point to erythrasma over these other conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Copper-orange fluorescence is characteristic of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* infections, particularly in burn wounds or folliculitis, not erythrasma.

items.stem: A 62-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of painful vesicles along the left forehead and scalp, following a dermatomal distribution. He also reports photophobia and mild eye redness in the left eye. His visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally, and extraocular movements are intact. There are no corneal abrasions or significant anterior chamber inflammation noted on initial slit-lamp examination by the ED physician. However, the patient describes a sensation of grittiness and foreign body in the left eye. Given the potential for serious ocular complications, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate urgent management step for herpes zoster involving the ophthalmic branch.
items.correctAnswerText: Refer the patient urgently to an ophthalmologist.
items.teachingPoint: Herpes zoster involving the ophthalmic division (V1) requires urgent ophthalmologic consultation due to the high risk of sight-threatening complications, even if initial examination appears unremarkable. Prompt specialist evaluation is paramount.
items.explanationCorrect: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) involves the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) and carries a significant risk of sight-threatening ocular complications, including keratitis, uveitis, and retinitis. Even with a seemingly normal initial slit-lamp examination, subtle findings or delayed complications can occur. Prompt ophthalmologic evaluation is crucial for comprehensive assessment and management to prevent vision loss. The patient's symptoms of photophobia, eye redness, and foreign body sensation warrant immediate specialist consultation.

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily.

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe topical erythromycin ointment for the left eye.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer the patient urgently to an ophthalmologist.

options.label: E
options.text: Apply topical corticosteroids to the affected skin lesions.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: While antiviral therapy (oral acyclovir) is essential for HZO, it should be initiated concurrently with or immediately following ophthalmologic evaluation, not as the sole initial step. Delaying ophthalmology referral to start antivirals is inappropriate given the potential for vision loss.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Topical antibiotics like erythromycin are used for bacterial conjunctivitis or prophylaxis, not for viral keratitis or uveitis associated with HZO. This would not address the underlying viral infection or potential intraocular inflammation.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Intravenous acyclovir is typically reserved for severe HZO (e.g., disseminated disease, immunocompromised patients, significant ocular involvement like acute retinal necrosis) or patients unable to take oral medication. Oral therapy is usually sufficient for uncomplicated HZO, and the primary immediate need is ophthalmologic assessment.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in active viral epithelial keratitis (like herpes simplex or zoster keratitis) as they can worsen the infection. They may be used later by an ophthalmologist for stromal keratitis or uveitis but should not be applied initially, especially without a definitive diagnosis from a specialist.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While antiviral therapy is crucial, it is not the *most* appropriate *next* step. The highest priority is to assess for and prevent potentially vision-threatening ocular complications via urgent ophthalmology consultation. Antiviral therapy should be started promptly, ideally in conjunction with or immediately after the referral.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of painful, unilateral vesicular eruption along his left forehead and scalp, consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO). He is otherwise healthy and not immunocompromised. Given the potential for serious ocular complications, what is the most appropriate next step in management?

items.teachingPoint: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus requires urgent ophthalmologic evaluation due to the high risk of sight-threatening complications, even if visual symptoms are absent initially. Antiviral therapy should be initiated promptly, ideally in coordination with the ophthalmologist's assessment.
items.explanationCorrect: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) involves the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) and carries a significant risk of sight-threatening ocular complications, including keratitis, uveitis, and retinitis, even in the absence of current visual symptoms. Prompt evaluation by an ophthalmologist is crucial to assess for ocular involvement and guide appropriate management, which may include topical antivirals, corticosteroids, or cycloplegics. Delaying this consultation can lead to irreversible vision loss.

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply topical mupirocin to the vesicles.

options.label: D

options.label: E

distractorExplanations.text: While initiating antiviral therapy (like acyclovir) is essential for HZO, it should ideally be done concurrently with or immediately following the ophthalmology consultation to ensure comprehensive management. distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Antiviral therapy is crucial, but the *most* urgent step is assessing for ocular involvement, which requires an ophthalmologist. Antivirals can be started concurrently or immediately after consultation, but the eye exam takes precedence due to the risk of vision loss.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Topical mupirocin is an antibiotic used for bacterial infections. While secondary bacterial infection of vesicles can occur, it's not the primary concern or the most urgent step in HZO management. Antiviral therapy is the mainstay.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Oral corticosteroids are sometimes used as adjunctive therapy in HZO to reduce inflammation and potentially decrease the risk of postherpetic neuralgia, but their use is controversial and should be decided in conjunction with the ophthalmologist, especially given potential risks like worsening viral infection or increased intraocular pressure. This is supportive care, not the most appropriate urgent management step.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of a slowly enlarging, well-demarcated, erythematous plaque on his left forearm. The lesion is asymptomatic but he notes decreased sensation within the plaque. He has no systemic symptoms, and his past medical history is unremarkable except for hypertension managed with lisinopril. Examination reveals a 4 cm, annular plaque with central clearing and a raised, indurated border. The skin within the plaque is notably hypoesthetic to light touch and pinprick compared to surrounding skin. There are no other lesions. A KOH preparation of scale from the active border is negative for fungal elements. A skin biopsy is performed.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish Hansen disease from cutaneous sarcoidosis and tinea corporis in a chronic hypoesthetic plaque eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Chronic skin lesions accompanied by objective sensory loss (hypoesthesia or anesthesia) should raise strong suspicion for Hansen disease (leprosy), even if the morphology mimics other dermatoses like tinea corporis or sarcoidosis. While other conditions can cause annular plaques, the presence of hypoesthesia is a critical diagnostic clue for leprosy.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with a chronic, well-demarcated, erythematous plaque with central clearing and an indurated border, accompanied by significant hypoesthesia within the lesion. This constellation of findings, particularly the objective sensory loss within a chronic skin lesion, is highly suggestive of Hansen disease (leprosy), specifically the tuberculoid form. The chronicity and morphology can mimic other conditions, but the hypoesthesia is a key distinguishing feature.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents with papules, plaques, or nodules, typically violaceous or erythematous, but sensory loss is not a characteristic feature. While lesions can be chronic, hypoesthesia is uncommon.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis typically presents as an annular plaque with central clearing and an active, scaling border. However, it is usually pruritic, and while inflammation can occur, significant objective hypoesthesia within the lesion is atypical. The negative KOH preparation also makes this less likely.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Granuloma annulare presents as annular or arcuate plaques, often on the extremities, but they are typically non-scaling, skin-colored or erythematous, and crucially, sensation is preserved. Hypoesthesia is not a feature.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Nummular eczema presents as coin-shaped, eczematous plaques, usually intensely pruritic, and associated with scaling, crusting, or weeping. Sensory loss is not characteristic.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Nummular eczema presents as coin-shaped, eczematous plaques, usually intensely pruritic, and associated with scaling, crusting, or weeping. Sensory loss is not characteristic.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging, erythematous plaque on his left forearm. He denies systemic symptoms, recent travel, or known exposure to tuberculosis. Physical examination reveals multiple similar, smaller lesions scattered on his trunk and extremities. A skin biopsy from the forearm lesion shows numerous foamy macrophages containing acid-fast bacilli, arranged in a palisading granuloma surrounding nerve bundles.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish Hansen disease from cutaneous sarcoidosis and tinea corporis in a chronic hypoesthetic plaque eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Hansen disease (leprosy) should be considered in patients presenting with chronic, hypoesthetic skin lesions, especially plaques. The definitive diagnosis relies on clinical findings combined with histopathology demonstrating acid-fast bacilli within macrophages, often associated with nerve involvement.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of chronic, hypoesthetic plaques is characteristic of Hansen disease. The key finding is the skin biopsy showing foamy macrophages containing acid-fast bacilli within a granuloma surrounding nerve bundles. This histopathology is pathognomonic for lepromatous leprosy.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous sarcoidosis can present with plaques, but they are typically non-hypoesthetic and biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas without acid-fast bacilli.

distractorExplanations.label: B

distractorExplanations.text: Granuloma annulare typically presents as annular plaques, often on the extremities, but they are non-hypoesthetic, non-indurated, and biopsy shows necrobiotic collagen surrounded by histiocytes and lymphocytes, not granulomas with acid-fast bacilli.

items.stem: A 17-year-old high school wrestler presents with a 3-week history of itchy, annular lesions with central clearing on his trunk and upper extremities. Oral terbinafine is a first-line agent for dermatophyte infections due to its fungicidal activity and excellent penetration into skin and nails. items.stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of persistent, erythematous, scaling papules and pustules primarily located on his scalp and upper back. He has tried multiple topical antifungal agents and topical corticosteroids without significant improvement. A bedside potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation from scale scraped from a scalp lesion is negative for fungal elements. Given the chronicity, morphology, and lack of response to empiric therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish a definitive diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish a definitive diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Recognize why deep or follicular dermatophyte infection may require biopsy or culture when bedside KOH is unrevealing.
items.correctAnswerText: Obtain skin biopsy for histopathology and fungal stains.
items.teachingPoint: In cases of suspected deep or follicular dermatophyte infection (e.g., kerion, chronic scalp tinea) where superficial KOH preparations are negative, a skin biopsy for histopathology and fungal stains is often necessary to establish a definitive diagnosis by visualizing fungal elements within deeper tissue structures.
items.explanationCorrect: Deep or follicular dermatophyte infections, such as kerion or chronic scalp tinea, often involve inflammation that can obscure fungal elements in superficial scrapings. The fungus may reside deeper within the hair follicle or dermis, making KOH preparation insensitive. A skin biopsy allows for examination of deeper tissue layers and specialized stains (e.g., PAS, GMS) to identify fungal hyphae within the stratum corneum, follicular epithelium, or dermis, providing a definitive diagnosis when superficial methods fail.

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat KOH preparation from multiple lesions.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform fungal culture of scrapings from active lesions.

options.label: C
options.text: Obtain skin biopsy for histopathology and fungal stains.

options.label: E
options.text: Consider alternative diagnoses such as seborrheic dermatitis or folliculitis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Repeating KOH is unlikely to be helpful if the initial preparation was negative and performed correctly, especially in suspected deep/follicular infection where fungal elements may not be present in superficial scales.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Fungal culture is a reasonable step but takes weeks for results. While it can detect fungi missed by KOH, biopsy offers a faster diagnosis and direct visualization of the organism within tissue, which is crucial for confirming deep involvement.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: While considering alternative diagnoses is important, empiric systemic therapy without a definitive diagnosis carries risks (side effects, drug interactions, potential for misdiagnosis). Establishing the correct diagnosis first is preferred, especially given the chronicity and lack of response to previous treatments.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: This is inappropriate. While biopsy is the best next step for diagnosis, initiating systemic therapy before confirming the fungal etiology is premature and potentially harmful. Alternative diagnoses must be ruled out or confirmed.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While these are potential differential diagnoses, the clinical presentation (chronic, scaling papules/pustules on scalp/back) is highly suggestive of a deep dermatophyte infection. Dismissing the possibility of tinea without further investigation like biopsy would be premature.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents 18 days after starting amoxicillin for a urinary tract infection. She reports fever, malaise, and a widespread pruritic rash that began as macules and papules but has evolved. On examination, she has diffuse erythema, scaling, and edema, particularly on her face and upper trunk. Mucous membranes are clear. Laboratory tests reveal leukocytosis with 15% eosinophils, elevated liver transaminases (AST 3x upper limit of normal, ALT 4x upper limit of normal), and mild lymphopenia. She denies recent travel or other new medications besides the amoxicillin.
items.leadIn: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate DRESS from an uncomplicated morbilliform drug eruption in a recently medicated patient.
items.correctAnswerText: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)
items.teachingPoint: DRESS syndrome is a severe drug reaction characterized by a delayed onset (typically 2-8 weeks), widespread rash, fever, lymphopenia, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement (commonly liver, kidney, or lung). Differentiating it from less severe morbilliform eruptions requires attention to the timing, systemic symptoms, and laboratory findings.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation, including the timing (18 days after drug initiation), widespread rash with facial/truncal involvement, fever, malaise, significant eosinophilia (>10%), lymphopenia, and elevated liver enzymes, is highly characteristic of DRESS syndrome. This systemic reaction typically occurs 2-8 weeks after starting a causative medication.

options.label: C
options.text: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Morbilliform drug eruptions are common but usually lack significant systemic symptoms like high fever, marked eosinophilia, lymphopenia, or organ involvement (e.g., hepatitis). They typically appear earlier (within 1-2 weeks) and resolve relatively quickly after drug withdrawal.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: AGEP is characterized by the rapid onset (usually within days) of widespread non-follicular pustules on an erythematous background, often accompanied by fever and neutrophilia, not typically eosinophilia or lymphopenia. The rash morphology described here (macules, papules, scaling, erythema, edema) is not typical for AGEP.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Urticarial drug eruptions present as transient wheals and are typically histamine-mediated, usually appearing within hours to days of drug exposure. While pruritic, they do not typically cause the systemic features (fever, eosinophilia, hepatitis, lymphopenia) seen in this patient.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: SJS involves mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital) and often presents with targetoid lesions or widespread epidermal detachment. This patient has clear mucous membranes, making SJS unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: This is incorrect because the patient lacks mucosal involvement and the rash morphology is not typical for SJS.

items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with a morbilliform rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and evidence of internal organ involvement (hepatitis, thrombocytopenia) approximately 2-3 weeks after starting a new medication (amoxicillin). This constellation of findings is characteristic of DRESS syndrome.

distractorExplanations.text: AGEP is characterized by the rapid onset (within 24-48 hours) of widespread non-follicular pustules on an erythematous background, often accompanied by fever and leukocytosis, but typically without significant lymphadenopathy or eosinophilia, and usually resolves quickly upon drug withdrawal.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Morbilliform drug eruption

items.stem: A 68-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, malaise, and painful oral erosions. He started taking allopurinol for gout 5 days prior. Physical examination reveals diffuse, tender erythema with scattered targetoid lesions and epidermal detachment involving approximately 10% of his body surface area. Mucous membrane involvement includes painful stomatitis and conjunctivitis. Vital signs are stable, but he is refusing oral intake due to pain. Given the clinical suspicion for Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), what is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step?
items.learningObjective: Identify the safest immediate management approach for suspected SJS/TEN.
items.correctAnswerText: Discontinue allopurinol and admit the patient for supportive care.
items.teachingPoint: The most critical initial step in managing suspected SJS/TEN is the immediate discontinuation of all potential offending medications, followed by prompt admission for intensive supportive care. Diagnostic procedures should not delay this crucial intervention.
items.explanationCorrect: The cornerstone of managing suspected SJS/TEN is immediate withdrawal of the offending medication. Supportive care in a specialized setting (burn unit or ICU) is crucial due to the high risk of complications like fluid loss, electrolyte imbalance, and infection. This patient's presentation strongly suggests SJS (epidermal detachment <10% is SJS, 10-30% is SJS/TEN overlap, >30% is TEN).

options.label: C
options.text: Discontinue allopurinol and admit the patient for supportive care.

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a skin biopsy for definitive diagnosis before initiating treatment.

options.label: E
options.text: Start prophylactic antibiotics to prevent secondary infection.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Corticosteroids are generally not recommended for SJS/TEN and may potentially worsen outcomes or increase infection risk. Their role remains controversial and unproven.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: IVIG has been studied in SJS/TEN, but its efficacy is uncertain, and it is not considered a standard first-line immediate treatment. It might be considered in specific severe cases, but withdrawal of the trigger and supportive care are paramount.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: While a biopsy can confirm the diagnosis, delaying essential management (stopping the drug, initiating supportive care) for diagnostic confirmation is inappropriate in a rapidly progressing condition like SJS/TEN. Clinical suspicion is sufficient to initiate immediate action.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Prophylactic antibiotics are generally not recommended unless there is evidence of active infection, as they do not prevent secondary infection and may contribute to antibiotic resistance or fungal overgrowth.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While supportive care is essential, initiating prophylactic antibiotics without evidence of infection is not the *most* appropriate immediate step. The priority is stopping the causative agent and providing general supportive measures like fluid management and wound care.
