items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of asymptomatic, skin-colored papules and nodules predominantly on her upper back and shoulders. She has no significant past medical history, and her medications are limited to occasional acetaminophen. Physical examination reveals multiple firm, non-pitting papules and nodules, some coalescing into plaques, in a sun-exposed distribution. A biopsy of a representative lesion shows dermal deposition of amorphous, eosinophilic material that stains positive with Congo red and exhibits apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
items.leadIn: The biopsy findings are characteristic of amyloid deposition in the skin. Based on the clinical presentation and histopathology, which condition is most likely?
items.learningObjective: Correlate Congo-red–positive eosinophilic deposits with the most likely cutaneous amyloidosis pattern or systemic implication.
items.teachingPoint: Cutaneous amyloidosis encompasses several distinct entities. Localized cutaneous amyloidosis (LCA) is characterized by asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, firm papules and nodules, typically in older adults, often in sun-exposed areas, with dermal amyloid deposition but no systemic involvement. Systemic amyloidosis presents with evidence of organ dysfunction and may have various cutaneous manifestations (e.g., purpura, waxy papules, macroglossia), while macular amyloidosis presents as diffuse hyperpigmented patches.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with asymptomatic, skin-colored papules and nodules in a sun-exposed distribution, which is the classic presentation of localized cutaneous amyloidosis (LCA). The biopsy confirms amyloid deposition (Congo red positive with apple-green birefringence). LCA typically occurs in older individuals, is usually asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, and lacks evidence of systemic involvement. The lesions are often found on the upper back, shoulders, and extremities.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Localized cutaneous amyloidosis (LCA) is the most likely diagnosis given the asymptomatic, localized papules/nodules in a sun-exposed area and confirmed dermal amyloid deposition without systemic signs.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic amyloidosis (AL type) is associated with plasma cell dyscrasias. While it can cause cutaneous lesions, they are often purpuric, ecchymotic, or involve the eyelids (periorbital purpura), and patients typically have systemic symptoms or evidence of underlying malignancy or monoclonal gammopathy. This patient's presentation is not typical for AL amyloidosis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic amyloidosis (AA type) is secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease). Cutaneous manifestations can occur but are less common than in AL amyloidosis and often associated with systemic symptoms related to the underlying inflammation. This patient has no history suggestive of a chronic inflammatory condition.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Macular amyloidosis presents as diffuse, non-indurated, yellowish-brown patches, typically in sun-exposed areas or intertriginous zones, often associated with sweating. The lesions are usually asymptomatic but may be pruritic. The patient's firm papules and nodules are inconsistent with macular amyloidosis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma can be associated with systemic amyloidosis (specifically, deposition of calcitonin-derived amyloid). While cutaneous amyloidosis can occur, it is rare, and the primary presentation would likely involve symptoms related to the thyroid tumor or its metastases. This patient's presentation does not suggest medullary thyroid carcinoma.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of asymptomatic, skin-colored papules and plaques primarily located on his lower extremities and trunk. He has no significant medical history other than well-controlled hypertension. Physical examination reveals multiple firm, non-pitting papules and plaques, some exhibiting a waxy appearance. A biopsy is performed from a representative lesion. Histopathology shows deposition of amorphous, eosinophilic material in the papillary dermis and around dermal blood vessels and adnexal structures. This material exhibits apple-green birefringence under polarized light after staining with Congo red. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: The histopathologic findings are characteristic of amyloid deposition. Based on the clinical presentation and biopsy results, which cutaneous amyloidosis is most strongly suggested?
items.learningObjective: Correlate Congo-red–positive eosinophilic deposits with the most likely cutaneous amyloidosis pattern or systemic implication.
items.teachingPoint: Localized cutaneous amyloidosis is a benign condition characterized by amyloid deposition confined to the skin, typically presenting as asymptomatic papules or plaques. It must be distinguished from systemic amyloidosis, which involves internal organs and carries a worse prognosis. The clinical presentation (skin-limited, asymptomatic lesions) combined with histopathology (dermal amyloid deposits) is key to diagnosing LCA.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with asymptomatic, skin-colored papules and plaques limited to the skin, which is the classic presentation of Localized Cutaneous Amyloidosis (LCA). The histopathology confirms amyloid deposition (Congo red positive, apple-green birefringence) in the dermis. LCA is typically idiopathic or associated with chronic inflammation or trauma, but it is not associated with systemic disease.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Localized cutaneous amyloidosis (LCA) is the most likely diagnosis given the asymptomatic, skin-limited papules/plaques and confirmed dermal amyloid deposition without evidence of systemic involvement.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic amyloidosis (AA type) is typically associated with chronic inflammatory conditions (like rheumatoid arthritis or chronic infections) and often presents with systemic symptoms (e.g., nephrotic syndrome, neuropathy, hepatomegaly) or more widespread skin lesions, which are absent here.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Macroglobulinemic purpura is associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia and typically presents with palpable purpura, bleeding, and systemic symptoms, none of which are described in this patient. While amyloid can be seen in cryoglobulinemia, the clinical picture doesn't fit.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disease characterized by tense bullae and urticarial plaques, not firm papules and plaques. Histopathology would show subepidermal blisters with eosinophils, not dermal amyloid deposits.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous small vessel vasculitis typically presents with palpable purpura, often on the lower extremities, and histopathology shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis (inflammation and destruction of blood vessel walls), not primary amyloid deposition.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with multiple asymptomatic, skin-colored papules and nodules on her upper back and scalp, present for several years. She has a history of early-onset colon cancer diagnosed at age 45. A biopsy of a nodule reveals a well-circumscribed dermal proliferation of mature adipocytes and foamy sebocytes, with some atypical cells showing large nuclei and prominent nucleoli, but no significant mitotic activity or necrosis. The lesion is negative for PTEN staining. Which hereditary cancer syndrome is most strongly associated with this histologic finding?
items.leadIn: Which hereditary cancer syndrome is most strongly associated with this histologic finding?
items.learningObjective: Correlate sebaceous neoplasia on histology with the hereditary cancer syndrome most likely to be relevant clinically.
items.teachingPoint: Multiple sebaceous neoplasms (adenomas, epitheliomas, carcinomas) are a hallmark cutaneous manifestation of Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome), which also predisposes to various internal malignancies, including breast, thyroid, endometrial, and colorectal cancer. While PTEN staining is typically lost in sebaceous carcinoma, it can be retained in sebaceous adenomas and sebaceomas.
items.explanationCorrect: The histologic description (mature adipocytes and foamy sebocytes, some atypia) is characteristic of a sebaceous adenoma or, given the atypia, potentially a sebaceoma (sebaceous carcinoma in situ). Sebaceous neoplasms, particularly multiple sebaceous adenomas, are strongly associated with Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome). The patient's history of early-onset colon cancer is also consistent with this syndrome, although PTEN mutations are less commonly implicated in colon cancer compared to other syndromes.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cowden syndrome is the correct answer as explained above.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyps, but not typically with sebaceous neoplasms.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is characterized by numerous colorectal adenomas and polyps, and while skin findings like epidermoid cysts and desmoid tumors can occur, sebaceous neoplasms are not a characteristic feature.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and retinal angiomas; it is not linked to sebaceous neoplasms.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B) involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas/marfanoid habitus; it has no association with sebaceous tumors.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with multiple, firm, skin-colored papules and nodules on his scalp and forehead that have been slowly enlarging over the past 10 years. The lesions are asymptomatic. On examination, there are numerous 3-10 mm, smooth, dome-shaped papules coalescing into larger plaques, particularly prominent along the hairline and extending onto the central forehead. A biopsy is performed from a representative lesion. Histopathology reveals nests of basaloid cells arranged in a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern with peripheral palisading and hyaline ring formation around keratinous cysts within the dermal component. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: The histopathologic findings are most consistent with:
items.learningObjective: Correlate an adnexal tumor pattern such as cylindroma or trichoepithelioma with the appropriate clinical diagnosis.
items.teachingPoint: Multiple cylindromas are a benign adnexal tumor characterized by specific histopathologic features including basaloid nests with peripheral palisading, a 'jigsaw puzzle' arrangement, and hyaline ring formation around keratinous cysts. This pattern distinguishes it from other adnexal tumors like trichoepithelioma or basal cell carcinoma.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of multiple, firm, skin-colored papules and nodules on the scalp and forehead in an older adult is characteristic of multiple cylindromas (also known as turban tumor when extensive). The histopathology described – nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern, and hyaline ring formation around keratinous cysts – is classic for cylindroma.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Multiple trichoepitheliomas typically present as smaller (1-3 mm), flesh-colored papules, often on the central face, and histologically show basaloid nests with horn cysts but lack the prominent hyaline rings and 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern described.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Disseminated superficial basal cell carcinoma presents as numerous small, pearly papules, often on the trunk, and histologically shows peripheral palisading of basaloid cells with retraction artifact but lacks the hyaline rings and distinct cystic structures seen in cylindroma.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Nevus sebaceus typically presents at birth or early childhood as a yellow-orange plaque on the scalp or face, becoming verrucous later. Histology shows epidermal hyperplasia, sebaceous gland hyperplasia, and apocrine differentiation, which is inconsistent with the description.

distractorExplanations.label: D

distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with multiple, firm, skin-colored papules and nodules on her scalp and forehead that have been slowly enlarging over 10 years. She has a family history of similar lesions in her mother and brother. On examination, the lesions are smooth, dome-shaped, and range from 2 mm to 1 cm in diameter. A biopsy is performed on one of the larger nodules. Histopathology reveals multiple islands of basaloid cells arranged in a jigsaw puzzle pattern, with peripheral palisading and hyaline ring formation surrounding adnexal structures resembling hair follicles and sweat ducts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Based on the clinical presentation and histopathologic findings, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Correlate an adnexal tumor pattern such as cylindroma or trichoepithelioma with the appropriate clinical diagnosis.
items.teachingPoint: Multiple trichoepitheliomas are characterized by multiple small, skin-colored papules and nodules, often on the face (especially forehead and scalp), and can be familial. Histologically, they show islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and hyaline ring formation surrounding rudimentary hair follicles and sweat ducts, often described as a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of multiple, firm, skin-colored papules and nodules on the scalp and forehead, especially with a family history, is highly suggestive of multiple trichoepitheliomas. The histopathology described – islands of basaloid cells in a jigsaw puzzle pattern with peripheral palisading and hyaline ring formation surrounding adnexal structures – is characteristic of trichoepithelioma. While Brooke-Spiegler syndrome involves cylindromas, the classic histology for cylindroma features eosinophilic hyaline rings surrounding ductal structures, not the described pattern.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Multiple trichoepitheliomas: This is the correct answer as the clinical presentation (multiple papules/nodules on scalp/forehead, family history) and classic histology (jigsaw puzzle basaloid islands, peripheral palisading, hyaline rings around adnexal structures) match.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Multiple cylindromas (Brooke-Spiegler syndrome): While Brooke-Spiegler syndrome involves multiple adnexal tumors including cylindromas, the described histology is not typical for cylindroma. Cylindromas typically show islands of basaloid cells with hyaline rings surrounding ductal structures, often in a 'drop-like' pattern, not the jigsaw puzzle pattern described.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Nevus sebaceus of Zoster: This presents as a yellowish, verrucous plaque, usually on the scalp, present since birth or early childhood. Histology shows epidermal hyperplasia, sebaceous gland hyperplasia, and apocrine differentiation, which does not match the description.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Disseminated superficial basal cell carcinoma: This presents as multiple small, pearly papules or nodules, often on the trunk. Histology shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, but typically lacks the prominent adnexal structures and hyaline rings described, and the clinical distribution is different.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous leiomyomatosis: This presents as multiple, firm, reddish-blue papules or nodules, often painful. Histology shows bundles of smooth muscle cells in the dermis, which is distinctly different from the basaloid proliferation described.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a chronic pruritic eruption. She reports a history of asthma and allergic rhinitis. In contrast, plaque psoriasis presents with well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale, often on extensor surfaces, and may exhibit the Auspitz sign.

Lichenification results from chronic rubbing and scratching, which is common in atopic dermatitis due to the intense pruritus. Excoriations are also more commonly seen in atopic dermatitis due to scratching.

items.teachingPoint: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a rare papulosquamous disorder characterized by diffuse erythema with fine, white scale and islands of sparing. The patient's history of atopic dermatitis may be a red herring, as PRP can occur in patients with a history of atopic disease.

distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma can present with erythroderma, but it typically has a more insidious onset and may show patches, plaques, or tumors. The clinical presentation and history are not typical for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a 10-year history of plaque psoriasis presents with widespread, thick, scaly plaques covering 12% of his body surface area. items.leadIn: Which of the following pathogenic pathways is the primary target of the newest class of biologic agents approved for plaque psoriasis?
items.learningObjective: Identify the psoriasis pathogenic pathway or biologic target most tightly linked to modern plaque-psoriasis therapy selection.
items.teachingPoint: The IL-23 pathway is the primary target of the newest class of biologic agents approved for plaque psoriasis, which include ustekinumab, guselkumab, and risankizumab. These agents target the p19 subunit of IL-23, which is crucial in the pathogenesis of psoriasis by promoting the differentiation of Th17 cells and the production of IL-17.

Given his significant comorbidities, his physician is concerned about the risks of systemic corticosteroids. Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for this patient?
items.leadIn: Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose an evidence-aligned treatment for localized bullous pemphigoid in an older adult at high risk from systemic corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: For localized bullous pemphigoid in patients at high risk from systemic corticosteroids, high-potency topical corticosteroids are the most appropriate first-line treatment to control the disease while minimizing systemic side effects.
items.explanationCorrect: Topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment is the most appropriate treatment for this patient with localized bullous pemphigoid. High-potency topical corticosteroids can effectively control the disease while minimizing the systemic side effects associated with oral corticosteroids, making them ideal for patients with significant comorbidities.

distractorExplanations.text: Oral dapsone is not typically used as a first-line treatment for bullous pemphigoid and may cause hemolytic anemia, especially in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is generally reserved for severe or refractory cases of bullous pemphigoid and is not necessary for this patient with localized disease.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Oral methotrexate is an immunosuppressive agent that is not typically used as a first-line treatment for localized bullous pemphigoid and carries its own set of potential adverse effects.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of a photosensitive rash on her face, scalp, and hands. She also reports fatigue and mild arthralgias. On examination, you note erythema and scaling on the cheeks and nose in a butterfly distribution, sparing the nasolabial folds. There are also erythematous patches and plaques on the dorsal hands with dilated follicular openings. The patient denies any history of new products or exposures.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus and allergic contact dermatitis using morphology and distribution.
items.teachingPoint: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) often presents with a characteristic butterfly rash on the face, sparing the nasolabial folds, and can be associated with systemic symptoms such as fatigue and arthralgias. The presence of dilated follicular openings (carpet tack sign) is a classic finding in cutaneous lupus.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of a photosensitive rash in a butterfly distribution, sparing the nasolabial folds, along with fatigue and arthralgias, is highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The presence of dilated follicular openings (carpet tack sign) is also a classic finding in cutaneous lupus.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis typically presents with pruritic, erythematous, and sometimes vesicular patches or plaques in areas of contact with the allergen. It does not typically present with a butterfly distribution or systemic symptoms.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatomyositis typically presents with a heliotrope rash (periorbital erythema with edema) and Gottron's papules (scaly erythematous papules over the knuckles). It is less likely to present with a butterfly distribution or systemic symptoms like fatigue and arthralgias.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Psoriasis typically presents with well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale. It does not typically present with a butterfly distribution or systemic symptoms. The distribution on the dorsal hands is less typical for psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus is the best answer as explained above.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Lichen planus typically presents with pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped papules and plaques. It does not typically present with a butterfly distribution or systemic symptoms. The morphology and distribution are not typical for lichen planus.

items.learningObjective: Differentiate dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus and allergic contact dermatitis using morphology and distribution.

items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of photosensitive rash on the face (butterfly rash), scalp (patchy alopecia), and hands, along with Raynaud's phenomenon (pain and swelling in fingers with cold exposure), is most consistent with cutaneous lupus erythematosus. The distribution and morphology of the lesions, as well as the associated symptoms, support this diagnosis.

items.explanationCorrect: Wood's light examination is the most helpful bedside test in this scenario. items.stem: A 45-year-old immigrant from Brazil presents with a 6-month history of an asymptomatic, hypopigmented plaque on the right shin. The patient reports decreased sensation within the plaque and occasional numbness in the right foot. Physical examination reveals a well-demarcated, hypopigmented plaque with induration and loss of light touch sensation. There is no regional lymphadenopathy. A punch biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with lymphocytes and a few Langhans-type giant cells. Acid-fast bacilli are identified on Fite stain.
items.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish Hansen disease from cutaneous sarcoidosis and tinea corporis in a chronic hypoesthetic plaque eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Tuberculoid leprosy (Hansen disease) is characterized by hypopigmented or erythematous plaques with induration and hypoesthesia, granulomatous inflammation, and identification of acid-fast bacilli on Fite stain. It is important to distinguish it from other granulomatous diseases like cutaneous sarcoidosis and lupus vulgaris, as well as from fungal infections like tinea corporis, due to differences in management and prognosis.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of a hypopigmented, hypoesthetic plaque with granulomatous inflammation and identification of acid-fast bacilli on Fite stain is most consistent with tuberculoid leprosy (Hansen disease). The decreased sensation and the presence of Langhans-type giant cells further support this diagnosis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a 15-year history of plaque psoriasis presents to your clinic for a follow-up visit. He has a history of multiple sclerosis and is concerned about worsening of his neurological symptoms with his current psoriasis treatment. On examination, he has stable plaque psoriasis covering 8% of his body surface area. His current medications include dimethyl fumarate for his multiple sclerosis and topical corticosteroids for his psoriasis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following systemic medications would be most appropriate to initiate for this patient's psoriasis?
items.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate medication choice or avoidance principle when treating psoriasis in a patient with demyelinating disease or heart failure risk.
items.teachingPoint: When treating psoriasis in a patient with multiple sclerosis or heart failure risk, it is important to consider the potential risks and benefits of each medication and to choose the most appropriate option. Apremilast is a good choice for this patient because it is generally well-tolerated and does not have the same risks of worsening neurological symptoms or heart failure as the other options.
items.explanationCorrect: Apremilast is the best choice for this patient because it is an oral phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor that is generally well-tolerated and does not have the same risks of worsening neurological symptoms or heart failure as the other options.

distractorExplanations.label: C

items.correctAnswerText: Referral to oncology for evaluation of the supraclavicular lymph node
items.teachingPoint: In patients with rapidly progressive acanthosis nigricans and systemic symptoms, a paraneoplastic syndrome should be suspected, and a thorough evaluation for an underlying malignancy is warranted. The presence of a palpable supraclavicular lymph node is a red flag for an underlying malignancy, and referral to oncology for further evaluation is the most appropriate next step.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of rapidly progressive acanthosis nigricans, weight loss, fatigue, subungual hemorrhages, and a palpable supraclavicular lymph node is highly suggestive of a paraneoplastic syndrome. The most appropriate next step is to refer the patient to oncology for evaluation of the supraclavicular lymph node, as this could indicate an underlying malignancy, such as lung cancer or lymphoma, which are common in patients with heavy smoking and alcohol use.

items.stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of heavy smoking presents with rapidly progressive, velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in the axillae, groin, and neck. The lesions have appeared over the past 3 months and are associated with mild pruritus. He reports unintentional weight loss of 10 pounds over the same period. Physical examination reveals thickened, hyperpigmented skin in the described areas, with no evidence of insulin resistance or other metabolic syndrome components.
items.leadIn: What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best workup step after recognizing a possible paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans is a cutaneous sign of underlying malignancy, often adenocarcinoma. Rapid diagnosis and management of the underlying malignancy are critical.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of rapidly progressive acanthosis nigricans, associated with weight loss, is highly suggestive of paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans. This condition is often associated with underlying malignancies, particularly adenocarcinoma of the lung, gastrointestinal tract, or genitourinary system. A thorough malignancy workup, including imaging and appropriate tumor markers, is essential to identify the underlying cause.

items.stem: A 3-month-old infant presents with a 2-week history of a scaly, erythematous rash involving the scalp, face, and diaper area. The rash is not itchy, and the infant has no family history of atopic diseases. The infant was born at term and has been healthy since birth. On examination, you note well-demarcated, greasy-appearing, yellowish scales on the scalp and in the skin folds of the neck and diaper area. There are no vesicles, pustules, or crusting.
items.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate infantile atopic dermatitis from seborrheic dermatitis in a young infant with eczematous rash.
items.teachingPoint: Seborrheic dermatitis in infants typically presents with greasy, yellowish scales in the skin folds and is not itchy. It is important to differentiate it from other inflammatory skin conditions to ensure appropriate management.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of a pruritic, scaling patch on his scalp with associated hair loss. On examination, you note an erythematous, scaly plaque with broken hairs and black dots. A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation confirms the diagnosis of tinea capitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the best treatment strategy for tinea capitis in a child, including household considerations.
items.teachingPoint: The mainstay of treatment for tinea capitis is oral antifungal therapy, with griseofulvin being the first-line agent. Topical treatments and adjunctive measures are important but not sufficient as standalone therapies. Additionally, household contacts and fomites should be evaluated and treated to prevent reinfection.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral griseofulvin is the first-line treatment for tinea capitis caused by Microsporum species, which is the most common cause in children. It is given at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks to ensure eradication of the infection.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy with a history of atopic dermatitis presents with a 2-day history of painful vesicular lesions on his face and hands. The lesions started as small red spots and rapidly progressed to fluid-filled blisters. He has a low-grade fever and appears irritable. His mother reports that he attends daycare and that several other children have had similar symptoms. On examination, you note grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, some of which are ruptured and crusted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate eczema coxsackium from eczema herpeticum and impetigo in an atopic child.
items.teachingPoint: Eczema coxsackium should be considered in atopic children presenting with vesicular lesions, especially in the context of a daycare outbreak. It is important to differentiate it from eczema herpeticum and impetigo, as the management and prognosis differ.
items.explanationCorrect: Eczema coxsackium is caused by coxsackievirus infection in patients with atopic dermatitis. It presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, similar to the description in the vignette. The history of daycare attendance and similar symptoms in other children supports a viral etiology.

items.leadIn: Select the best answer:
items.learningObjective: Identify the mechanistic principle of selective photothermolysis that explains why different lasers treat different lesions.
items.correctAnswerText: Selective photothermolysis relies on matching the pulse duration to the thermal relaxation time of the target chromophore.
items.teachingPoint: The key teaching point is that selective photothermolysis depends on matching the laser pulse duration to the thermal relaxation time of the target chromophore, ensuring effective lesion treatment while minimizing collateral damage.
items.explanationCorrect: This answer is correct because selective photothermolysis is based on the principle that the laser pulse duration is matched to the thermal relaxation time of the target, allowing selective heating and destruction of the lesion while sparing surrounding tissue.

options.label: A
options.text: Laser energy is absorbed by water molecules, causing rapid vaporization of the lesion.

options.label: B
options.text: The laser wavelength is chosen to match the absorption peak of melanin, ensuring selective heating of pigmented structures.

options.label: C
options.text: Selective photothermolysis relies on matching the pulse duration to the thermal relaxation time of the target chromophore.

options.label: D
options.text: Laser energy is non-selectively absorbed by all tissue components, leading to uniform heating.

options.label: E
options.text: The laser beam is focused to a point that minimizes scatter and maximizes penetration depth.

distractorExplanations.text: This distractor focuses on beam focusing rather than the timing mechanism essential for selective photothermolysis.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man underwent Mohs micrographic surgery for a basal cell carcinoma on his nose. On postoperative day 1, he presents with an expanding, tender hematoma at the surgical site. items.leadIn: Select the safest immediate next step for an expanding postoperative hematoma after dermatologic surgery.
items.learningObjective: Select the safest immediate next step for an expanding postoperative hematoma after dermatologic surgery.

items.teachingPoint: In differentiating atopic dermatitis from plaque psoriasis, flexural distribution with lichenification strongly favors AD, whereas extensor predominance, silvery scale, and well-demarcated borders favor psoriasis. Pruritus is common to both.
items.explanationCorrect: Atopic dermatitis (AD) classically favors flexural surfaces such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae, especially in adolescents and adults. While plaque psoriasis typically affects extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, and sacrum, the prominent involvement of flexural areas with lichenification and excoriations is a hallmark clinical clue strongly favoring AD. Although psoriasis can occasionally involve flexures (inverse psoriasis), it typically presents as well-demarcated, shiny erythematous patches without significant scale due to moisture, whereas AD in these areas often shows chronic lichenification and scaling from scratching.

options.text: The presence of silvery scale on the plaques

options.label: B
options.text: The distribution involving the antecubital and popliteal fossae

options.label: C
options.text: A personal history of seasonal allergic rhinitis

options.label: D
options.text: The intense pruritus associated with the lesions

options.label: E
options.text: The well-demarcated borders of the erythematous plaques

distractorExplanations.text: Silvery scale is a classic feature of plaque psoriasis, not atopic dermatitis. AD typically presents with ill-defined erythema, excoriations, and lichenification rather than thick silvery scale.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Flexural involvement with lichenification is a key discriminating feature of AD in adults.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: While a personal history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis) supports the diagnosis of AD, it is not a clinical finding on physical examination. The question asks for a discriminating *clinical* clue from the presentation that favors AD over psoriasis in this specific eruption. Furthermore, while atopy is associated with AD, it can also be present in the general population without dermatologic disease.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Intense pruritus is a hallmark of both atopic dermatitis and plaque psoriasis, making it a poor discriminating feature between the two conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Well-demarcated borders are more characteristic of plaque psoriasis. Atopic dermatitis lesions typically have ill-defined, diffuse borders.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a chronic, intensely pruritic eruption that has waxed and waned for the past 15 years. Physical examination reveals well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the extensor surfaces of his elbows and knees. However, closer inspection reveals subtle lichenification and excoriations over the flexural aspects of his wrists. His mother reports that he has had childhood asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, and his paternal grandmother suffers from similar skin complaints. Which of the following clinical features most strongly favors a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis over plaque psoriasis in this patient?
items.leadIn: Which of the following clinical features most strongly favors a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis over plaque psoriasis in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate atopic dermatitis from plaque psoriasis in a chronic pruritic eruption by identifying the discriminating clinical clues that most strongly favor atopic dermatitis.
items.teachingPoint: Flexural involvement is a key discriminating feature of atopic dermatitis in adults and older children, whereas plaque psoriasis typically favors extensor surfaces. Personal or family history of the atopic triad (atopic dermatitis, asthma, allergic rhinitis) also supports a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis.
items.explanationCorrect: While this patient presents with features classically associated with plaque psoriasis (extensor involvement, well-demarcated plaques, silvery scale), the presence of lesions in flexural areas (such as the wrists) strongly favors atopic dermatitis. Flexural involvement is a hallmark of atopic dermatitis in older children and adults, whereas plaque psoriasis predominantly affects extensor surfaces. The patient's personal history of asthma and allergic rhinitis (the atopic triad) further supports this diagnosis.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of an intensely pruritic, erythematous, scaly plaque on the volar aspect of her right wrist. She was previously diagnosed with atopic dermatitis and has used twice-daily emollients and high-potency topical corticosteroids for 8 weeks without improvement. The eruption is strictly localized to the right wrist, sparing her flexural creases and other typical atopic sites. She denies occupational exposures to chemicals or metals. Physical examination reveals a well-demarcated, lichenified plaque measuring 3 cm by 4 cm on the volar wrist. There is no evidence of secondary infection or systemic symptoms.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for recalcitrant eczematous dermatitis that is labeled 'atopic dermatitis' but remains localized, treatment-resistant, or distribution-atypical.
items.correctAnswerText: Patch testing to evaluate for allergic contact dermatitis
items.teachingPoint: Localized, treatment-resistant eczematous dermatitis with an atypical distribution for atopic dermatitis should raise suspicion for allergic contact dermatitis. Patch testing is the diagnostic gold standard and should be performed before escalating to systemic therapies or assuming refractory atopic dermatitis.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient presents with a localized, treatment-resistant eczematous plaque that is atypical for atopic dermatitis (volral wrist, sparing flexural creases). Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a common mimic of atopic dermatitis and frequently presents as localized, recalcitrant eczema. Given the failure of standard atopic dermatitis therapies (emollients and high-potency topical corticosteroids) and the atypical distribution, ruling out ACD via patch testing is the most appropriate next step. Identifying a specific allergen allows for targeted avoidance and potential resolution of the dermatitis.

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe a course of oral prednisone with a tapering dose

options.label: C
options.text: Perform patch testing to evaluate for allergic contact dermatitis

options.label: E
options.text: Apply a topical calcineurin inhibitor twice daily

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic methotrexate is a second-line systemic agent for severe, widespread atopic dermatitis or psoriasis. It is not indicated for a localized plaque that has not yet been fully evaluated for other causes like ACD. Escalating to systemic immunosuppression without a confirmed diagnosis is inappropriate.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Oral prednisone may provide temporary relief for acute flares of eczema but is not a long-term solution. It does not address the underlying cause of localized, treatment-resistant dermatitis and carries significant systemic side effects with prolonged use. It does not replace the need for diagnostic evaluation.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Patch testing is the correct next step. (See explanation_correct)

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Oral cyclosporine is a potent immunosuppressant used for severe, refractory atopic dermatitis. Like methotrexate, it is reserved for widespread disease after other treatments fail and is not appropriate as a next step for a localized lesion where the diagnosis itself (ACD vs. AD) remains uncertain.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are effective for atopic dermatitis and can be used as steroid-sparing agents. However, if the patient has already failed high-potency topical corticosteroids and the distribution is atypical, switching to another topical anti-inflammatory without ruling out ACD is unlikely to be effective and delays appropriate diagnostic testing.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for a chronic, pruritic rash on her left sole that has persisted for 8 months. She was previously diagnosed with atopic dermatitis and treated with potent topical corticosteroids and emollients without improvement. The eruption is strictly localized to the lateral aspect of her left foot, sparing the right foot and all other areas. Physical examination reveals well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques with mild lichenification. There is no history of psoriasis or fungal infection in her family.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for recalcitrant eczematous dermatitis that is labeled 'atopic dermatitis' but remains localized, treatment-resistant, or distribution-atypical.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform a KOH preparation and fungal culture
items.teachingPoint: Unilateral, treatment-resistant scaly plaques on the feet in a patient with atopic dermatitis should prompt evaluation for tinea pedis (KOH prep/culture) before escalating therapy, as the distribution is atypical for eczema and fungal infections can mimic or coexist with inflammatory dermatoses.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is B. While the patient has a history of atopic dermatitis, the strictly unilateral, localized nature of the eruption on the sole is highly atypical for atopic dermatitis. Unilateral, treatment-resistant scaly plaques on the feet should always raise suspicion for tinea pedis (dermatophytosis), even in patients with a known history of eczema. A KOH preparation and fungal culture are the most appropriate next steps to rule out a superficial fungal infection before escalating immunosuppressive therapy or pursuing other systemic treatments. Missing this diagnosis could lead to inappropriate treatment and worsening of the condition.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform a KOH preparation and fungal culture

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Oral terbinafine is an appropriate treatment for confirmed tinea pedis, but it should not be initiated empirically without first confirming the diagnosis via microscopy and/or culture, especially in a recalcitrant case where differential diagnoses are broad.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. See explanation for correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Oral cyclosporine is a potent systemic immunosuppressant reserved for severe, widespread atopic dermatitis or other inflammatory conditions that have failed multiple topical and systemic therapies. It is inappropriate here given the localized nature of the disease and the high suspicion for an infectious etiology.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Calcipotriene is a vitamin D analog used primarily for plaque psoriasis. While psoriasis can present with scaly plaques, the distribution and history make a fungal infection more likely. Treating empirically with a psoriasis medication without ruling out tinea could mask the infection or worsen it (tinea incognito).

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Discontinuing topical steroids and observing is not appropriate for a symptomatic, chronic rash that has already failed first-line therapy. Furthermore, abrupt cessation of potent topical steroids can sometimes cause a rebound flare or perioral/perifacial dermatitis if used on the face, though less relevant here. Observation does not address the likely underlying infectious cause.

items.stem: A 24-year-old healthy male presents with a two-week history of an itchy rash. The eruption began 10 days ago on his trunk as a single, asymptomatic, 4-cm erythematous plaque with a fine collarette of scale at the periphery. Two days later, multiple smaller, 1- to 2-cm oval erythematous plaques with similar peripheral scaling appeared on his trunk and proximal extremities in a 'Christmas tree' distribution. He denies recent medication changes, fever, or mucosal involvement.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish pityriasis rosea from secondary syphilis and morbilliform drug eruption in a generalized papulosquamous eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Pityriasis rosea is distinguished from secondary syphilis and drug eruptions by the presence of a herald patch, a 'Christmas tree' distribution along skin cleavage lines, sparing of the palms and soles, and absence of mucosal involvement or recent medication changes.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for pityriasis rosea. The initial large, asymptomatic plaque with peripheral scaling represents the herald patch. This is followed days later by a generalized eruption of smaller, oval plaques arranged along the skin cleavage lines (Langer's lines), creating a characteristic 'Christmas tree' pattern on the back. The absence of mucosal involvement and recent medication use further supports this self-limited viral-associated exanthem.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Secondary syphilis can present with a generalized papulosquamous eruption, but it typically involves the palms and soles (which are spared here), often includes mucous patches, and lacks a herald patch or a 'Christmas tree' distribution. A serologic test for syphilis would be negative in pityriasis rosea.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Pityriasis rosea is characterized by a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption along skin cleavage lines.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Morbilliform drug eruptions are typically symmetric, pruritic, and maculopapular. They occur 1-2 weeks after starting a new medication (which this patient denies) and do not feature a herald patch or the specific peripheral scaling seen in pityriasis rosea.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Guttate psoriasis presents with numerous small, discrete, salmon-pink papules and plaques covered by silvery scale, typically following a streptococcal pharyngitis. It lacks the herald patch and the specific distribution pattern of pityriasis rosea.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis typically presents as annular, erythematous plaques with a raised, scaly border and central clearing. It is usually localized or asymmetric and does not follow the generalized 'Christmas tree' distribution of pityriasis rosea.

judgeRuns.globalComment: This is a high-quality, well-constructed board-style question. It provides sufficient clinical clues to allow for a definitive diagnosis while requiring the examinee to differentiate between common differentials.

items.stem: A 24-year-old previously healthy man presents with a 1-week history of an itchy rash that began on his trunk and spread to his proximal extremities. Two weeks prior, he noticed a single, asymptomatic, 4-cm salmon-colored plaque on his back with a collarette of scale that he ignored. The current eruption consists of numerous smaller, oval, salmon-colored patches and plaques with peripheral scaling. The long axes of these lesions are oriented parallel to the skin tension lines on his back, creating a "Christmas tree" pattern. He denies recent medication changes, systemic symptoms, or sick contacts.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish pityriasis rosea from secondary syphilis and morbilliform drug eruption in a generalized papulosquamous eruption.
items.teachingPoint: The presence of a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption of oval, salmon-colored patches with peripheral scaling oriented along skin tension lines (Christmas tree distribution) is diagnostic of pityriasis rosea and helps distinguish it from secondary syphilis, drug eruptions, and other papulosquamous disorders.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for pityriasis rosea. The initial lesion described is the herald patch, which precedes the generalized eruption by 1 to 2 weeks. The secondary eruption typically consists of multiple oval, salmon-colored patches with a fine peripheral scale (collarette) that align along the cleavage lines of the skin, often described as a "Christmas tree" distribution. This condition is typically self-limited and does not require specific treatment beyond symptomatic care for pruritus.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Secondary syphilis can present with a generalized papulosquamous eruption and is an important differential diagnosis. However, it typically involves the palms and soles, lacks a herald patch or Christmas tree distribution, and is often asymptomatic. The presence of the herald patch and specific orientation on the back strongly favors pityriasis rosea.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Pityriasis rosea matches the herald patch, Christmas tree distribution, and timeline described.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: A morbilliform drug eruption typically presents with symmetric, pruritic macules and papules that coalesce. It requires a history of new medication use (usually within 1-2 weeks of onset) and lacks the herald patch and specific orientation on the cleavage lines seen in this patient.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Nummular eczema presents with coin-shaped, intensely pruritic, exudative or crusted plaques. It typically affects the extremities more than the trunk and does not feature a herald patch or a Christmas tree distribution.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Guttate psoriasis presents with numerous small, drop-like (guttate), erythematous papules and plaques with silvery scale, often following a streptococcal pharyngitis. It lacks the herald patch and does not typically align along skin tension lines in a Christmas tree pattern.

judgeRuns.globalComment: This is an excellent, high-quality board-style question. items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of his worsening skin condition. He has a 10-year history of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, characterized by thick, erythematous plaques with silvery scale covering 25% of his total body surface area, primarily on his extensor surfaces and scalp. He has failed multiple topical therapies including high-potency corticosteroids and vitamin D analogs. His past medical history is significant for Crohn disease, diagnosed 5 years ago, which is currently well-controlled with infliximab. He reports that his psoriasis has been increasingly refractory to topical treatments and is significantly impacting his quality of life. He asks about starting systemic therapy for his psoriasis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Select the best systemic option for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in a patient with concomitant inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: In patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and concomitant inflammatory bowel disease, ustekinumab is a preferred systemic therapy because it targets the IL-12/IL-23 pathway, which is implicated in the pathogenesis of both conditions. This allows for simultaneous control of both dermatologic and gastrointestinal manifestations, avoiding the potential exacerbation of IBD associated with IL-17 inhibitors.
items.explanationCorrect: Ustekinumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the p40 subunit of interleukin (IL)-12 and IL-23. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of both moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and Crohn disease. Given that this patient has concomitant inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), ustekinumab is the optimal systemic choice as it effectively treats both conditions simultaneously, addressing his refractory psoriasis while maintaining control of his Crohn disease.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of intensely pruritic, coin-shaped lesions on his lower legs. The lesions are typically more exudative and crusted than psoriatic plaques, which usually feature thick silvery scale and are located on extensor surfaces.

items.teachingPoint: Nummular dermatitis is characterized by coin-shaped, pruritic, eczematous plaques often triggered or exacerbated by xerosis and hot showers, particularly in older adults during winter. Differentiation from tinea corporis relies on the lack of central clearing and active border, while differentiation from psoriasis involves the presence of weeping/crusting and lack of silvery scale.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of well-circumscribed, coin-shaped (nummular), pruritic, erythematous, and weeping or crusting plaques on the extremities of an older adult with background xerosis, particularly during winter months or after hot showers, is classic for nummular dermatitis. Hot water and harsh soaps disrupt the skin barrier, leading to this eczematous reaction.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis typically presents with annular plaques featuring a scaly, active border and central clearing. The absence of central clearing and the presence of uniform scaling/crusting throughout the lesion make this diagnosis unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Plaque psoriasis usually presents with thick, silvery scale on well-demarcated plaques, often located on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, or lumbosacral area. The lesions are typically less pruritic and lack the weeping or crusting seen in this patient.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer (nummular dermatitis).

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Stasis dermatitis occurs in the setting of chronic venous insufficiency and typically presents with erythema, scaling, and hyperpigmentation (hemosiderin deposition) in the medial lower legs or ankles. It is usually bilateral and associated with edema, which are not described here.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis usually corresponds to the area of exposure (e.g., clothing, plants, cosmetics) and may present with vesicles or linear arrangements. The discrete, coin-shaped plaques on the shins without a clear exposure history favor nummular dermatitis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of intensely pruritic, thickened plaques on his anterior shins. A skin biopsy confirms hypertrophic lichen planus. He has been using clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment twice daily under occlusion for 8 weeks without significant improvement in symptoms or lesion thickness. The lesions are localized to both shins, covering approximately 10% of his total body surface area. He has no history of systemic disease or liver dysfunction.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose an appropriate treatment escalation strategy for extensive hypertrophic lichen planus that has not responded to high-potency topical corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: For extensive or recalcitrant hypertrophic lichen planus that fails high-potency topical corticosteroids, systemic oral retinoids are a preferred next-line therapy. Intralesional steroids are reserved for localized lesions, and NB-UVB is often less effective than PUVA or systemic agents due to poor penetration through hyperkeratotic plaques.
items.explanationCorrect: Hypertrophic lichen planus is a challenging variant of LP that often requires aggressive therapy due to the significant epidermal hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis. When high-potency topical corticosteroids fail, systemic therapies are indicated for extensive or recalcitrant disease. Systemic oral retinoids (such as acitretin or isotretinoin) are a well-established second-line treatment for hypertrophic LP, effectively reducing epidermal thickness and pruritus. Given the extent of his disease (10% TBSA) and failure of topical therapy, escalating to a systemic agent is the most appropriate next step.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Intralesional corticosteroids are excellent for localized, recalcitrant hypertrophic LP. However, this patient has extensive disease covering 10% TBSA on both shins, making intralesional injections impractical and potentially painful due to the number of required injections.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are primarily used for facial, intertriginous, or mucosal LP to avoid corticosteroid-induced atrophy. They are generally less effective for thick, hyperkeratotic plaques on the shins compared to retinoids or phototherapy.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy is a valid treatment for classic LP, but hypertrophic LP often responds poorly to NB-UVB due to the thick stratum corneum limiting light penetration. Psoralen plus UVA (PUVA) is preferred over NB-UVB for hypertrophic variants if phototherapy is chosen, but systemic retinoids are a more direct and reliable escalation for extensive disease.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Topical keratolytics (e.g., salicylic acid) can help reduce hyperkeratosis and improve the penetration of topical steroids. However, since high-potency steroids with occlusion have already failed, keratolytics alone are insufficient as a standalone escalation strategy for extensive hypertrophic LP.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of intensely pruritic, thickened plaques on his shins. Physical examination reveals well-demarcated, violaceous, hyperkeratotic plaques measuring 3 to 5 cm in diameter on both anterior lower legs. A punch biopsy confirms hypertrophic lichen planus. The patient has been applying clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment twice daily under occlusion for 8 weeks without significant improvement in pruritus or plaque thickness. He has no history of liver disease, diabetes, or hypertension.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

First-line therapy typically involves high-potency topical corticosteroids, often under occlusion. When extensive or recalcitrant disease fails to respond to optimized topical therapy, systemic agents are indicated. Oral methotrexate is a well-established first-line systemic treatment for widespread or severe hypertrophic lichen planus due to its efficacy and favorable safety profile compared to other systemic options. It effectively reduces inflammation and pruritus.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for diffuse, painful redness and scaling involving nearly his entire body. He has a 15-year history of plaque psoriasis but stopped treatment two weeks ago due to cost. He reports chills, fatigue, and a 10-pound weight loss over the past month. On examination, his skin is diffusely erythematous and scaly with mild facial edema. Vital signs show a temperature of 37.8°C (100°F), heart rate of 105/min, and blood pressure of 95/60 mmHg. Laboratory studies reveal mild leukocytosis and hypoalbuminemia.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Manage erythrodermic psoriasis by identifying the safest immediate disposition and first-line stabilization strategy.
items.correctAnswerText: Admit to the hospital for intravenous hydration and topical emollients
items.teachingPoint: Erythrodermic psoriasis requires immediate hospital admission for fluid resuscitation and topical therapy. Systemic corticosteroids are generally contraindicated due to the risk of rebound pustular psoriasis upon withdrawal.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient presents with erythrodermic psoriasis, a severe and potentially life-threatening complication characterized by diffuse erythema and scaling involving >90% of the body surface area. The loss of skin barrier function leads to significant transcutaneous fluid and protein loss, resulting in hypovolemia, hypoalbuminemia, and high-output cardiac failure. The immediate priority is hospital admission for stabilization, which includes aggressive intravenous hydration to correct fluid deficits and the application of topical emollients (often with mild corticosteroids) to restore barrier function and reduce inflammation. Systemic corticosteroids are generally avoided due to the risk of precipitating a severe flare or pustular psoriasis upon withdrawal.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to worsening redness and peeling of his skin over 2 weeks. He has a known history of plaque psoriasis but has been nonadherent to his topical therapies for several months. He reports fatigue, chills, and subjective fevers but denies new medication use or recent infections. On examination, he is diaphoretic and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min). His entire body surface area is diffusely erythematous and covered with fine, white scaling. There are scattered areas of superficial desquamation but no frank pustules or bullae. Laboratory studies reveal mild leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and hypoalbuminemia. His blood pressure is 108/65 mm Hg.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Manage erythrodermic psoriasis by identifying the safest immediate disposition and first-line stabilization strategy.
items.correctAnswerText: Admit to a burn unit or intensive care setting for aggressive fluid resuscitation and supportive care
items.teachingPoint: Erythrodermic psoriasis is a dermatologic emergency characterized by >90% body surface area erythema and scaling, leading to significant transcutaneous fluid loss, thermoregulatory failure, and high-output cardiac strain. The immediate priority is admission to a burn unit or intensive care setting for aggressive supportive care, including fluid resuscitation and hemodynamic monitoring. Specific systemic therapies should be initiated only after the patient is stabilized.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient presents with erythrodermic psoriasis, a severe and potentially life-threatening inflammatory skin condition characterized by generalized erythema and scaling involving >90% of the body surface area. The most critical immediate management step is recognizing the hemodynamic and metabolic instability associated with erythroderma. Extensive cutaneous inflammation leads to massive vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and profound fluid/protein loss through the skin barrier, mimicking a burn injury. Patients often develop high-output cardiac failure, hypothermia, and electrolyte imbalances. Therefore, the safest immediate disposition is admission to a specialized setting such as a burn unit or intensive care unit where aggressive fluid resuscitation, thermoregulation, and close hemodynamic monitoring can be provided. Supportive care is the cornerstone of initial stabilization before initiating specific systemic therapies.

This is the safest initial disposition to stabilize the patient before specific antipsoriatic therapy is considered.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of an intensely pruritic, scaly eruption that began on his face and neck before spreading to his trunk and extremities. Despite high-potency topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines, the rash has worsened. Examination reveals diffuse erythema with overlying fine, white scales. Notably, there are islands of sparing around the mouth and eyes. On his palms, there is marked hyperkeratosis with orange-brown discoloration and sharp demarcation at the wrist. Follicular hyperkeratotic papules are scattered across his extensor surfaces, coalescing into plaques with a characteristic orange-brown hue. Skin biopsy demonstrates alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in both vertical and horizontal directions, along with follicular plugging and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish pityriasis rubra pilaris from erythrodermic psoriasis and chronic eczematous dermatitis in a difficult papulosquamous case.
items.teachingPoint: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is distinguished from erythrodermic psoriasis and chronic eczematous dermatitis by its clinical features (follicular hyperkeratotic papules, orange-brown discoloration, islands of sparing, palmoplantar keratoderma with sharp demarcation) and pathognomonic histology (alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in vertical and horizontal directions, i.e., checkerboard pattern).
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of follicular hyperkeratotic papules, orange-brown discoloration, palmoplantar keratoderma with sharp demarcation, and islands of sparing is classic for pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP). The histologic finding of alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in both vertical (checkerboard) and horizontal directions is pathognomonic for PRP. These features reliably distinguish it from other papulosquamous disorders.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erythrodermic psoriasis typically presents with well-demarcated erythema and thick, silvery scales. While it can cause diffuse redness and scaling, it lacks the characteristic follicular papules, orange-brown hue, islands of sparing, and palmoplantar keratoderma with sharp demarcation seen in PRP. Histology would show regular acanthosis, thinning of the suprapapillary plates, and parakeratosis with neutrophils (Munro microabscesses).

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Chronic eczematous dermatitis can present with erythema, scaling, and pruritus. However, it typically lacks the follicular hyperkeratotic papules, orange-brown discoloration, islands of sparing, and the specific palmoplantar findings described. Histology would show spongiosis (intercellular edema), which is absent in this case.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Sezary syndrome is a leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presenting with erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating atypical T-cells (Sezary cells). While it can cause erythroderma and scaling, it does not typically present with follicular papules, islands of sparing, or the specific histologic findings of alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis. Pruritus is common, but the clinical and histologic features point elsewhere.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), particularly mycosis fungoides, can present with patches, plaques, and tumors. Erythrodermic CTCL is a possibility in erythroderma cases, but it typically lacks the follicular papules, islands of sparing, and orange-brown keratoderma. Histology would show epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes, Pautrier microabscesses, and cerebriform nuclei.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Sezary syndrome is a leukemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presenting with erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating atypical T-cells (Sezary cells). While it can cause erythroderma and scaling, it does not typically present with follicular papules, islands of sparing, or the specific histologic findings of alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis. Pruritus is common, but the clinical and histologic features point elsewhere.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents for follow-up of a chronic, pruritic rash involving her upper and lower eyelids. She was previously treated with triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% cream twice daily for two weeks, which provided excellent clearance. However, she is concerned about the potential side effects of prolonged topical corticosteroid use on her thin eyelid skin, such as skin atrophy and telangiectasias. She has had multiple recurrences over the past year, requiring intermittent steroid courses for flares. items.explanationCorrect: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs), such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, are FDA-approved for the short-term and noncontinuous chronic management of atopic dermatitis. They are particularly useful as maintenance therapy for sensitive areas like the eyelids, face, and intertriginous regions because they do not cause skin atrophy or carry the risk of steroid-induced glaucoma and cataracts. Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment is effective for controlling inflammation and pruritus in chronic eyelid dermatitis while avoiding the adverse effects associated with prolonged topical corticosteroid use.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered by silvery scale on his elbows and knees. He has no joint pain or nail pitting. Skin biopsy reveals marked epidermal hyperplasia, confluent parakeratosis, and neutrophilic microabscesses in the stratum corneum. Dermoscopy shows dotted vessels on a pink background with white scales. The patient is being evaluated for systemic therapy due to extensive disease burden (>10% BSA). Which of the following pathogenic mechanisms is most directly targeted by first-line biologic agents for this condition?
items.leadIn: Which of the following pathogenic mechanisms is most directly targeted by first-line biologic agents for this condition?
items.learningObjective: Identify the psoriasis pathogenic pathway or biologic target most tightly linked to modern plaque-psoriasis therapy selection.
items.correctAnswerText: Inhibition of interleukin-12 and interleukin-23 to modulate Th17 cell differentiation
items.teachingPoint: The pathogenesis of plaque psoriasis is primarily driven by the IL-23/Th17 axis. First-line biologic therapies increasingly target IL-23 (e.g., guselkumab, risankizumab) to achieve high rates of clearance by interrupting the upstream cytokine driver.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is C. Psoriasis is primarily driven by the Th17 pathway, with interleukin-23 (IL-23) playing a central role in the survival, expansion, and maintenance of pathogenic Th17 cells. First-line biologic therapies for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, such as guselkumab, risankizumab, and tildrakizumab, are monoclonal antibodies that specifically target the p19 subunit of IL-23. This targeted approach effectively interrupts the cytokine cascade that leads to keratinocyte hyperproliferation and inflammation, resulting in high rates of complete or near-complete clearance. While IL-17 inhibitors are also first-line, the question asks for the pathogenic mechanism most tightly linked to modern therapy selection, and IL-23 inhibition represents a highly specific upstream target in the psoriasis pathway.

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibition of interleukin-17A and its downstream signaling cascade

options.label: B
options.text: Neutralization of tumor necrosis factor-alpha to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine release

options.label: C
options.text: Inhibition of interleukin-12 and interleukin-23 to modulate Th17 cell differentiation

options.label: D
options.text: Blocking of CD52 to deplete circulating and tissue-infiltrating T lymphocytes

options.label: E
options.text: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-4 to reduce intracellular cAMP degradation

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Inhibition of interleukin-17A (e.g., secukinumab, ixekizumab) is indeed a first-line biologic strategy for plaque psoriasis. However, IL-23 inhibition (Option C) is considered more upstream in the pathogenic cascade. By targeting IL-23, these agents prevent the initial differentiation and maintenance of Th17 cells, which then produce IL-17A. Therefore, IL-23 inhibition is often viewed as a more fundamental interruption of the disease pathway.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) inhibitors (e.g., adalimumab, etanercept) were among the first biologics approved for psoriasis. While effective and still used, particularly in patients with comorbid inflammatory bowel disease or psoriatic arthritis, they are not the most specific agents for the Th17-driven pathogenesis of plaque psoriasis. TNF-α inhibitors have a broader immunosuppressive profile and are generally considered after or alongside IL-23/IL-17 inhibitors in the treatment algorithm for isolated plaque psoriasis.
