distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Alemtuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against CD52, used in multiple sclerosis and certain leukemias. It causes profound lymphocyte depletion and is not indicated for psoriasis due to its significant safety profile, including risk of opportunistic infections and secondary malignancies. It does not target the specific Th17 pathway central to psoriasis pathogenesis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitors, such as crisaborole, are used for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis and sometimes off-label for psoriasis. They work by increasing intracellular cAMP, which reduces inflammation. However, they are not first-line systemic biologics for extensive plaque psoriasis and do not target the IL-23/Th17 axis.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of persistent, well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery scales on his extensor surfaces and scalp. He has failed topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogs. A biopsy reveals marked epidermal hyperplasia, confluent parakeratosis with neutrophilic microabscesses in the stratum corneum, and dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae. Flow cytometry of lesional skin T-cells demonstrates a distinct upregulation of the transcription factor RORγt and increased production of IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-23 compared to lesional skin from a patient with chronic plaque eczema. In selecting a targeted biologic therapy, which of the following pathogenic mechanisms is most directly implicated in the maintenance and amplification of this specific cytokine cascade?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate biologic target to address the underlying pathogenic cascade in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Identify the psoriasis pathogenic pathway or biologic target most tightly linked to modern plaque-psoriasis therapy selection.
items.teachingPoint: Modern biologic therapy for plaque psoriasis increasingly targets the IL-23/Th17 axis. Interleukin-23 (IL-23) is the upstream driver that maintains Th17 cell populations and subsequent production of IL-17A, IL-17F, and other inflammatory cytokines. Selecting an agent targeting the IL-23 p19 subunit provides specific blockade of this pathogenic cascade, leading to sustained clearance and remission in plaque psoriasis.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is Interleukin-23 p19 subunit inhibition. The vignette describes classic plaque psoriasis with a specific immunologic profile highlighting the IL-23/Th17 axis. Interleukin-23 (IL-23) is a key cytokine produced by antigen-presenting cells that drives the differentiation and maintenance of Th17 cells, which in turn produce IL-17A, IL-17F, and other inflammatory mediators. While IL-17 inhibitors are highly effective, IL-23 acts upstream in this pathway, making it a critical target for long-term disease modulation and clearance. Targeting the p19 subunit of IL-23 specifically blocks this upstream driver without affecting other cytokines sharing the p40 subunit.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Interleukin-17A inhibition is a valid and highly effective treatment for plaque psoriasis. However, IL-23 acts upstream of IL-17A in the pathogenic cascade. Targeting IL-23 is often considered more comprehensive for modulating the entire Th17 pathway and maintaining long-term remission, as it prevents the initial drive of IL-17 production. While both are correct therapeutic targets, IL-23 inhibition is more tightly linked to the upstream pathogenic mechanism described (IL-23 driving IL-17 production).

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) inhibition is effective for psoriasis but acts through a different pathway. TNF-α contributes to inflammation and angiogenesis but does not directly drive the specific IL-23/Th17 axis highlighted in the vignette. It is a broader anti-inflammatory target rather than one specific to the RORγt/IL-23/IL-17 cascade.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Interleukin-12/23 p40 subunit inhibition targets both IL-12 and IL-23, as they share the p40 subunit. While effective, it is less specific than targeting the IL-23 p19 subunit alone. The vignette emphasizes the IL-23/Th17 axis; therefore, a more specific agent (anti-p19) is the superior choice for targeting this precise pathway without affecting IL-12-dependent Th1 responses.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Interleukin-23 p19 subunit inhibition is the correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibition reduces inflammation by increasing intracellular cAMP levels, leading to decreased production of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines. It is a broader mechanism and does not specifically target the IL-23/Th17 axis. PDE-4 inhibitors are typically used as topical or oral small molecules rather than targeted biologics for this specific pathway.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of intensely pruritic, tense blisters on his trunk and extremities. He reports that the lesions began as erythematous urticarial plaques before developing into blisters. Examination reveals multiple intact bullae on an erythematous base, with scattered erosions where blisters have ruptured. There is no oral mucosal involvement. Direct immunofluorescence of a perilesional skin biopsy demonstrates linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris in a subepidermal-versus-intraepidermal blistering presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense blisters, pruritus, lack of mucosal involvement, and linear IgG/C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence. Pemphigus vulgaris is distinguished by flaccid blisters, frequent mucosal involvement, and intercellular IgG deposition within the epidermis.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of tense blisters on an erythematous base without mucosal involvement, combined with the characteristic direct immunofluorescence finding of linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone, is diagnostic for bullous pemphigoid. The intensely pruritic prodrome with urticarial plaques is also highly characteristic of this subepidermal autoimmune blistering disease.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Pemphigus vulgaris typically presents with flaccid blisters that rupture easily, leaving painful erosions. Mucosal involvement is almost universal. Direct immunofluorescence shows a reticular or 'chicken-wire' pattern of IgG deposition within the epidermis (intercellular space), not along the basement membrane.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense blisters, often preceded by pruritic urticarial plaques. It spares the mucous membranes in most cases and shows linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane zone.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks) and is associated with celiac disease. Direct immunofluorescence reveals granular IgA deposition in the dermal papillae, not linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita can clinically mimic bullous pemphigoid with tense blisters, but it typically involves trauma-prone areas (hands, feet) and may show scarring or milia. Direct immunofluorescence is similar to bullous pemphigoid, but salt-split skin testing would show binding on the floor (dermal side), whereas bullous pemphigoid binds to the roof (epidermal side). The classic presentation described here is more typical of bullous pemphigoid.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis features tense blisters and vesicles, often in a 'cluster of jewels' arrangement. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane zone, not IgG and C3.

items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris in a subepidermal-versus-intraepidermal blistering presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense bullae, intense pruritus, lack of mucosal involvement, subepidermal blistering (absence of intraepidermal split), and linear IgG/C3 deposition at the basement membrane zone. items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of intensely pruritic, tense bullae on an erythematous base without mucosal involvement is highly characteristic of bullous pemphigoid. Histologically, bullous pemphigoid features a subepidermal blister (intraepidermal split is absent). Direct immunofluorescence typically shows linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Pemphigus vulgaris typically presents with flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving painful erosions and frequent mucosal involvement. items.stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with a two-week history of painful oral ulcers that have progressed to erosions, making it difficult for her to eat or drink. She reports a new onset of widespread, fragile blisters on her trunk and extremities that rupture easily. Physical examination reveals scattered flaccid bullae with positive Nikolsky sign on the trunk and diffuse erythematous erosions covering her buccal mucosa. She appears lethargic and has dry mucous membranes with a heart rate of 105 beats per minute. items.teachingPoint: In patients with suspected pemphigus vulgaris presenting with severe mucosal involvement and inability to tolerate oral intake, immediate management must prioritize intravenous fluid resuscitation for dehydration while simultaneously obtaining diagnostic biopsies to confirm the diagnosis and initiate systemic immunosuppression.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of fragile blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, and severe mucosal erosions is highly suggestive of pemphigus vulgaris. The immediate priority in a patient who cannot tolerate oral intake due to severe mucosal disease is correcting dehydration and maintaining hemodynamic stability through intravenous fluid resuscitation. Concurrently, obtaining a biopsy for routine histology and direct immunofluorescence is essential to confirm the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris, which requires prompt initiation of systemic immunosuppressive therapy (such as corticosteroids and rituximab) to prevent further progression and complications. Biopsy of a perilesional blister is the gold standard for diagnosis.

items.explanationCorrect: This patient’s clinical presentation is classic for dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), an autoimmune blistering disease strongly associated with celiac disease. DH is characterized by the deposition of IgA immune complexes at the tips of the dermal papillae, which is best demonstrated by direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of perilesional skin. This finding distinguishes DH from other immunobullous disorders and is considered the diagnostic gold standard.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a pruritic, grouped vesicular rash on his extensor elbows and knees. He reports recent episodes of chronic diarrhea and bloating. Skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blisters with numerous neutrophils forming microabscesses at the tips of the dermal papillae. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is performed to confirm the diagnosis. Which of the following findings would most likely be observed on DIF?
items.leadIn: Which of the following findings would most likely be observed on direct immunofluorescence?
items.learningObjective: Recognize the key immunopathologic finding that distinguishes dermatitis herpetiformis from other immunobullous disorders.
items.correctAnswerText: Granular deposition of IgA at the dermal papillae tips
items.teachingPoint: Dermatitis herpetiformis is distinguished by granular IgA deposition at the dermal papillae tips on direct immunofluorescence, correlating with its pathogenesis involving IgA autoantibodies against epidermal transglutaminase and its strong association with celiac disease.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient's clinical presentation (pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces, associated gastrointestinal symptoms) and histology (subepidermal blisters with neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae) are classic for dermatitis herpetiformis (DH). DH is strongly associated with celiac disease. The hallmark immunopathologic finding on direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is granular deposition of IgA at the tips of the dermal papillae in approximately 90-100% of cases. This distinguishes DH from other subepidermal blistering diseases like bullous pemphigoid, which typically shows linear IgG and/or C3 along the basement membrane zone.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Linear deposition of IgG along the basement membrane zone is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid, not dermatitis herpetiformis. Bullous pemphigoid typically presents with tense bullae on the trunk and flexural areas in elderly patients, without the specific neutrophilic papillary microabscesses or gluten sensitivity seen in DH.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Granular deposition of IgA at the dermal papillae tips is the correct finding for dermatitis herpetiformis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Linear deposition of C3 along the basement membrane zone can be seen in bullous pemphigoid or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, but it is not the primary diagnostic feature of DH. While C3 may be present in DH, IgA deposition is the defining and most specific finding.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Granular deposition of IgG in the epidermis (intercellular spaces) is characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris, an intraepidermal blistering disease caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins. Pemphigus vulgaris presents with flaccid blisters and positive Nikolsky sign, not subepidermal blisters.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Linear deposition of fibrinogen along the basement membrane zone is a nonspecific finding that can be seen in many subepidermal blistering diseases and even some inflammatory dermatoses. It is not specific for diagnosing dermatitis herpetiformis.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of intensely pruritic, tense bullae on erythematous bases confined to the flexural aspects of his upper extremities. He has a history of severe congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, recent osteoporotic fractures, and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. A skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. Given his comorbidities, systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose an evidence-aligned treatment for localized bullous pemphigoid in an older adult at high risk from systemic corticosteroids.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate high-potency topical clobetasol propionate ointment twice daily
items.teachingPoint: High-potency topical corticosteroids are the first-line treatment for localized bullous pemphigoid and should be preferred over systemic therapies in elderly patients with significant comorbidities to minimize adverse effects.
items.explanationCorrect: High-potency topical corticosteroids (e.g., clobetasol propionate) are considered first-line therapy for localized bullous pemphigoid. This approach provides effective disease control while avoiding the significant systemic adverse effects associated with oral corticosteroids, such as worsening heart failure, hyperglycemia, and bone loss. For limited disease burden, topical therapy is highly effective and preferred in patients with significant comorbidities.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of an itchy, erythematous rash on her face and neck that worsens with sun exposure. Physical examination reveals a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, along with discrete scaly papules on her extensor forearms. A punch biopsy of a forearm lesion demonstrates interface dermatitis with basal layer vacuolization, a thickened basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence (lupus band test), and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. The patient reports no joint pain, oral ulcers, chest pain, or fever.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best evaluation step when cutaneous lupus erythematosus is newly diagnosed and systemic disease has not yet been assessed.
items.correctAnswerText: Order a comprehensive metabolic panel and urinalysis with protein-to-creatinine ratio
items.teachingPoint: Upon diagnosis of cutaneous lupus erythematosus, clinicians must screen for subclinical systemic involvement (SLE). Initial evaluation should include a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis with protein-to-creatinine ratio, and autoantibody testing (ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA), even in asymptomatic patients.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient has newly diagnosed cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE). Even in the absence of systemic symptoms, it is essential to screen for subclinical or early systemic involvement (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, SLE). Renal disease is a major cause of morbidity in SLE and can be asymptomatic initially. A comprehensive metabolic panel (to assess renal function) and a urinalysis with protein-to-creatinine ratio are the most appropriate, high-yield initial screening tests for lupus nephritis.

options.label: B
options.text: Order a comprehensive metabolic panel and urinalysis with protein-to-creatinine ratio

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe high-potency topical corticosteroids and advise strict sun avoidance

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a bone marrow biopsy to evaluate for cytopenias

options.label: E
options.text: Order an echocardiogram to assess for pericardial effusion

items.teachingPoint: All patients with a new diagnosis of cutaneous lupus erythematosus should undergo baseline screening for systemic involvement, including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis, regardless of the absence of systemic symptoms.
items.explanationCorrect: Even in the absence of systemic symptoms, patients newly diagnosed with cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) require baseline screening for asymptomatic systemic involvement. A complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis are essential to evaluate for hematologic abnormalities (e.g., cytopenias), renal dysfunction, and proteinuria, which may indicate early systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Identifying subclinical disease alters management and prognosis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a persistent rash on her face, hands, and chest that has worsened over the past 3 months. She reports significant fatigue and proximal muscle weakness, noting difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair. Examination reveals violaceous papules over the dorsal interphalangeal joints (Gottron papules), a heliotrope rash with periorbital edema, and erythematous macules on the anterior chest in a V-distribution. She denies joint pain, photosensitivity-related systemic symptoms, or recent exposure to new topical products.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus and allergic contact dermatitis using morphology and distribution.
items.teachingPoint: Dermatomyositis is characterized by pathognomonic cutaneous findings such as Gottron papules and heliotrope rash, often accompanied by proximal muscle weakness. Differentiating it from cutaneous lupus erythematosus and allergic contact dermatitis relies on recognizing these specific morphological features, their distribution, and the presence of systemic muscle involvement.
items.explanationCorrect: The presence of Gottron papules (violaceous papules over the dorsal interphalangeal joints) and a heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital edema) are pathognomonic cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis. Combined with proximal muscle weakness (difficulty combing hair and rising from a chair) and fatigue, this clinical picture strongly supports the diagnosis of dermatomyositis. The V-sign on the chest is also a classic photosensitive distribution associated with this condition.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus typically presents with a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds and does not cause Gottron papules or significant proximal muscle weakness. While photosensitivity is common, the specific morphology and distribution described are not characteristic of lupus.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis usually presents with pruritic, vesicular, or eczematous plaques at sites of exposure. It does not explain the proximal muscle weakness or the pathognomonic Gottron papules and heliotrope rash seen in this patient.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatomyositis is the correct diagnosis, as explained above.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Polymorphous light eruption presents with pruritic papules, plaques, or vesicles in sun-exposed areas but lacks the specific features of Gottron papules, heliotrope rash, and proximal muscle weakness. It is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out autoimmune conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic sclerosis can cause hand changes and skin tightening, but it typically presents with sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and Raynaud phenomenon. It does not cause Gottron papules or the specific inflammatory myopathy symptoms described here.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of an intensely pruritic and photosensitive rash. Examination reveals symmetric, erythematous to violaceous papules over the dorsal aspects of her metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, which are slightly scaly. She also has a diffuse erythema on her face and neck that spares the nasolabial folds. Her proximal muscle strength is intact on examination, and she denies any recent exposure to new topical medications or plants. Laboratory studies show an elevated creatine kinase level of 210 U/L (reference range: 30-190 U/L).
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus and allergic contact dermatitis using morphology and distribution.
items.teachingPoint: Gottron papules are pathognomonic for dermatomyositis. Differentiating dermatomyositis from cutaneous lupus relies on the presence of violaceous papules over the joints and a photosensitive facial rash that spares the nasolabial folds, whereas lupus malar rashes typically involve the nasolabial folds and lack specific knuckle involvement.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for dermatomyositis, specifically the Gottron papules (violaceous, scaly papules over the MCP and IP joints) and a photosensitive facial rash that spares the nasolabial folds. Although her muscle strength is intact and CK is only mildly elevated, amyopathic dermatomyositis or early disease can present with prominent cutaneous findings before significant myopathy develops. The distribution and morphology of the lesions are highly specific for this condition.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis typically presents with acute, vesicular, and weeping plaques in areas of exposure. It does not characteristically cause violaceous papules over the joints or a photosensitive facial rash sparing the nasolabial folds.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Discoid lupus erythematosus presents with well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques that often lead to follicular plugging and central atrophy with scarring. While it can be photosensitive, the specific distribution over the knuckles (Gottron papules) is pathognomonic for dermatomyositis, not lupus.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatomyositis

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Polymorphous light eruption is a common photodermatosis characterized by pruritic papules or plaques in sun-exposed areas, but it typically spares the face and does not cause violaceous papules over the joints or elevated muscle enzymes.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause a malar rash, but this rash typically involves the nasolabial folds. Furthermore, SLE does not characteristically present with Gottron papules over the dorsal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a persistent rash. Over the past two months, she has developed an erythematous, scaly eruption on her face and upper chest that worsens with sun exposure. She also reports proximal muscle weakness, noting difficulty rising from a chair and combing her hair. Physical examination reveals an erythematous, violaceous rash on the upper eyelids with mild periorbital edema (heliotrope rash) and erythematous papules over the dorsal aspects of her metacarpophalangeal joints (Gottron papules). Serum creatine kinase is mildly elevated at 180 U/L. The dermatologist suspects dermatomyositis and orders a muscle biopsy, which confirms the diagnosis of adult-onset dermatomyositis. Given her age and new diagnosis, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the appropriate malignancy-oriented workup step for newly diagnosed adult dermatomyositis.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids and schedule a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
items.teachingPoint: Adult-onset dermatomyositis is associated with a significantly increased risk of underlying malignancy. A comprehensive age-appropriate cancer screening, including CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, should be performed at the time of diagnosis.
items.explanationCorrect: Dermatomyositis in adults is strongly associated with an underlying malignancy, particularly ovarian, lung, breast, gastrointestinal, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The risk of malignancy is highest within the first three years following diagnosis, but screening should occur at the time of initial presentation. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is a critical component of the initial malignancy workup in adult patients with dermatomyositis. Additionally, initiating high-dose systemic corticosteroids is the standard first-line treatment to control inflammation and muscle weakness. Therefore, combining immediate treatment with a comprehensive malignancy screen is the most appropriate next step.

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids and schedule a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

options.label: B
options.text: Order anti-Jo-1 antibodies to evaluate for antisynthetase syndrome and associated interstitial lung disease

options.label: C
options.text: Begin methotrexate therapy as first-line treatment and defer malignancy screening until symptoms resolve

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a comprehensive skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence to rule out lupus erythematosus

options.label: E
options.text: Refer for ophthalmologic evaluation and start topical corticosteroids to manage the cutaneous manifestations

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is essential for malignancy screening in adult dermatomyositis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with antisynthetase syndrome, which can present with dermatomyositis-like features. However, while testing for myositis-specific antibodies is useful for prognostication and identifying associated interstitial lung disease, it does not replace the immediate need for a comprehensive malignancy screen in an older adult with new-onset disease.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Methotrexate is a common steroid-sparing agent used in dermatomyositis, but it is not first-line monotherapy for acute disease. Furthermore, deferring malignancy screening until symptoms resolve is incorrect because the risk of occult malignancy must be assessed at diagnosis to guide long-term prognosis and management.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: While lupus erythematosus can cause heliotrope-like rashes, the presence of Gottron papules and proximal muscle weakness strongly points to dermatomyositis. A skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence is not the priority over malignancy screening in a patient with a clinical diagnosis of adult-onset dermatomyositis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Ophthalmologic evaluation is not a standard initial step for dermatomyositis unless there are specific visual complaints. Topical corticosteroids may help cutaneous symptoms but do not address the systemic nature of the disease or the critical need for malignancy screening.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of progressive proximal muscle weakness and a photosensitive rash on his face, neck, and upper chest. Physical examination reveals heliotrope discoloration of the eyelids with periorbital edema, Gottron papules over the knuckles, and violaceous macules on the upper chest (V-sign). Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated creatine kinase level of 1,200 U/L and positive anti-Mi-2 antibodies. Given his new diagnosis of dermatomyositis, what is the most appropriate next step in management to address potential underlying malignancy?
items.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step in management to address potential underlying malignancy?
items.learningObjective: Identify the appropriate malignancy-oriented workup step for newly diagnosed adult dermatomyositis.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform age-appropriate cancer screening, including colonoscopy and CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis
items.teachingPoint: Adult-onset dermatomyositis carries a significant risk of underlying malignancy. A comprehensive, age-appropriate cancer screening workup, including CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis in addition to standard screenings (e.g., colonoscopy), should be performed promptly upon diagnosis.
items.explanationCorrect: Dermatomyositis in adults is strongly associated with an increased risk of underlying malignancy, particularly ovarian, lung, pancreatic, gastric, colorectal, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The malignancy risk is highest within the first 3 years following diagnosis. Therefore, a thorough and immediate age-appropriate malignancy screening is indicated. This typically includes a detailed history and physical examination, basic laboratory studies, and standard cancer screenings appropriate for the patient's age and sex (e.g., colonoscopy, mammography, Pap smear) plus additional targeted imaging such as a CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to detect occult solid tumors.

options.label: A
options.text: Order a PET-CT scan of the entire body

options.label: B
options.text: Perform age-appropriate cancer screening, including colonoscopy and CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids without further workup

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain a tumor marker panel including CA-125, CEA, and AFP

options.label: E
options.text: Schedule a routine follow-up in 6 months for repeat malignancy screening

distractorExplanations.text: While PET-CT is highly sensitive and sometimes used in refractory cases or when standard screening is negative but suspicion remains high, it is not the recommended initial step due to its high cost, radiation exposure, and potential for false-positive findings. Standard age-appropriate screening and CT imaging are the established first-line approaches.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Age-appropriate screening combined with cross-sectional imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) is the standard of care for detecting occult malignancies in newly diagnosed adult dermatomyositis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Although high-dose systemic corticosteroids are the first-line treatment for the inflammatory symptoms of dermatomyositis, ignoring the high association with malignancy would be negligent. The workup for underlying cancer must occur concurrently with or prior to initiating immunosuppressive therapy, as treating the malignancy often improves the dermatomyositis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Tumor marker panels lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity to serve as a primary screening tool for occult malignancy in dermatomyositis. They are generally reserved for monitoring known cancers rather than initial diagnosis, as elevated levels can occur in benign conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Delaying malignancy screening for 6 months is inappropriate given the strong and immediate association between adult-onset dermatomyositis and cancer. Early detection of an underlying malignancy significantly improves patient prognosis, as treating the cancer often leads to improvement in the dermatomyositis symptoms.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of painful, non-blanching violaceous lesions on her lower extremities. The lesions are palpable and range from 3 to 8 mm in diameter, with some coalescing into larger plaques. She recently recovered from a mild upper respiratory infection but denies joint pain, abdominal pain, or hematuria. Physical examination reveals symmetric palpable purpura on the distal lower legs without ulceration or necrosis. A punch biopsy is performed to evaluate for small-vessel vasculitis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate biopsy strategy and expected histopathologic finding?
items.learningObjective: Correlate palpable purpura with the optimal biopsy strategy and histopathologic pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Biopsy a fresh papule or early purpuric lesion; neutrophilic infiltration with nuclear dust around postcapillary venules
items.teachingPoint: For suspected leukocytoclastic vasculitis, biopsy a fresh lesion (e.g., papule or early purpura) within 24-48 hours to capture neutrophilic infiltration and nuclear dust around postcapillary venules. Older lesions may only show nonspecific hemosiderin deposition.
items.explanationCorrect: The optimal biopsy strategy for suspected leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV) is a fresh, early lesion such as a papule or early purpuric macule, typically within the first 24 to 48 hours of appearance. Biopsying older or resolving lesions may yield nonspecific findings like hemosiderin deposition due to prior hemorrhage. Histopathologically, LCV is characterized by a neutrophilic infiltrate targeting the postcapillary venules of the superficial dermis, accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis and leukocytoclasis (nuclear dust).

options.label: A
options.text: Biopsy a necrotic ulcer; fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall

options.label: B
options.text: Biopsy a fresh papule or early purpuric lesion; neutrophilic infiltration with nuclear dust around postcapillary venules

options.label: C
options.text: Biopsy a resolving hyperpigmented macule; hemosiderin deposition in the dermis

options.label: D
options.text: Biopsy a vesicle containing clear fluid; subepidermal blister with eosinophils

options.label: E
options.text: Biopsy a tense bulla; linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane zone

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Biopsying a necrotic ulcer may show fibrinoid necrosis, but it is not the optimal site for diagnosing early LCV and may complicate wound care. Ulcers often represent a later, more destructive stage of vasculitis rather than the diagnostic early inflammatory phase.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Biopsying a fresh papule or early purpuric lesion yields the highest diagnostic yield for LCV. The histopathology will show neutrophilic infiltration with nuclear dust around postcapillary venules, confirming the diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: A resolving hyperpigmented macule primarily shows hemosiderin deposition and sparse inflammation. While consistent with prior hemorrhage, it lacks the acute inflammatory changes required to diagnose active vasculitis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: A vesicle with clear fluid and subepidermal blistering with eosinophils suggests a bullous autoimmune disease (e.g., bullous pemphigoid) or an arthropod bite reaction, not LCV.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of painful, raised purpuric lesions on her lower extremities. She reports arthralgias and mild abdominal discomfort over the past week but denies fever, hemoptysis, or hematuria. Physical examination reveals palpable purpura and urticarial plaques on the bilateral shins, with no mucosal involvement. She recently completed a 10-day course of amoxicillin for sinusitis. You plan to perform a skin biopsy to confirm the suspected diagnosis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnostic evaluation?
items.learningObjective: Correlate palpable purpura with the optimal biopsy strategy and histopathologic pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform a punch biopsy including subcutaneous fat from the edge of an early purpuric lesion
items.teachingPoint: For suspected leukocytoclastic vasculitis presenting as palpable purpura, the diagnostic standard is a deep punch biopsy extending into the subcutaneous fat taken from an early lesion (24-48 hours old) to visualize neutrophilic vasculitis, fibrinoid necrosis, and leukocytoclasis in small vessels.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of palpable purpura, arthralgias, and recent antibiotic use is highly suggestive of leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV), likely cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis secondary to a drug reaction. The optimal biopsy strategy for suspected LCV involves a punch biopsy that extends into the subcutaneous fat to evaluate the deep dermis and subcutis, where small vessels are located. The biopsy should be taken from an early lesion (within 24-48 hours) to capture the acute inflammatory phase characterized by neutrophilic infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, and leukocytoclasis. Sampling the edge of a lesion helps avoid central ulceration or secondary changes.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis presents with a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer on her left shin that began after minor trauma. The lesion has violaceous, undermined borders and a necrotic base. A biopsy demonstrates dense neutrophilic infiltration without evidence of vasculitis or infection. She is currently maintained on mesalamine and has a history of frequent flares requiring systemic corticosteroids. Her current ulcer is refractory to wide local excision and sharp debridement, which exacerbated the lesion size due to pathergy. She is hemodynamically stable with no signs of systemic infection.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial systemic therapy for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate initial systemic therapy for pyoderma gangrenosum with pathergy and associated inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a sterile neutrophilic dermatosis often associated with IBD. Pathergy is common, so surgical debridement should be avoided. First-line systemic therapy for severe or refractory cases involves high-dose corticosteroids combined with cyclosporine to achieve rapid disease control.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for pyoderma gangrenosum (PG), a neutrophilic dermatosis strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Pathergy is a hallmark feature, meaning trauma exacerbates the lesion. Initial systemic therapy for rapidly progressive or refractory PG typically involves high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) often combined with a steroid-sparing agent like cyclosporine to achieve rapid control and facilitate tapering. Cyclosporine is particularly effective for PG due to its inhibition of T-cell activation and neutrophil migration. While treating the underlying IBD is crucial, PG often requires targeted immunosuppression.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam are broad-spectrum antibiotics used for infected ulcers or necrotizing fasciitis. PG is a sterile neutrophilic process; antibiotics are only indicated if secondary infection is proven, which was ruled out by the biopsy and clinical context.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic corticosteroids and cyclosporine is the correct answer. This combination provides rapid anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects necessary to halt the progression of PG, especially in the setting of pathergy and IBD association.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Subcutaneous granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) can actually exacerbate PG by increasing neutrophil counts and activation. It is contraindicated in the treatment of PG.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide is a valid treatment for small, stable PG lesions. However, this patient has a rapidly enlarging ulcer with pathergy and a history of IBD flares. Intralesional injection carries a high risk of worsening pathergy and is insufficient for systemic control or large, aggressive lesions.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic methotrexate is a steroid-sparing agent that can be used for maintenance therapy in PG. However, it has a slow onset of action (weeks to months) and is not appropriate for the initial management of rapidly progressive, painful, or pathergy-prone lesions where rapid control is needed.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis presents with a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer on the anterior shin. The lesion began as a pustule 10 days ago and has progressed to a 6-cm necrotic ulcer with violaceous, undermined borders. Minor trauma from scratching the area significantly worsened the lesion's size and pain (pathergy). Inflammatory markers are elevated, and a biopsy shows dense neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis or infection. She is currently taking mesalamine but reports frequent flares of her colitis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial systemic therapy for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate initial systemic therapy for pyoderma gangrenosum with pathergy and associated inflammatory bowel disease.
items.teachingPoint: Infliximab is the preferred initial systemic therapy for moderate-to-severe pyoderma gangrenosum associated with inflammatory bowel disease, as it effectively treats both the cutaneous and gastrointestinal manifestations by targeting TNF-alpha-driven inflammation.
items.explanationCorrect: Infliximab, a TNF-alpha inhibitor, is the preferred initial systemic therapy for moderate-to-severe pyoderma gangrenosum (PG), particularly when associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). It effectively treats both the cutaneous lesions and the underlying colitis, addressing the pathogenic immune dysregulation. PG is a neutrophilic dermatosis driven by excessive inflammatory cytokine production, and TNF-alpha blockade directly targets this pathway. While corticosteroids are often used initially for rapid control, infliximab is superior in patients with concurrent IBD due to its dual efficacy and steroid-sparing benefits.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: High-dose oral prednisone is frequently used for rapid control of PG but is not ideal as initial monotherapy in this patient due to the need for long-term management of both PG and IBD. It lacks the disease-modifying potential of TNF inhibitors and carries significant long-term adverse effects, making it a less optimal choice when infliximab is available.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Cyclosporine is an effective alternative for PG, particularly in patients who cannot tolerate corticosteroids or TNF inhibitors. However, it is not preferred as initial therapy in patients with concurrent IBD because it does not treat the underlying colitis and carries risks of nephrotoxicity and hypertension with long-term use.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Methotrexate is a slower-acting immunosuppressant that may be used for mild-to-moderate PG or as a steroid-sparing agent. It is less effective than infliximab for rapid control of severe, pathergy-prone lesions and does not provide the same robust efficacy for active IBD.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Dapsone is primarily used for neutrophilic dermatoses with a significant eosinophilic or bullous component, such as dermatitis herpetiformis or linear IgA disease. It has limited efficacy in PG and is not appropriate as initial therapy for this patient with active IBD.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for a urinary tract infection. On day 3 of his stay, he develops sudden onset of fever and painful, erythematous plaques on his left forearm. The lesions are edematous with a smooth surface and lack vesicles or bullae. He is hemodynamically stable but tachycardic due to the infection. Physical examination reveals no lymphangitic streaking, and the surrounding skin is warm but not fluctuant. The patient has no history of recent trauma to the area.
items.leadIn: Which of the following clinical features is most helpful in distinguishing this patient's cutaneous condition from bacterial cellulitis?

items.correctAnswerText: Tender, edematous plaques with a smooth surface
items.teachingPoint: In an acutely ill patient, the presence of tender, edematous plaques with a smooth surface strongly suggests Sweet syndrome over bacterial cellulitis, which typically presents with diffuse erythema and ill-defined borders.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis). While fever and systemic symptoms can occur in both Sweet syndrome and bacterial cellulitis, the morphology of the lesions is a key discriminator. Sweet syndrome typically presents with tender, edematous (pseudovesicular) plaques or nodules that have a smooth, non-purulent surface. Bacterial cellulitis usually presents with diffuse, ill-defined erythema and warmth rather than discrete, smooth-surfaced plaques. Although lymphangitic streaking is absent in this case, its presence would strongly favor cellulitis; however, its absence does not definitively rule out cellulitis. The rapid onset and extremity location are seen in both conditions.

items.leadIn: Which of the following histopathologic findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of Sweet syndrome over bacterial cellulitis?
items.learningObjective: Identify the discriminating feature that separates Sweet syndrome from bacterial cellulitis in an acutely ill patient.
items.correctAnswerText: Dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis
items.teachingPoint: The histopathologic hallmark of Sweet syndrome is a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate without true vasculitis (no fibrinoid necrosis or significant endothelial swelling). This finding helps distinguish it from bacterial cellulitis, which may show similar neutrophils but often includes microabscesses or secondary vasculitic changes, and from primary small-vessel vasculitides.
items.explanationCorrect: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) is characterized by a dense, diffuse infiltrate of mature neutrophils in the upper to mid-dermis. A key discriminating histopathologic feature that separates it from bacterial cellulitis and vasculitic processes is the absence of true leukocytoclastic vasculitis (i.e., no fibrinoid necrosis or endothelial swelling of vessel walls). While both conditions can present with neutrophils, the lack of vascular damage in Sweet syndrome is a hallmark diagnostic criterion.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of tense blisters and erosions on her trunk, extremities, and oral mucosa. She reports occasional itching but no pain. Physical examination reveals flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving erythematous erosions. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows a linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is ordered to identify the specific autoantibody target associated with this clinical and histopathologic presentation.
items.leadIn: Which of the following autoantigens is most likely targeted in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Identify the autoantigen target most consistent with a given immunobullous disease and clinical presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins, primarily BPAG2 (180 kDa) and BPAG1 (230 kDa). Clinical features include tense blisters, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of tense blisters, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone is classic for bullous pemphigoid (BP). BP is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins, primarily BPAG2 (also known as type XVII collagen) and less commonly BPAG1. The 180 kDa protein (BPAG2/BP180) is the most common target antigen in BP, making it the correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Desmoglein 1 is the primary target in pemphigus foliaceus, which presents with superficial blisters and crusting on the scalp and trunk. It does not involve mucous membranes, and immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposition in the epidermis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Desmoglein 3 is targeted in pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune disease characterized by flaccid bullae and mucosal involvement. It features a positive Nikolsky sign, and immunofluorescence reveals intercellular IgG deposition in the epidermis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: BPAG1 (230 kDa) is a hemidesmosomal protein that can be targeted in bullous pemphigoid, but it is less commonly the primary target than BPAG2. Additionally, antibodies against BPAG1 are more frequently associated with mucous membrane pemphigoid or linear IgA bullous dermatosis in some contexts, though BPAG2 remains the hallmark antigen for classic BP.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: BPAG2 (180 kDa) is the correct answer as explained.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a two-month history of severe, pruritic vesicles and bullae predominantly located on the extensor surfaces of her elbows, knees, buttocks, and posterior scalp. Direct immunofluorescence reveals granular IgA deposits along the dermal papillae. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blistering with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermal papillae. She denies any gastrointestinal symptoms, but her family history is notable for celiac disease in her mother and sister. Which of the following autoantigens is most likely targeted by circulating antibodies in this patient?
items.leadIn: Which of the following autoantigens is most likely targeted by circulating antibodies in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Identify the autoantigen target most consistent with a given immunobullous disease and clinical presentation.
items.teachingPoint: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae and targets epidermal transglutaminase (eTG). It is strongly associated with celiac disease.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of grouped, intensely pruritic vesicles and bullae on extensor surfaces, combined with granular IgA deposits along the dermal papillae and neutrophilic microabscesses on histology, is classic for dermatitis herpetiformis (DH). DH is an extra-intestinal manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy. The primary autoantigens targeted by IgA antibodies in DH are epidermal transglutaminase (eTG), also known as transglutaminase 3, and tissue transglutaminase (tTG). IgA antibodies against these enzymes lead to the characteristic histologic and immunofluorescence findings.

distractorExplanations.label: A

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermal transglutaminase is the correct target for dermatitis herpetiformis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Laminin-332 antibodies are associated with anti-laminin-332 mucous membrane pemphigoid, which presents with severe scarring and blistering of the mucosal surfaces.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, which can present with trauma-induced blistering on extensor surfaces. However, direct immunofluorescence typically shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone, not granular IgA.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging, pruritic rash on his right forearm that began 3 months ago. He initially noticed a small, erythematous papule that slowly expanded outward. Over the past 4 weeks, he applied over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream twice daily without relief. The eruption has since become more intensely pruritic and erythematous, with some central clearing that is less distinct than before. He has no history of atopic dermatitis, and there are no signs of systemic illness.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish tinea incognito from eczematous dermatitis in a patient whose eruption worsened after empiric topical corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: Tinea incognito should be suspected in patients with a chronic, pruritic, expanding rash that fails to improve or worsens after the application of topical corticosteroids. Steroids mask the inflammatory signs of dermatophytosis, leading to atypical morphology and delayed diagnosis. KOH preparation is essential for confirmation.
items.explanationCorrect: Tinea incognito is a dermatophyte infection whose clinical presentation has been altered by prior treatment with topical corticosteroids. Corticosteroids reduce local inflammation and pruritus initially but also suppress the immune response, allowing the fungus to proliferate more extensively. This leads to a broader, less scaly, and poorly marginated plaque that often lacks the classic annular appearance of tinea corporis. The history of worsening despite steroid use and the presence of an expanding, pruritic lesion strongly point to this diagnosis. A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation would reveal branching hyphae.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Nummular dermatitis typically presents as discrete, coin-shaped, erythematous, and scaly plaques. While it is pruritic, it does not typically worsen or change morphology significantly with the use of topical corticosteroids; in fact, steroids are a primary treatment. The lack of distinct coin-shaped lesions and the history of steroid failure make this less likely.

distractorExplanations.label: B

distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis can present as an erythematous, pruritic plaque. However, it usually improves with topical corticosteroids rather than worsening or expanding. The history of an initially small papule slowly expanding over months is more characteristic of a fungal infection than a contact reaction, which often appears acutely or subacutely after exposure.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Pityriasis rosea typically begins with a herald patch followed by a generalized eruption of smaller, oval, scaly plaques in a 'Christmas tree' distribution on the trunk. It is usually self-limiting and does not present as a solitary, slowly expanding forearm plaque that worsens with steroids.

It is typically asymptomatic (non-pruritic) and does not scale or worsen with topical corticosteroids. items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of an expanding, pruritic rash on her trunk. Two weeks ago, a primary care physician diagnosed eczema and prescribed clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment twice daily. The rash initially improved slightly but has since rapidly expanded into a large, annular plaque with central clearing and an active, scaly border. The center of the lesion now appears relatively flat and hypopigmented compared to the active edge. There is no history of contact with animals or recent travel.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish tinea incognito from eczematous dermatitis in a patient whose eruption worsened after empiric topical corticosteroids.
items.teachingPoint: Tinea incognito is a dermatophyte infection whose typical clinical features are altered by the prior use of topical corticosteroids. It often presents with expanded, less scaly, and more inflammatory annular plaques. Clinicians should suspect tinea incognito in patients with worsening or atypical eczematous eruptions after steroid use and perform a KOH preparation to confirm the diagnosis.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of an expanding annular plaque with central clearing and an active, scaly border is highly suggestive of tinea corporis. The worsening and morphological alteration (loss of typical scale, central hypopigmentation, and rapid expansion) following the application of a potent topical corticosteroid is characteristic of tinea incognito. Corticosteroids suppress the local inflammatory response, masking typical signs while allowing the dermatophyte to proliferate unchecked.

distractorExplanations.text: Granuloma annulare presents as smooth, flesh-colored to erythematous papules arranged in an annular pattern. It is typically asymptomatic, lacks scale, and does not change significantly or worsen with topical corticosteroid use.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Erythema annulare centrifugum presents with slowly expanding annular plaques with a trailing scale. However, it does not typically exhibit the rapid expansion and morphological alteration seen after steroid use, nor is it associated with fungal proliferation.

distractorExplanations.text: Pityriasis rosea usually begins with a herald patch followed by a Christmas tree distribution of smaller, oval, scaly plaques. It is self-limiting and does not typically present as a single expanding annular plaque that worsens with topical steroids.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Granuloma annulare is often considered in the differential for annular lesions, but it lacks scale and inflammation. Pityriasis rosea has a distinct distribution and herald patch.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man with a history of moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis presents to the emergency department due to a rapidly progressive rash over the past 2 days. He reports fever, malaise, and severe pruritus at the sites of his chronic dermatitis. Physical examination reveals numerous monomorphic, 2- to 4-mm vesicles and punched-out erosions with hemorrhagic crusting superimposed on his typical flexural eczematous plaques. There is no evidence of lymphadenopathy or corneal involvement.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for suspected eczema herpeticum in a patient with atopic dermatitis.
items.teachingPoint: Eczema herpeticum presents as monomorphic vesicles and punched-out erosions in patients with pre-existing skin barrier defects like atopic dermatitis. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt systemic antiviral therapy.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of monomorphic vesicles, punched-out erosions, and hemorrhagic crusting in a patient with atopic dermatitis is classic for eczema herpeticum (Kaposi varicelliform eruption). This is a dermatologic emergency caused by disseminated herpes simplex virus infection. Immediate initiation of systemic antiviral therapy, such as oral acyclovir (or intravenous acyclovir for severe cases), is the most appropriate next step to prevent serious complications like viremia, secondary bacterial infection, and ocular involvement.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform a KOH preparation of the vesicular fluid

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. Oral acyclovir is the treatment of choice for mild-to-moderate eczema herpeticum.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Topical tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor used for maintenance therapy of atopic dermatitis. It has no antiviral activity and would not treat the underlying HSV infection; furthermore, applying immunomodulators to an active viral eruption is contraindicated.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic corticosteroids are generally contraindicated in the acute setting of eczema herpeticum because they can further suppress local and systemic immunity, potentially exacerbating the viral replication and leading to more widespread dissemination.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Topical mupirocin is a topical antibiotic used for impetigo or secondary bacterial superinfection (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus). While secondary infection can occur, the primary pathology here is viral, and mupirocin would not address the disseminated HSV infection.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: A KOH preparation is used to diagnose fungal infections (e.g., tinea corporis). Tinea typically presents with annular, scaly plaques with an active border, not monomorphic vesicles and punched-out erosions. A viral culture or PCR would be the appropriate diagnostic test if confirmation is needed, but treatment should not be delayed.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive thickening, discoloration, and crumbling of all ten toenails over the past two years. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, well-controlled hypertension, and chronic kidney disease with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 45 mL/min/1.73 m². On examination, there is severe distal and lateral subungual hyperkeratosis with proximal nail plate involvement in multiple digits. A potassium hydroxide preparation and fungal culture confirm Trichophyton rubrum onychomycosis. The patient desires a curative treatment and is willing to undergo monitoring for potential adverse effects.
items.leadIn: Which of the following systemic treatment strategies is most appropriate for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic therapy approach for confirmed onychomycosis when nail disease is extensive and matrix-involving.
items.correctAnswerText: Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 weeks
items.teachingPoint: Oral terbinafine is the first-line systemic treatment for extensive, matrix-involving dermatophyte onychomycosis. It is preferred over azoles due to superior efficacy, fungicidal activity, and a favorable safety profile. Dose adjustment is not required for mild to moderate renal impairment.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral terbinafine is the first-line systemic therapy for extensive, matrix-involving onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum. It is fungicidal, has high cure rates, and does not require routine liver function monitoring in patients without pre-existing severe hepatic disease. While caution is advised in renal impairment, terbinafine is primarily metabolized by the liver and does not require dose adjustment for mild to moderate renal dysfunction (eGFR >30 mL/min).

options.label: A
options.text: Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily continuously for 12 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily in pulse therapy for four cycles

options.label: D

options.label: E

distractorExplanations.label: C

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Topical ciclopirox is indicated for mild to moderate onychomycosis involving less than 50% of the nail plate and not involving the matrix. It is inappropriate for extensive, matrix-involving disease due to poor penetration and low cure rates.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressive thickening, discoloration, and subungual hyperkeratosis of all 20 nails. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and well-controlled hypertension. A nail clipping sent for potassium hydroxide preparation and fungal culture confirms dermatophyte infection involving the distal, lateral, and proximal nail matrices. He has failed multiple courses of topical ciclopirox lacquer due to poor adherence and lack of efficacy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic therapy approach for confirmed onychomycosis when nail disease is extensive and matrix-involving.
items.correctAnswerText: Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 weeks
items.teachingPoint: Oral terbinafine is the preferred first-line systemic treatment for extensive dermatophyte onychomycosis involving the nail matrix, due to its superior efficacy and favorable safety profile compared to other systemic antifungals.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral terbinafine is the first-line systemic therapy for extensive onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes. It achieves high concentrations in the nail plate and matrix, providing the highest cure rates among available antifungals. A 12-week course is standard for toenail involvement, especially when the matrix is affected.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a painful, burning rash on his left forehead and scalp that began three days ago. He reports mild prodromal tingling in the same area prior to lesion onset. Examination reveals grouped vesicles on an erythematous base confined strictly to the left forehead, sparing the nasal tip and not crossing the midline. He has no history of recent travel, new skincare products, or ocular symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish herpes zoster ophthalmicus from allergic contact dermatitis and HSV in a unilateral painful facial eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus presents as a painful, unilateral vesicular eruption in the V1 distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Differentiation from HSV and contact dermatitis relies on recognizing the dermatomal pattern, prodromal neuralgia, and characteristic pain rather than pruritus.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of a unilateral, painful, vesicular eruption confined to a single dermatome (V1 branch of the trigeminal nerve) is classic for herpes zoster ophthalmicus. The prodromal pain/tingling and the sharp midline demarcation strongly support this diagnosis over other causes of facial vesicles. Although the nasal tip is spared (Hutchinson sign negative), V1 involvement still warrants ophthalmology evaluation to rule out ocular complications.

options.label: B
options.text: Allergic contact dermatitis to hair dye

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) typically presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, but lesions are usually localized to the vermilion border of the lips or perioral region (herpes labialis). While HSV can occur on the forehead, it is less likely to be strictly unilateral with a dermatomal distribution and prominent prodromal neuralgia in an immunocompetent adult.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is typically pruritic rather than painful. It often presents with erythema, edema, and vesicles but follows a distribution corresponding to the allergen exposure (e.g., hairline for dye) and frequently crosses the midline. The sharp dermatomal cutoff and neuropathic pain make this diagnosis unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. See explanation_correct.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Impetigo contagiosa typically presents with honey-colored crusts rather than clear vesicles on an erythematous base. It is more common in children, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, and does not follow a strict dermatomal pattern or cause significant prodromal pain.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Cellulitis presents with diffuse erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness rather than grouped vesicles. It does not typically follow a dermatomal distribution and is less likely to present with the sharp midline demarcation seen in this patient.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of severe, burning pain and erythema on the left side of his face. He denies ocular pain or visual changes, but his left eye appears mildly injected.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish herpes zoster ophthalmicus from allergic contact dermatitis and HSV in a unilateral painful facial eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus should be suspected in patients with unilateral, painful, vesicular eruptions following the V1 dermatome. Involvement of the nasal tip (Hutchinson sign) suggests nasociliary nerve involvement and warrants urgent ophthalmologic evaluation due to the high risk of sight-threatening ocular complications.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of severe unilateral pain, a dermatomal distribution (V1 branch of the trigeminal nerve), and grouped vesicles on an erythematous base is classic for herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO). Immediate antiviral therapy and ophthalmologic evaluation are critical.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis typically presents with pruritus rather than severe pain, and the rash is often bilateral or corresponds to a specific exposure pattern rather than a strict dermatome. Vesicles may be present but are usually less grouped and not accompanied by the severe neuropathic pain described.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) can cause grouped vesicles, but it is typically localized to the vermilion border of the lips (herpes labialis) or perioral region. While HSV can be painful, it rarely involves the entire V1 dermatome or presents with Hutchinson sign. Recurrent HSV lesions are usually smaller and resolve faster.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is the correct diagnosis based on the dermatomal distribution, severe pain, and Hutchinson sign.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Cellulitis presents with diffuse erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness rather than grouped vesicles. It is a bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and does not follow a strict dermatomal pattern or present with vesicles.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Impetigo is characterized by honey-colored crusted lesions, typically in children. It presents with superficial vesicles or bullae that rupture easily, but it is not associated with severe neuropathic pain or a dermatomal distribution.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with advanced dementia is admitted to a long-term care facility for placement. Two days after admission, he develops severe pruritus and excoriated papules on his trunk and extremities. Skin scraping confirms Sarcoptes scabiei infestation. The facility's infection control committee convenes to address potential exposure among other residents and staff. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in outbreak management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in outbreak management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the best outbreak-control strategy for institutional scabies exposure.
items.correctAnswerText: Treat all residents and staff who had close contact with the patient within the past month.
items.teachingPoint: In institutional scabies outbreaks, the cornerstone of management is simultaneous pharmacologic treatment of all residents and staff who had close contact with the index patient within the preceding 2 to 6 weeks, regardless of clinical symptoms.
items.explanationCorrect: Scabies outbreaks in institutional settings require mass treatment of all close contacts, regardless of symptom status. Because the incubation period for primary scabies is 2 to 6 weeks, anyone exposed within the past month may be incubating the infestation. Simultaneous treatment of all close contacts prevents reinfestation and halts transmission.

options.label: A
options.text: Treat only the newly admitted patient with topical permethrin.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer oral ivermectin prophylactically to all facility staff.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat all residents and staff who had close contact with the patient within the past month.

options.label: D
options.text: Restrict facility admissions for 4 weeks and perform environmental decontamination only.

options.label: E
options.text: Treat the patient and all household contacts of facility staff.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Treating only the index patient ignores asymptomatic carriers and close contacts who are incubating the infestation, leading to rapid reinfestation and continued outbreak spread.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Prophylactic ivermectin for all staff is unnecessary and potentially harmful; treatment should be targeted to close contacts. Additionally, topical permethrin or oral ivermectin are both acceptable for treatment, but mass prophylaxis without indication is not recommended.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Mass treatment of close contacts within the exposure window is the standard of care for institutional scabies outbreaks.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Restricting admissions does not address the existing infestation in residents and staff. Environmental decontamination is adjunctive but insufficient without simultaneous pharmacologic treatment of all close contacts.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Household contacts of staff are not considered close institutional contacts requiring mass treatment unless they reside with the index patient or have direct household exposure. The primary focus must be on facility residents and staff.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to a long-term care facility for postoperative rehabilitation. Three days after admission, he develops intense pruritus and a papular rash on his wrists and finger webs. Skin scraping reveals scabies mites. Shortly after, three other residents in the same wing report similar symptoms. The facility has strict infection control protocols. What is the most appropriate next step in management to prevent further transmission?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management to prevent further transmission?
items.learningObjective: Identify the best outbreak-control strategy for institutional scabies exposure.
items.correctAnswerText: Treat all residents, staff, and close contacts of the diagnosed patients simultaneously with topical permethrin or oral ivermectin.
items.teachingPoint: In institutional outbreaks of scabies, simultaneous treatment of all residents and staff, regardless of symptoms, is the most effective strategy to control transmission. Environmental decontamination should be performed concurrently.
items.explanationCorrect: In institutional settings such as long-term care facilities, nursing homes, or psychiatric hospitals, scabies can rapidly spread due to close contact and often delayed diagnosis. The cornerstone of outbreak control is the simultaneous treatment of all affected individuals, close contacts, and often all residents and staff within the facility, regardless of symptoms. This 'mass treatment' approach is necessary because subclinical or incubating infestations are common, and treating only symptomatic individuals leaves a reservoir for reinfestation. Topical permethrin 5% cream or oral ivermectin are first-line therapies.

options.label: A
options.text: Treat only the newly diagnosed patient and his immediate roommates with permethrin 5% cream.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer oral ivermectin to the diagnosed patient and treat all facility staff who have had contact with him.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat all residents, staff, and close contacts of the diagnosed patients simultaneously with topical permethrin or oral ivermectin.

options.label: D
options.text: Isolate the affected residents in a negative-pressure room and treat them with topical permethrin twice weekly for four weeks.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform environmental decontamination of the facility and treat only symptomatic residents with oral ivermectin.
