distractorExplanations.text: Oral ivermectin is effective for scabies, but treating only the diagnosed patient and staff ignores other potentially infected residents. Furthermore, simultaneous mass treatment of all contacts is required to break the cycle of transmission in a closed population.

distractorExplanations.label: C

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Negative-pressure isolation rooms are not required for scabies, which is transmitted via direct skin-to-skin contact or fomites. Additionally, treating with permethrin twice weekly for four weeks is an excessive regimen not indicated for standard scabies management.

The standard of care is prompt initiation of systemic antiviral therapy (e.g., oral valacyclovir) to limit viral replication and reduce the risk of complications. Urgent ophthalmology consultation is mandatory for a comprehensive slit-lamp examination to detect subtle ocular involvement that may require additional targeted therapy, even if initial screening is normal.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful, unilateral rash involving his right forehead and scalp that began 12 hours ago. He reports a burning sensation in the area prior to rash onset and notes new-onset photophobia and mild tearing of the right eye. Physical examination reveals grouped vesicles on an erythematous base strictly confined to the V1 distribution of the trigeminal nerve. There is no evidence of corneal involvement on gross inspection, but slit-lamp examination is not immediately available.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate urgent management step for herpes zoster involving the ophthalmic branch.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate oral valacyclovir therapy and arrange urgent ophthalmology consultation
items.teachingPoint: Herpes zoster in the V1 dermatome requires immediate systemic antiviral therapy and urgent ophthalmology consultation to prevent sight-threatening complications, regardless of whether ocular symptoms are initially apparent.
items.explanationCorrect: Herpes zoster involving the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve is a medical emergency due to the high risk of sight-threatening complications, such as keratitis, uveitis, and optic neuritis. The presence of photophobia and tearing raises strong suspicion for ocular involvement even if gross inspection is normal. Immediate initiation of systemic antiviral therapy (e.g., oral valacyclovir, famciclovir, or IV acyclovir) is required to halt viral replication and reduce the risk of ocular complications. Urgent ophthalmology consultation is mandatory for a formal slit-lamp examination to assess for corneal dendrites and intraocular inflammation.

options.text: Initiate oral valacyclovir therapy and arrange urgent ophthalmology consultation

options.label: B
options.text: Apply topical acyclovir cream to the affected skin lesions only

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe oral corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and pain

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Observation is inappropriate because delayed treatment increases the risk of permanent vision loss and chronic postherpetic neuralgia. V1 zoster requires immediate intervention.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man from Guatemala presents with a 6-month history of an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging plaque on his left cheek. He recalls a minor insect bite in the area that never fully healed. The lesion is slightly erythematous with central hypopigmentation and fine scaling at the periphery. Sensory examination reveals markedly decreased light touch, pinprick, and temperature sensation over the plaque compared to adjacent skin. There is no regional lymphadenopathy, and his systemic examination is unremarkable.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish Hansen disease from cutaneous sarcoidosis and tinea corporis in a chronic hypoesthetic plaque eruption.
items.teachingPoint: Sensory loss (hypoesthesia) in a chronic cutaneous plaque is the key clinical feature distinguishing Hansen disease from other granulomatous, infectious, or inflammatory dermatoses such as cutaneous sarcoidosis, tinea corporis, and cutaneous leishmaniasis.
items.explanationCorrect: The presence of a chronic, slowly enlarging plaque with central hypopigmentation and marked sensory loss (hypoesthesia) is the hallmark of Hansen disease (leprosy). Sensory deficits are a defining feature that distinguishes leprosy from other granulomatous or scaly dermatoses. Although cutaneous leishmaniasis can cause chronic plaques, it is typically ulcerated and not hypoesthetic. Tinea corporis presents with an annular, scaly plaque but retains normal sensation. Cutaneous sarcoidosis presents with non-caseating granulomas and normal sensation. Mycobacterium marinum typically causes nodules or plaques along lymphatic channels (sporotrichoid spread) and is not hypoesthetic.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous leishmaniasis typically presents as a chronic, non-healing ulcer with raised borders and indurated base. It does not cause sensory loss (hypoesthesia).

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis presents as an annular, erythematous plaque with central clearing and active scaly borders. Sensation is preserved.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Hansen disease (lepromatous leprosy)

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous sarcoidosis presents as firm, erythematous to violaceous papules or plaques. Sensation is intact, and histology shows non-caseating granulomas.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Mycobacterium marinum infection typically presents as nodules, plaques, or ulcers in a sporotrichoid pattern following aquatic exposure. Sensation is preserved.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man from rural Brazil presents with a 10-month history of an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging lesion on his left forearm. He recalls a minor abrasion in the area that never fully healed. Examination reveals a solitary, well-demarcated, erythematous plaque with slightly raised borders and central atrophy on the volar aspect of his forearm. The lesion is completely hypoesthetic to pinprick and temperature sensation, but light touch is preserved. There are no other skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, or cranial nerve deficits. A skin biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas in the dermis and subcutaneous fat with a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate surrounding adnexal structures and nerves. Acid-fast bacilli are not visualized on standard Ziehl-Neelsen staining, but a PCR assay for Mycobacterium leprae is positive.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Distinguish Hansen disease from cutaneous sarcoidosis and tinea corporis in a chronic hypoesthetic plaque eruption.
items.teachingPoint: The presence of a chronic granulomatous plaque accompanied by localized hypoesthesia (especially to temperature and pinprick) is the clinical hallmark of leprosy. This sensory deficit distinguishes it from other cutaneous granulomatous conditions like sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris, or granuloma annulare, which are typically non-hypoesthetic.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a solitary, hypoesthetic plaque with central atrophy and raised borders is highly characteristic of tuberculoid leprosy. The key distinguishing feature from other granulomatous conditions is the loss of sensation (hypoesthesia), particularly to temperature and pinprick, while light touch is often preserved until late stages. The histology showing perineural and periadnexal granulomas, combined with a positive PCR for Mycobacterium leprae, confirms the diagnosis. The absence of visible acid-fast bacilli on standard staining is common in tuberculoid leprosy due to the strong cell-mediated immune response that limits bacterial proliferation.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous sarcoidosis typically presents with asymptomatic, non-hypoesthetic plaques or papules. While it also features noncaseating granulomas, the hallmark of leprosy—sensory loss and perineural inflammation—is absent. Furthermore, sarcoidosis would not yield a positive PCR for M. leprae.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Tinea corporis presents as an annular, scaly plaque with a raised border and central clearing. It is pruritic rather than asymptomatic, does not cause hypoesthesia, and histology would show fungal hyphae in the stratum corneum rather than deep dermal granulomas.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Leprosy (Hansen disease)

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Granuloma annulare presents as asymptomatic, flesh-colored to erythematous papules or plaques in an annular configuration. It lacks sensory deficits, and histology typically shows palisading granulomas with mucin deposition in the dermis without significant perineural involvement.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Lupus vulgaris (cutaneous tuberculosis) presents as reddish-brown plaques with 'apple-jelly' nodules on diascopy. Although it is a granulomatous disease, it does not cause sensory loss. Histology would show caseating or noncaseating granulomas with a positive PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, not M. leprae.

items.stem: A 19-year-old male collegiate wrestler presents with a 2-week history of multiple, intensely pruritic, annular erythematous plaques with central clearing and a scaly, advancing border on his trunk, thighs, and upper arms. He has failed to improve after 1 week of over-the-counter topical clotrimazole applied twice daily. Physical examination reveals approximately 15 distinct lesions, the largest measuring 6 cm in diameter. He has no systemic symptoms and no signs of kerion or tinea capitis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate treatment strategy for extensive tinea corporis in a contact-sport athlete.
items.correctAnswerText: Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 2 weeks
items.teachingPoint: Extensive tinea corporis, failure of topical therapy, and contact-sport participation are indications for oral antifungal treatment. Terbinafine is a first-line agent due to its fungicidal activity, short course duration, and once-daily dosing.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral antifungal therapy is indicated for extensive tinea corporis (multiple lesions, large surface area involvement), failure of topical therapy, and in patients participating in contact sports to prevent transmission and ensure rapid resolution. Terbinafine is highly effective against dermatophytes, has a convenient once-daily dosing schedule, and requires only a short 2-week course for tinea corporis. It is generally preferred due to its fungicidal activity and favorable pharmacokinetics.

items.stem: A 16-year-old male high school wrestler presents with a 2-week history of multiple pruritic, annular, scaly plaques on his trunk and upper extremities. Several lesions have coalesced into large, geographic patches covering approximately 40% of his body surface area. He has tried an over-the-counter clotrimazole cream twice daily for 10 days with minimal improvement. He is scheduled to return to wrestling in 5 days and requires clearance to participate. Vital signs are normal, and there is no evidence of secondary bacterial infection or tinea capitis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate treatment strategy for extensive tinea corporis in a contact-sport athlete.
items.correctAnswerText: Oral griseofulvin for 4 weeks and clear him to participate after 1 week of therapy
items.teachingPoint: Extensive tinea corporis (>20-30% BSA) or lesions refractory to topical therapy require systemic antifungal treatment. For contact-sport athletes, return to participation is generally permitted after at least 1 week of systemic antifungal therapy, provided lesions are improving and covered.
items.explanationCorrect: Extensive tinea corporis covering a large body surface area (>20-30%) or lesions refractory to topical therapy requires systemic antifungal treatment. Oral griseofulvin is a first-line agent for extensive dermatophyte infections, particularly in contact sports. Clearing an athlete for participation typically requires at least 1 week of systemic antifungal therapy to ensure the infection is no longer highly contagious, along with clinical improvement. Griseofulvin's efficacy in tinea corporis is well-established, and the 1-week rule for return to play balances contagion risk with athletic participation.

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe oral terbinafine for 2 weeks and clear him immediately after the first dose

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe oral griseofulvin for 4 weeks and clear him to participate after 1 week of therapy

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While oral terbinafine is an excellent first-line systemic agent for tinea corporis, clearing the athlete immediately after one dose is unsafe. Systemic antifungals require a minimum of 1 week of therapy to significantly reduce contagion risk and ensure clinical response.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Oral griseofulvin is appropriate for extensive tinea corporis. Clearing the athlete after 1 week of systemic therapy aligns with standard guidelines to minimize transmission risk in contact sports while allowing continued treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Oral itraconazole is a valid alternative systemic agent. However, clearing the athlete based solely on the absence of scaling is subjective and may not adequately ensure reduced contagion. The 1-week systemic therapy rule is a more standardized and reliable criterion for return to play.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Topical ketoconazole shampoo as a body wash is an adjunctive therapy for widespread or recurrent tinea corporis but is insufficient as monotherapy for extensive, refractory disease. It does not replace the need for systemic treatment in this scenario.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of an expanding, pruritic plaque on his right forearm. He has tried over-the-counter clotrimazole twice daily for 4 weeks without improvement. Physical examination reveals a well-demarcated, erythematous plaque with central clearing and an active, scaly border. A bedside potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of the scale demonstrates no hyphae or spores. The lesion is now becoming tender and developing small pustules along the advancing edge.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management to establish a definitive diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Recognize why deep or follicular dermatophyte infection may require biopsy or culture when bedside KOH is unrevealing.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform a deep skin biopsy for histopathology and culture
items.teachingPoint: Bedside KOH preparations have high sensitivity for superficial dermatophyte infections but may be falsely negative in deep follicular (Majocchi granuloma) or dermal fungal infections. When clinical suspicion remains high despite negative KOH, a deep skin biopsy for histopathology (with special stains) and culture is required to confirm the diagnosis.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation suggests tinea corporis, but the negative KOH and lack of response to topical antifungals raise suspicion for a deeper or follicular dermatophyte infection (e.g., Majocchi granuloma) or an alternative diagnosis such as granulomatous dermatitis. Bedside KOH is highly sensitive for superficial fungal infections but frequently yields false-negative results when the infection involves the hair follicle, deeper dermis, or is obscured by significant inflammation or crusting. A deep skin biopsy allows for histopathologic evaluation (e.g., PAS stain to highlight fungi in the dermis or follicle) and tissue culture, which are necessary for definitive diagnosis when superficial sampling is non-diagnostic.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform a deep skin biopsy for histopathology and culture

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat KOH preparation with a different magnification

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain a bacterial wound culture and start oral cephalexin

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Empiric oral antifungal therapy is inappropriate without a confirmed diagnosis, especially given the negative KOH. The lesion may represent Majocchi granuloma, which requires oral therapy, but it could also be a deep bacterial infection or inflammatory condition. Treating without confirmation risks inappropriate therapy and delayed diagnosis of potentially serious conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in suspected fungal infections as they can mask the clinical presentation, promote deeper invasion (tinea incognito), and worsen the infection. This would be harmful without excluding a fungal etiology definitively.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Repeating the KOH with different magnification is unlikely to yield a different result if the initial preparation was adequate. The sensitivity of KOH depends on the depth and density of fungal elements; if superficial scale is negative, changing magnification will not detect deep follicular or dermal fungi.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While pustules suggest possible bacterial involvement, the primary lesion is chronic, annular, and scaly with central clearing, which is classic for dermatophytosis. Bacterial superinfection can occur but is not the primary pathology. Treating for bacteria without ruling out fungal causes delays appropriate management.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of an asymptomatic, erythematous, scaly plaque on his left shin. He reports it began as a small papule and slowly expanded. He has no history of diabetes, immunosuppression, or recent travel. Physical examination reveals a 4-cm annular plaque with central clearing and a raised, scaly border. Bedside potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of the active margin demonstrates no hyphae or spores. He was treated with topical clotrimazole for 2 weeks without improvement.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management to confirm the diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Recognize why deep or follicular dermatophyte infection may require biopsy or culture when bedside KOH is unrevealing.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform a skin biopsy for histopathology and fungal culture
items.teachingPoint: Bedside KOH preparations may be falsely negative in deep or follicular dermatophyte infections (e.g., Majocchi granuloma) because the organisms reside deeper than the superficial scale. Biopsy with special stains (PAS/GMS) and tissue culture are required for definitive diagnosis when clinical suspicion remains high despite negative superficial testing.
items.explanationCorrect: Deep or follicular dermatophyte infections (e.g., Majocchi granuloma) often extend beyond the superficial stratum corneum into the hair follicle or dermis. Bedside KOH preparations only sample the superficial scale and may be falsely negative if the organism is sequestered deeper in the follicular infundibulum or dermis. A skin biopsy allows for histopathologic evaluation (e.g., PAS stain to highlight fungal elements within follicles or dermis) and tissue culture, which are necessary to definitively diagnose these deeper variants when superficial testing is negative.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a diffuse, pruritic rash that began on his trunk and spread to his extremities over the past 10 days. He was started on amoxicillin-clavulanate for a sinus infection one week ago. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Physical examination reveals confluent erythematous macules and papules covering 60% of his body surface area. There is mild facial edema. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 14,000/mm³ with an absolute eosinophil count of 2,500/mm³ and an atypical lymphocyte percentage of 15%. Liver function tests reveal a mild elevation in alanine aminotransferase (ALT 65 U/L).
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate DRESS from an uncomplicated morbilliform drug eruption in a recently medicated patient.
items.teachingPoint: DRESS syndrome is characterized by a triad of rash, hematologic abnormalities (eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis), and internal organ involvement (most commonly hepatitis) occurring 2 to 8 weeks after drug initiation. Facial edema and fever are also common clinical clues that help differentiate it from a simple morbilliform drug eruption.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of a morbilliform rash, fever, facial edema, lymphadenopathy (implied by systemic involvement), eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, and hepatic involvement occurring 2 to 8 weeks after initiating a high-risk medication (amoxicillin-clavulanate) is classic for Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS). The systemic symptoms and laboratory abnormalities distinguish it from a simple morbilliform eruption.

distractorExplanations.text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) typically presents with sterile, non-follicular pustules on an erythematous base and is usually associated with neutrophilia rather than eosinophilia. It also typically has a shorter latency period (days).

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: DRESS syndrome is the correct diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: An uncomplicated morbilliform drug eruption presents with a maculopapular rash but lacks the systemic features seen here, such as high fever, facial edema, significant eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, and organ involvement (hepatitis).

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Serum sickness-like reactions typically present with urticaria, arthralgias, and fever but do not feature the prominent eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, or hepatic inflammation characteristic of DRESS.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Urticarial vasculitis presents with urticarial lesions that last longer than 24 hours, are often painful rather than pruritic, and may leave behind purpura or hyperpigmentation. It does not typically cause the systemic eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytosis seen in this patient.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man is evaluated for a widespread rash that began 10 days ago after starting allopurinol for gout. He reports mild pruritus but denies fever, mucosal involvement, or facial swelling. Examination reveals a symmetric, blanching, erythematous maculopapular eruption involving 60% of his body surface area. Vital signs are normal. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 7,200/mm³ with 5% eosinophils and a normal liver function panel. Renal function is within normal limits.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate DRESS from an uncomplicated morbilliform drug eruption in a recently medicated patient.
items.teachingPoint: Morbilliform drug eruptions are the most common cutaneous adverse drug reactions, presenting as symmetric, pruritic maculopapular rashes without systemic symptoms or laboratory abnormalities. DRESS syndrome must be distinguished by the presence of fever, organ involvement (e.g., hepatitis), and hematologic abnormalities such as eosinophilia.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with a classic morbilliform (maculopapular) drug eruption. Key features supporting this diagnosis include the typical latency period (7-14 days), symmetric distribution, blanching nature of the rash, absence of systemic symptoms (fever, organ involvement), and normal laboratory values (no eosinophilia or transaminitis). This is the most common type of drug eruption and is generally benign, resolving upon discontinuation of the offending agent.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) typically presents with widespread sterile pustules on an erythematous base, often accompanied by fever and neutrophilia. It usually has a shorter latency period (days) compared to morbilliform eruptions or DRESS. The absence of pustules, fever, and neutrophilia in this patient makes AGEP unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) is characterized by a triad of rash, fever, and internal organ involvement (most commonly liver or kidney), along with hematologic abnormalities such as eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis. This patient lacks fever, organ dysfunction (normal LFTs and renal function), and eosinophilia, making DRESS incorrect.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Morbilliform drug eruption is the most common type of cutaneous adverse drug reaction. It presents as a symmetric, pruritic, erythematous maculopapular rash that typically appears 7-14 days after drug initiation. It is limited to the skin without systemic symptoms or laboratory abnormalities, exactly matching this patient's presentation.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Serum sickness-like reactions typically present with urticaria, fever, and arthralgias/arthritis, often appearing 1-3 weeks after drug exposure. While allopurinol can cause serum sickness-like reactions, this patient lacks fever and joint symptoms, and his rash is maculopapular rather than urticarial.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a severe mucocutaneous reaction characterized by epidermal detachment (<10% BSA), prominent mucosal involvement, and targetoid lesions. This patient has no mucosal involvement, no epidermal detachment, and a blanching maculopapular rash, ruling out SJS.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to rapidly progressive skin pain and blistering that began 2 days ago. He started a new medication for chronic back pain 10 days prior. Examination reveals widespread erythematous macules, atypical targetoid lesions on the trunk, and extensive epidermal detachment involving approximately 30% of his total body surface area. Mucosal surfaces, including the oral cavity and conjunctivae, are significantly eroded. The patient appears dehydrated and is in visible distress.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the safest immediate management approach for suspected SJS/TEN.
items.correctAnswerText: Discontinue the suspected offending agent and initiate supportive wound care
items.teachingPoint: The immediate and most critical management step for suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) is the prompt discontinuation of the suspected offending drug and initiation of aggressive supportive care, including fluid resuscitation and wound management. Controversial therapies like systemic corticosteroids or IVIG should not delay these foundational interventions.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) overlap, given the mucosal involvement and extensive epidermal detachment (>10% but <30%). The absolute cornerstone of management in SJS/TEN is the immediate identification and discontinuation of the suspected causative drug. Furthermore, early transfer to a specialized burn or intensive care unit for aggressive supportive care—particularly fluid and electrolyte management, temperature control, nutritional support, and meticulous wound care—is critical to reducing mortality. Delaying the removal of the offending agent increases morbidity and mortality.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer subcutaneous epinephrine and transfer to the intensive care unit

options.label: C
options.text: Discontinue the suspected offending agent and initiate supportive wound care

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a punch biopsy of an early lesion for histopathologic evaluation

options.label: E
options.text: Start intravenous immunoglobulin therapy pending specialist consultation

distractorExplanations.text: Systemic corticosteroids remain controversial in SJS/TEN. While some centers use them early to halt progression, others associate their use with increased risks of infection and impaired wound healing. They are not the universally accepted first-line immediate step compared to drug cessation and supportive care.

distractorExplanations.label: B

This patient's presentation of blistering, mucosal erosion, and epidermal detachment is characteristic of a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR), not IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.

The clinical diagnosis is often sufficient to warrant immediate action in a clear-cut case.

However, its use is controversial and not standardized as a first-line immediate intervention over drug cessation and supportive care. It does not replace the critical need to stop the offending medication.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of recurrent, pruritic wheals and angioedema that have persisted for 6 months. She takes cetirizine 10 mg daily, but the lesions continue to appear daily and occasionally interfere with her work. She has no history of asthma, aspirin sensitivity, or thyroid disease. Physical examination reveals several 2- to 4-cm erythematous, edematous plaques on the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count with differential, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the best step-up therapy for chronic spontaneous urticaria that persists despite standard-dose second-generation antihistamines.
items.teachingPoint: For chronic spontaneous urticaria refractory to standard-dose second-generation H1-antihistamines, the recommended next step is to increase the antihistamine dose up to fourfold before considering omalizumab or other advanced therapies.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient has chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) that is inadequately controlled with standard-dose second-generation H1-antihistamines. According to the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) and international EAACI/GA²LEN/EDF/WAO guidelines, the recommended step-up therapy for CSU refractory to standard doses is to increase the dose of the second-generation antihistamine up to fourfold. Increasing cetirizine from 10 mg to 20 mg daily is a safe, evidence-based next step before escalating to biologic agents or immunosuppressants.

options.label: D

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Omalizumab is a highly effective biologic therapy indicated for CSU that remains uncontrolled despite antihistamine up-dosing. Up-dosing the current agent is preferred.

distractorExplanations.text: Short courses of oral corticosteroids may be used for severe, acute exacerbations or breakthrough symptoms in CSU. items.learningObjective: Choose the best step-up therapy for chronic spontaneous urticaria that persists despite standard-dose second-generation antihistamines.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a 1-day history of a painful, well-demarcated violaceous patch on his glans penis. He notes that an identical lesion appeared in the exact same location 6 months ago after taking a pill for a urinary tract infection. The current episode began approximately 30 minutes after he took the same medication for a new infection. He denies fever, malaise, or mucosal involvement elsewhere. Examination reveals a single 2-cm dusky erythematous to violaceous plaque with mild central edema and no frank blistering.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate fixed drug eruption from erythema multiforme and herpes simplex recurrence.
items.teachingPoint: Fixed drug eruption is characterized by the recurrence of a well-demarcated, erythematous to violaceous plaque at the same anatomical site upon re-exposure to a specific offending medication. Recognizing this temporal and spatial recurrence is key to distinguishing it from other recurrent dermatoses like herpes simplex or erythema multiforme.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a well-demarcated, dusky violaceous plaque that recurs in the exact same location upon re-exposure to a specific medication is pathognomonic for a fixed drug eruption. The rapid onset after re-challenge and lack of systemic symptoms further support this diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erythema multiforme typically presents with targetoid lesions on the extremities and is frequently associated with herpes simplex virus infection or Mycoplasma pneumoniae, rather than a single recurrent plaque at the same site after drug ingestion.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Fixed drug eruption

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Herpes simplex virus infection usually presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base rather than a solitary, well-demarcated violaceous plaque. While it can recur at the same site, the temporal relationship to drug ingestion and the morphology are inconsistent with HSV.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Bullous pemphigoid typically presents in elderly patients as tense bullae on urticarial or erythematous plaques, often involving the flexural surfaces. It does not present as a solitary violaceous plaque on the genitalia.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Syphilis typically presents as a painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) in the primary stage. The lesion described is painful and violaceous, and the recurrent nature tied to medication use rules out an infectious etiology like syphilis.

items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate fixed drug eruption from erythema multiforme and herpes simplex recurrence.
items.teachingPoint: Fixed drug eruption is characterized by the recurrence of well-demarcated, dusky erythematous or violaceous plaques at the exact same anatomical site upon re-exposure to a specific offending medication, often leaving behind residual hyperpigmentation.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a solitary, well-demarcated, dusky erythematous to violaceous plaque that recurs at the exact same site upon re-exposure to a specific offending drug is classic for a fixed drug eruption (FDE). The history of preceding hyperpigmentation and the absence of systemic symptoms or widespread lesions further support this diagnosis. The glans penis is a common site for FDEs.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erythema multiforme typically presents with targetoid lesions, often involving the extremities and palms/soles. It is frequently triggered by infections (e.g., HSV) or drugs but usually presents with multiple lesions rather than a solitary, recurring plaque at the exact same site.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection can recur at the same site and involve the genitalia. However, HSV lesions typically present as grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that evolve into ulcers, often preceded by prodromal pain or tingling. They do not typically leave behind persistent hyperpigmentation in the same manner as FDE, and the trigger is usually stress or illness rather than a specific medication.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Lichen planus typically presents as pruritic, purple, polygonal papules and plaques, often on the flexor wrists or ankles. While it can involve the genitalia, it does not characteristically recur at the exact same site triggered by a specific medication.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease that typically affects the elderly. It presents with tense bullae on erythematous or urticarial plaques, usually widespread rather than a solitary recurring plaque. It is not triggered by acute re-exposure to a specific medication in this manner.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of rapidly progressive, intensely pruritic hives covering her trunk and extremities. She also reports throat tightness and mild shortness of breath after taking amoxicillin for a dental infection earlier today. On examination, her blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg, heart rate is 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. She has diffuse wheals with surrounding erythema, but no visible oropharyngeal edema. Her lungs are clear to auscultation.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the next best step when urticaria is accompanied by features concerning for anaphylaxis.
items.teachingPoint: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate administration of intramuscular epinephrine. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjunctive only and must never delay or replace epinephrine in patients with respiratory compromise, hypotension, or progressive symptoms.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient is experiencing anaphylaxis, a severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction. The diagnosis is clinical and based on the rapid onset of skin/mucosal involvement (urticaria) plus respiratory compromise (throat tightness, shortness of breath, tachypnea) or reduced blood pressure. Even with normal oxygen saturation and clear lungs initially, respiratory symptoms in the setting of widespread urticaria after a high-risk drug exposure mandate immediate treatment with intramuscular epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh. Epinephrine is the first-line therapy because it rapidly reverses vasodilation, decreases mucosal edema, and stabilizes mast cells. Delaying epinephrine administration increases the risk of progression to respiratory failure or cardiovascular collapse.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer intravenous diphenhydramine and oral prednisone

options.label: C
options.text: Perform immediate skin prick testing to amoxicillin

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain a complete blood count with differential and serum tryptase level

options.label: E
options.text: Administer intramuscular epinephrine followed by intravenous methylprednisolone

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Intramuscular epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjunctive therapies for anaphylaxis but should never replace epinephrine as the initial intervention. They do not address upper airway edema or hypotension and have a delayed onset of action. Relying solely on these agents in the setting of respiratory compromise is dangerous and contraindicated.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Skin prick testing is used to identify IgE-mediated allergens but has no role in the acute management of anaphylaxis. It should only be performed after the patient has fully recovered and is off antihistamines, typically weeks later in an outpatient setting.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Serum tryptase can support the diagnosis of anaphylaxis by documenting mast cell degranulation, but it should be drawn 1-2 hours after symptom onset and does not change the immediate management. A complete blood count is nonspecific in this acute setting. Diagnostic testing should never delay life-saving treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: While corticosteroids are often administered after epinephrine to potentially prevent biphasic reactions, they do not replace the need for immediate epinephrine. Furthermore, adding intravenous methylprednisolone to the correct answer makes this option incorrect because epinephrine is the sole priority. The phrasing implies a sequence or equal importance, but epinephrine must be given first and alone as the immediate next step.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of an enlarging, asymptomatic plaque on his right shin. He recalls being bitten by a mosquito 3 weeks ago at the exact site of the lesion, which initially appeared as an intensely pruritic papule. The plaque is now 6 cm in diameter, warm to the touch, and has a slightly indurated border with surrounding erythema. He is otherwise healthy, takes no medications, and has no systemic symptoms such as fever or chills. Laboratory evaluation reveals a peripheral eosinophil count of 1,200/μL (normal <500/μL). A punch biopsy of the lesion demonstrates a dense dermal infiltrate composed predominantly of eosinophils with flame figures and no organisms on Gram stain.

items.teachingPoint: Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis) is characterized clinically by recurrent, erythematous, indurated plaques and histologically by dermal eosinophilic infiltrates with 'flame figures' (collagen coated with eosinophil granule proteins). After excluding bacterial cellulitis, first-line therapy for extensive or symptomatic lesions is a tapering course of oral systemic corticosteroids.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation and histologic findings (dense eosinophilic infiltrate with flame figures) are diagnostic of Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis). This condition is a benign, self-limited but often recurrent eosinophilic dermatosis. Because bacterial infection has been reasonably excluded by the absence of systemic symptoms, normal white blood cell count aside from eosinophilia, and negative Gram stain, the first-line treatment for symptomatic or extensive lesions is systemic corticosteroids (e.g., oral prednisone). A tapering course over several weeks is typically effective in resolving the inflammatory plaques and preventing early recurrence.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of progressive facial swelling, fever, and a pruritic rash. Two weeks ago, he was prescribed lamotrigine for new-onset seizures after a motor vehicle accident. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Examination reveals a morbilliform eruption involving the trunk and extremities, facial edema with periorbital swelling, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 14,000/mm3 with 25% eosinophils and an elevated liver transaminase level. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's condition?
items.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's condition?
items.learningObjective: Recognize the immunologic and temporal features that distinguish DRESS from other severe cutaneous adverse reactions.
items.correctAnswerText: Reactivation of human herpesvirus-6 or other latent viruses within the context of drug-specific CD8+ T-cell infiltration
items.teachingPoint: DRESS syndrome is distinguished by a 2- to 8-week latency period, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement. Its pathophysiology uniquely involves the reactivation of latent herpesviruses (especially HHV-6) alongside drug-specific T-cell responses, differentiating it from other severe cutaneous adverse reactions.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient's clinical presentation is classic for Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) syndrome. DRESS is a severe cutaneous adverse reaction characterized by a latency period of 2 to 8 weeks after drug initiation, fever, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, hematologic abnormalities (particularly eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytosis), and internal organ involvement, most commonly the liver. The pathophysiology involves a complex interplay between drug-specific T-cell responses and the reactivation of latent viruses, most notably human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6), but also Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus. The reactivation of these viruses is thought to contribute to the systemic symptoms and prolonged clinical course.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct cytotoxic T-cell activation against drug-modified host proteins without viral reactivation

options.label: C
options.text: Reactivation of human herpesvirus-6 or other latent viruses within the context of drug-specific CD8+ T-cell infiltration

options.label: D
options.text: Formation of immune complexes leading to complement activation and neutrophilic vasculitis

options.label: E
options.text: Epidermal keratinocyte apoptosis mediated by Fas-Fas ligand interactions resulting in widespread epidermal detachment

distractorExplanations.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation describes the mechanism of immediate hypersensitivity reactions, such as urticaria and anaphylaxis. distractorExplanations.text: Direct cytotoxic T-cell activation without viral reactivation is a feature of other drug eruptions like maculopapular exanthems, but it does not account for the specific viral reactivation component that is a hallmark of DRESS pathogenesis and contributes to its severity and systemic nature.

These conditions may present with fever and rash but typically lack the profound eosinophilia, facial edema, and specific latency period associated with DRESS.

These conditions present with mucosal involvement and widespread skin detachment rather than the facial edema, lymphadenopathy, and eosinophilia characteristic of DRESS.

Histology reveals spongiform subcorneal and intraepidermal pustules, papillary dermal edema, and a mixed infiltrate with eosinophils. Differentiating AGEP from generalized pustular psoriasis is critical, as the former typically resolves rapidly upon withdrawal of the offending drug, whereas the latter requires systemic immunosuppressive therapy.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a 10-day history of progressive facial swelling, fever, and a widespread rash. He was started on allopurinol 14 days ago for gout flares and has been taking it daily. Physical examination reveals diffuse, edematous, erythematous macules and papules covering more than 50% of his body surface area, prominent facial edema, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis with 18% eosinophilia, an absolute eosinophil count of 2.5 × 10^9/L, and elevated transaminases (AST 140 U/L, ALT 165 U/L). Renal function is normal. items.teachingPoint: For suspected DRESS syndrome, immediate discontinuation of the culprit drug is paramount. For moderate cases without life-threatening organ failure, oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg/day) is the first-line systemic treatment, while IV steroids are reserved for severe visceral involvement.

Oral prednisone at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day is the standard first-line therapy for moderate DRESS without life-threatening organ failure, allowing for gradual tapering over weeks to months. IV steroids are typically reserved for severe cases with hemodynamic instability or severe visceral organ involvement (e.g., severe hepatitis, pneumonitis).

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of progressive hair loss on the vertex and occipital scalp. She reports mild burning and tenderness over the affected areas. Examination reveals patchy hair loss with perifollicular erythema and scaling, along with focal areas of smooth, shiny skin indicating scarring. There are no signs of nail pitting or onycholysis. Given the mixed clinical features and uncertainty regarding the specific subtype of scarring alopecia, a biopsy is requested to guide therapy. Which of the following approaches is most appropriate for obtaining diagnostic tissue in this scenario?
items.leadIn: Which of the following approaches is most appropriate for obtaining diagnostic tissue in this scenario?
items.learningObjective: Identify the most appropriate biopsy approach for active scarring alopecia when the subtype remains uncertain.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform a single 6-mm punch biopsy from the active border of the lesion, ensuring both involved and uninvolved skin are included.
items.teachingPoint: When diagnosing scarring alopecia, a 6-mm punch biopsy should be performed at the active border of the lesion to capture both inflamed and unaffected skin, maximizing diagnostic yield. Biopsying the center of a scar often yields non-diagnostic end-stage fibrosis.
items.explanationCorrect: For the diagnosis of scarring alopecias, a 6-mm punch biopsy is preferred over smaller biopsies because it provides a full-thickness sample of the hair follicle, including the subcutaneous fat and surrounding tissue. This allows for adequate assessment of the extent of follicular destruction, inflammation pattern, and fibrosis. Biopsying the active border (the leading edge) is crucial because it captures both the actively inflamed tissue and adjacent unaffected skin, providing a clear transition zone that aids in distinguishing between different subtypes of scarring alopecia (e.g., lichen planopilaris vs. frontal fibrosing alopecia vs. discoid lupus erythematosus). Center-only biopsies may only show end-stage fibrosis, which is often non-diagnostic.

options.label: A
options.text: Perform a single 4-mm punch biopsy from the center of the smooth, scarred area.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform a single 6-mm punch biopsy from the active border of the lesion, ensuring both involved and uninvolved skin are included.

options.label: C
options.text: Perform a 4-mm punch biopsy from the center of the lesion and submit it for direct immunofluorescence.

options.label: D
options.text: Perform a single 6-mm punch biopsy from the center of the lesion and submit it for routine histopathology only.

options.label: E
options.text: Perform a 4-mm punch biopsy from the center of the lesion and submit it for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Biopsying the center of a scarred area often yields only end-stage fibrosis with a complete loss of follicular structures. This 'burned-out' tissue is frequently non-diagnostic and fails to show the characteristic inflammatory patterns required for subtype classification.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. A 6-mm punch biopsy at the active border provides a comprehensive sample of both diseased and healthy tissue, maximizing diagnostic yield for scarring alopecias.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: While direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is essential for diagnosing lupus erythematosus and lichen planopilaris, it requires a fresh, snap-frozen sample or specific transport media. Standard histopathology alone is insufficient for these diagnoses, but a biopsy from the center of a scar may still lack diagnostic architecture even if sent for DIF. Furthermore, DIF is typically performed on a separate biopsy or the same punch if specifically requested with appropriate handling, but the primary error here is biopsying the center of a scar where diagnostic follicles may be absent.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: A 4-mm punch biopsy is often too small to adequately capture the full depth of the hair follicle and surrounding subcutaneous fat, potentially leading to sampling error. Additionally, biopsying the center of a scar may miss active inflammation.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Microbiologic cultures are indicated if an infectious etiology (such as tinea capitis or kerion) is strongly suspected based on clinical features like pustules, purulent discharge, or significant lymphadenopathy. However, in a patient with established scarring and perifollicular erythema without signs of acute infection, cultures are low yield. Histopathologic evaluation is the primary diagnostic modality for inflammatory scarring alopecias.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive thickening and discoloration of his fingernails. He reports occasional itching on his scalp but denies joint pain or systemic symptoms. Examination reveals pitting of the nail plates, shortening and crumbling of the distal free edges, and a yellow-brown discoloration extending proximally from the nail bed. Several nails also demonstrate oil-drop-like salmon patches on the distal nail plates. The surrounding skin shows well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the extensor surfaces of his elbows. There is no evidence of subungual hyperkeratosis that can be easily scraped away, and fungal cultures are pending.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate nail psoriasis from onychomycosis and nail lichen planus.
items.teachingPoint: Psoriatic nail dystrophy is distinguished from onychomycosis and lichen planus by the presence of nail plate pitting, oil-drop (salmon) patches on the nail bed, and concurrent cutaneous psoriasis. Onychomycosis typically features subungual hyperkeratosis without pitting, while lichen planus is characterized by dorsal pterygium and nail thinning.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for psoriatic nail disease. Key distinguishing features include nail plate pitting, onycholysis with oil-drop (salmon patch) discoloration, and distal nail bed crumbling. The presence of concurrent cutaneous psoriasis (silvery plaques on elbows) strongly supports this diagnosis. While fungal infection can cause thickening and discoloration, the specific combination of pitting, oil-drop lesions, and skin findings points to psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Onychomycosis typically presents with subungual hyperkeratosis that can often be scraped away, distal lateral onycholysis, and yellow-brown discoloration. However, it does not cause nail plate pitting or salmon patches, and the concurrent cutaneous findings are specific to psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Nail lichen planus typically presents with thinning of the nail plate, longitudinal ridging (trachyonychia), dorsal pterygium formation, and sometimes complete nail destruction (anonychia). It lacks the oil-drop lesions and pitting seen in psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer - see above.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Traumatic onychodystrophy usually affects a single nail or nails corresponding to specific trauma. It may cause subungual hematoma or onycholysis but does not explain the multiple nail involvement, pitting, oil-drop lesions, or concurrent cutaneous psoriasis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Yellow nail syndrome is characterized by slow-growing, thickened, yellow nails with lymphedema and respiratory abnormalities. It does not present with pitting, oil-drop lesions, or associated cutaneous psoriasis.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive changes to his fingernails. He reports that the nails have become thickened and discolored, initially on the third digits of both hands. He denies any history of trauma or exposure to fungi. On examination, there is pitting of the nail plate on multiple digits, including the thumbs and great toes. The distal edges of the nails show subungual hyperkeratosis, and there is a characteristic 'oil drop' discoloration (salmon patch) visible on the third fingernails. The surrounding skin is erythematous with silvery scaling.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate nail psoriasis from onychomycosis and nail lichen planus.
items.teachingPoint: Nail psoriasis is distinguished from onychomycosis and nail lichen planus by the presence of pitting, subungual hyperkeratosis, and the pathognomonic 'oil drop' (salmon patch) sign. Lichen planus typically causes scarring changes like dorsal pterygium, while onychomycosis lacks pitting and the oil drop sign.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for nail psoriasis. Key clinical features include nail pitting (the most common finding), subungual hyperkeratosis, and the pathognomonic 'oil drop' or salmon patch discoloration. The presence of silvery scaling on the surrounding skin strongly supports a diagnosis of psoriasis over other nail disorders. While onychomycosis can cause thickening and discoloration, it typically lacks pitting and the specific oil drop sign.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Dermatophyte onychomycosis typically presents with distal lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO), characterized by yellow-brown discoloration, subungual debris, and onycholysis. While it can cause nail thickening, pitting is not a feature of fungal infection, and the 'oil drop' sign is absent. Fungal cultures or KOH prep would be negative in this case.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Nail psoriasis is the correct diagnosis, so no distractor explanation needed for B.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Lichen planus of the nail typically presents with thinning of the nail plate, longitudinal ridging (onychorrhexis), dorsal pterygium formation (scarring of the proximal nail fold), and sometimes total nail dystrophy or anonychia. It does not typically present with pitting, oil drop discoloration, or subungual hyperkeratosis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Onychogryphosis is a thickening and curvature of the nail, resembling a ram's horn, usually caused by chronic trauma or neglect in elderly patients. It does not present with pitting, oil drop discoloration, or silvery scaling.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Yellow nail syndrome is characterized by slow-growing, thickened, yellow-green nails with loss of the lunula and cuticle. It is often associated with lymphedema and respiratory diseases (e.g., bronchiectasis, pleural effusions). It does not present with pitting or oil drop discoloration.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of symmetric, hyperpigmented patches on her cheeks and forehead. She reports the discoloration worsens during summer months but partially fades in winter. She denies any preceding inflammatory skin disease, trauma, or use of topical bleaching agents, but admits to inconsistent sunscreen use. Dermoscopy reveals a reticular brown pattern with no telangiectasias, and Wood lamp examination accentuates the pigmentation. Which of the following clinical features would most reliably distinguish this condition from postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and exogenous ochronosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following clinical features would most reliably distinguish this condition from postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and exogenous ochronosis?
items.learningObjective: Identify the bedside discriminator that separates melasma from postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and exogenous ochronosis.
items.correctAnswerText: Symmetric distribution across sun-exposed facial areas
items.teachingPoint: Symmetric distribution of hyperpigmented patches on sun-exposed facial areas is a key clinical discriminator for melasma, helping to distinguish it from postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (often localized to sites of inflammation) and exogenous ochronosis (characterized by blue-black discoloration and follicular plugging).
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for melasma, characterized by symmetric, hyperpigmented macules and patches on sun-exposed facial areas (cheeks, forehead, upper lip). While melasma can be associated with sun exposure, its hallmark is the symmetric distribution. Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) typically occurs at sites of prior inflammation or trauma and lacks this symmetric, sun-exposed pattern. Exogenous ochronosis presents with blue-black discoloration and follicular plugging, often with a mottled appearance, rather than the symmetric brown patches of melasma. Therefore, symmetry and distribution are key bedside discriminators.

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of a history of preceding inflammatory skin disease

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of black or blue-gray dots and globules on dermoscopy

options.label: C
options.text: Symmetric distribution across sun-exposed facial areas

options.label: D
options.text: Worsening of pigmentation with exposure to visible light

options.label: E
options.text: Reversibility upon strict sun avoidance and topical therapy

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: A history of preceding inflammatory skin disease is a risk factor for postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), not melasma. While helpful to identify PIH, it does not reliably distinguish melasma from exogenous ochronosis, which is caused by topical hydroquinone use and not necessarily preceded by inflammation.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Dermoscopic findings can help differentiate these conditions, but the absence of black/blue-gray dots and globules is more specific for ruling out exogenous ochronosis. Melasma typically shows a reticular pattern, and PIH can show various patterns depending on the depth of pigment. While useful, this is a dermoscopic finding rather than a primary bedside clinical discriminator compared to distribution.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Symmetric distribution across sun-exposed facial areas is a hallmark of melasma and helps distinguish it from PIH (often localized to sites of injury) and exogenous ochronosis (which can be asymmetric or associated with specific application areas).

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Melasma and PIH are primarily exacerbated by ultraviolet (UV) radiation, not visible light. While some studies suggest visible light may play a role in melasma, it is not the primary discriminator. Exogenous ochronosis is also primarily related to hydroquinone toxicity and sun exposure, but the light spectrum itself is not a reliable distinguishing feature at the bedside.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: All three conditions—melasma, PIH, and exogenous ochronosis—can potentially improve with sun avoidance and topical therapies (though exogenous ochronosis is notoriously difficult to treat). Therefore, reversibility or response to therapy does not reliably distinguish between them.

items.teachingPoint: Wood lamp examination is a valuable bedside tool to differentiate melasma from exogenous ochronosis. Exogenous ochronosis presents with characteristic brownish-black speckles or blue-gray hues under Wood lamp, whereas melasma shows accentuated pigmentation without these specific speckles.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for melasma, characterized by symmetric hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed areas (malar cheeks, forehead) that worsens with UV exposure. Melasma typically shows accentuation of pigmentation under Wood lamp if it is epidermal, but it lacks the pathognomonic brownish-black speckles or blue-gray hues seen in exogenous ochronosis. Exogenous ochronosis, often resulting from prolonged use of hydroquinone-containing creams, is characterized by these specific speckled patterns under Wood lamp. Therefore, the absence of these speckles helps rule out exogenous ochronosis and supports the diagnosis of melasma.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of progressive darkening of the nail plate on his right thumb. He reports no recent trauma to the digit and denies pain or bleeding. Examination reveals a single, irregularly bordered brown-to-black band measuring 4 mm in width extending from the proximal nail fold to the free edge. The pigmentation crosses onto the adjacent proximal nail fold skin, and there is no evidence of subungual hemorrhage or psoriatic changes. The patient has a history of chronic sun exposure but no personal or family history of melanoma.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best step for a concerning longitudinal melanonychia suspicious for nail unit melanoma.
items.correctAnswerText: Punch biopsy of the proximal nail matrix and bed
items.teachingPoint: In adults with longitudinal melanonychia, high-risk features such as a single band wider than 3 mm, irregular borders, and Hutchinson sign (pigmentation of the proximal nail fold) strongly suggest nail unit melanoma. These patients require prompt biopsy of the nail matrix and bed for histopathologic evaluation.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient presents with longitudinal melanonychia that exhibits several high-risk features for nail unit melanoma, including adult onset, a single band greater than 3 mm in width, irregular borders, and Hutchinson sign (pigmentation extending to the proximal nail fold). In adults, especially those over 50 years of age, these clinical findings warrant histopathologic evaluation to rule out melanoma. A longitudinal incisional biopsy or punch biopsy of the proximal nail matrix and bed is the standard next step to obtain a definitive diagnosis while preserving as much of the nail unit architecture as possible for future reconstruction if necessary.

options.label: A
options.text: Observation with serial photography and reassurance

options.label: B
options.text: Application of topical corticosteroids to the nail fold

options.label: C
options.text: Punch biopsy of the proximal nail matrix and bed

options.label: D
options.text: Total excision of the entire nail unit with the nail plate removed

options.label: E
options.text: Laser therapy targeting the pigmented band

distractorExplanations.text: Observation with serial photography is inappropriate given the high-risk clinical features. While longitudinal melanonychia can be benign, particularly in children and darker-skinned adults with multiple bands, the presence of Hutchinson sign and a single wide band in an older adult mandates biopsy to exclude malignancy.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Topical corticosteroids are used for inflammatory conditions such as lichen planus or psoriasis. This patient lacks signs of inflammation, nail dystrophy typical of lichen planus (e.g., pterygium formation), or psoriatic changes. While other features like a history of stress or positive pull test can be seen in both conditions (or suggest non-scarring processes generally), the lack of inflammatory scalp changes is the key feature that effectively rules out active scarring alopecia in this vignette.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 3-month history of sudden, diffuse hair shedding. She reports finding large amounts of hair in her shower drain and on her pillowcases, though she has not noticed any distinct bald patches. She recalls a severe episode of high fever and dehydration from gastroenteritis approximately 3 months ago that required hospitalization. She has no personal or family history of alopecia areata, and her menstrual cycles have been regular. Physical examination reveals a normal scalp without erythema, scaling, or scarring. Hair pull test is positive with 5-7 telogen hairs per grip. Dermoscopy shows a normal density of terminal and vellus hairs with no black dots, exclamation mark hairs, or broken hairs. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the most appropriate next step for diffuse acute telogen effluvium once serious mimics have been excluded.
items.correctAnswerText: Reassure the patient and schedule follow-up in 3 months
items.teachingPoint: Acute telogen effluvium is a self-limiting condition triggered by physiologic stressors. Once scarring alopecias and inflammatory mimics are excluded clinically, the mainstay of management is patient reassurance and observation, as spontaneous regrowth typically occurs within 6 to 9 months.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for acute telogen effluvium (TE), triggered by a significant physiologic stressor such as severe illness, fever, or surgery approximately 2-3 months prior to the onset of shedding. The diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by a positive pull test and dermoscopic findings of normal hair density without signs of scarring or inflammation. Once serious mimics like alopecia areata, secondary syphilis, and lupus erythematosus have been clinically excluded (as suggested by the normal scalp exam and dermoscopy), no further diagnostic testing or pharmacologic intervention is required. TE is self-limiting, and hair regrowth typically occurs spontaneously within 6 to 9 months after the inciting event. Reassurance and observation are the most appropriate management strategies.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of progressive, painful erosions on her gingiva and buccal mucosa. She reports that the lesions occasionally bleed during brushing and are accompanied by desquamative blisters on her scalp, which have left areas of scarring alopecia. Examination reveals diffuse erythematous and erosive gingivitis with white, lacy striae on the adjacent buccal mucosa. A punch biopsy of an intact blister shows a subepithelial split with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate and direct immunofluorescence demonstrates linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate mucous membrane pemphigoid from erosive lichen planus and recurrent aphthosis in chronic oral disease.
items.teachingPoint: Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) is characterized by chronic, scarring mucosal erosions (often desquamative gingivitis) and potentially cutaneous involvement. Diagnosis relies on histology showing a subepithelial blister and direct immunofluorescence demonstrating linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane zone. It must be distinguished from erosive lichen planus (which has band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and fibrinogen DIF) and pemphigus vulgaris (which has intraepidermal acantholysis and intercellular IgG DIF).
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of chronic, painful gingival erosions (desquamative gingivitis) and scarring alopecia is highly suggestive of a mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) spectrum disorder. The key diagnostic findings are the subepithelial blister split on histology and, most importantly, the linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence (DIF). This distinguishes it from lichen planus and pemphigus. Note: Cicatricial pemphigoid is an older term largely synonymous with MMP, but MMP is the preferred modern terminology for this clinical entity.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erosive lichen planus can present with desquamative gingivitis and white striae (Wickham striae), which are present in this patient. However, histology would show a hyperkeratotic epidermis with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, not a subepithelial split. DIF would show fibrinogen deposition at the basement membrane, not linear IgG/C3.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Mucous membrane pemphigoid

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis presents with recurrent, discrete, round ulcers with a yellow-gray pseudomembrane and erythematous halo. It is not chronic, progressive, or associated with scarring alopecia. Histology shows nonspecific inflammation without subepithelial splits or linear immunofluorescence.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Pemphigus vulgaris causes flaccid blisters and erosions. Histology shows an intraepidermal split (acantholysis), not a subepithelial split. DIF demonstrates intercellular deposition of IgG throughout the epidermis (chicken-wire pattern), not linear basement membrane deposition.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Cicatricial pemphigoid is a historical term often used interchangeably with mucous membrane pemphigoid. However, in modern classification and board examinations, 'Mucous membrane pemphigoid' is the preferred and more accurate diagnostic term for this clinical presentation involving mucous membranes and scarring alopecia. The immunofluorescence pattern described is classic for MMP.

However, the item is fundamentally flawed because it includes two synonymous terms (MMP and Cicatricial pemphigoid) as options. In a high-stakes examination, if two options represent the same medical diagnosis, the item is invalid. The question shifts from testing clinical diagnosis to testing nomenclature preference.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of progressive oral discomfort and difficulty eating. She reports that her gums are often tender, bleed easily with brushing, and occasionally form blisters that rupture to leave painful ulcers. Examination reveals diffuse erythema and desquamative gingivitis with scattered white, reticulated striae on the buccal mucosa. There are no cutaneous lesions or nail changes. Direct immunofluorescence of a perilesional biopsy shows linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate mucous membrane pemphigoid from erosive lichen planus and recurrent aphthosis in chronic oral disease.
items.teachingPoint: Desquamative gingivitis is a clinical descriptor, not a specific diagnosis. Mucous membrane pemphigoid must be distinguished from erosive lichen planus and other blistering diseases. Linear IgG/C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence is pathognomonic for mucous membrane pemphigoid, whereas lichen planus shows fibrinogen deposition and pemphigus vulgaris shows intercellular IgG.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's clinical presentation of desquamative gingivitis, recurrent oral blisters/ulcers, and the key histopathologic finding of linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence is diagnostic of mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP). Although white reticulated striae can suggest lichen planus, the immunofluorescence pattern is definitive for MMP. The absence of skin or nail involvement does not rule out MMP, as it can be limited to mucous membranes.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erosive lichen planus can present with desquamative gingivitis and white striae. However, direct immunofluorescence in lichen planus typically shows a shaggy band of fibrinogen at the basement membrane zone, not linear IgG and C3 deposition.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Mucous membrane pemphigoid

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis presents with discrete, round/oval ulcers with a yellow-gray pseudomembrane and erythematous halo. It does not cause desquamative gingivitis, blistering, or basement membrane zone immunofluorescence deposits.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Pemphigus vulgaris typically presents with flaccid bullae and painful erosions on the oral mucosa. However, direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular (chicken-wire) IgG deposition within the epidermis, not linear basement membrane deposition.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Discoid lupus erythematosus can cause oral lesions and may show immunofluorescence at the basement membrane zone. However, it typically presents with well-demarcated plaques, follicular plugging, and atrophy on the skin. Oral lesions are usually central erythema with peripheral radiating striae, and DIF typically shows granular IgG/IgM/C3 deposition rather than the linear pattern seen in MMP.
