items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of depigmented patches on her forearms and perioral region. She recalls a severe allergic contact dermatitis reaction to hair dye approximately 8 months ago that resolved completely. The patches are well-demarcated and milky white in color, with no scale or residual erythema. Wood lamp examination reveals accentuated fluorescence of the lesions. A punch biopsy is performed to clarify the diagnosis.
items.leadIn: Which histopathologic finding would most reliably distinguish this patient's condition from postinflammatory hypopigmentation?
items.learningObjective: Identify the most useful discriminator between vitiligo and postinflammatory hypopigmentation.
items.correctAnswerText: Absence of melanocytes in the basal layer
items.teachingPoint: The most reliable histopathologic discriminator between vitiligo and postinflammatory hypopigmentation is the presence versus absence of melanocytes in the epidermis. Vitiligo shows complete loss of melanocytes, whereas PIH retains melanocytes with reduced melanin content.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of vitiligo, characterized by acquired depigmentation. The key histopathologic discriminator between vitiligo and postinflammatory hypopigmentation (PIH) is the status of melanocytes. In vitiligo, there is a complete absence or near-complete depletion of melanocytes in the epidermis. In contrast, PIH typically shows a preserved number of melanocytes but with decreased melanin production and transfer. Therefore, the absence of melanocytes confirms vitiligo.

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of melanocytes in the basal layer

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased number of melanosomes within keratinocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Increased melanin in the stratum corneum

options.label: D
options.text: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction

options.label: E
options.text: Basal layer vacuolization with apoptotic keratinocytes

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. Absence of melanocytes is the hallmark of vitiligo.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Decreased number of melanosomes within keratinocytes is characteristic of postinflammatory hypopigmentation, where melanocytes are present but functionally impaired or have reduced melanin transfer. This finding would support PIH rather than vitiligo.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Increased melanin in the stratum corneum is not a specific discriminator and may be seen in various conditions, including hyperpigmentation or normal skin turnover. It does not help distinguish between vitiligo and PIH.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction is seen in interface dermatitides such as lichen planus or lupus erythematosus. While inflammation may precede PIH, this finding is not specific to either vitiligo or PIH and does not address melanocyte presence.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Basal layer vacuolization with apoptotic keratinocytes is characteristic of interface dermatitis (e.g., lichen planus, lupus erythematosus). This finding indicates active inflammation and tissue damage, which may precede PIH but does not distinguish vitiligo from PIH.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of depigmented patches on her forearms and around the mouth. She reports a severe allergic contact dermatitis to nickel jewelry 8 months ago that resolved with topical corticosteroids. Since the rash cleared, she noticed pale patches developing exactly where the dermatitis occurred, as well as new symmetrically distributed macules on her forearms and perioral area. On examination, there are well-demarcated ivory-white macules with no scale or atrophy. Wood lamp examination reveals bright blue-white fluorescence of the lesions.
items.leadIn: Which of the following findings would best distinguish this patient's condition from postinflammatory hypopigmentation?
items.learningObjective: Identify the most useful discriminator between vitiligo and postinflammatory hypopigmentation.
items.correctAnswerText: Absence of melanocytes on skin biopsy
items.teachingPoint: The most useful discriminator between vitiligo and postinflammatory hypopigmentation is the presence of melanocytes in the epidermis. Vitiligo is characterized by an absence of melanocytes, whereas PIH retains normal melanocyte counts with impaired pigment production or transfer.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is highly suggestive of vitiligo, an acquired depigmenting disorder characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of melanocytes. The key discriminator between vitiligo and postinflammatory hypopigmentation (PIH) is the presence or absence of melanocytes in the epidermis. In vitiligo, histopathology typically shows a complete absence of melanocytes in the affected skin. In contrast, PIH retains normal numbers of melanocytes; the hypopigmentation results from impaired melanin transfer or decreased melanogenesis following inflammation. Therefore, a skin biopsy demonstrating an absence of melanocytes is the most definitive way to distinguish vitiligo from PIH.

options.label: C
options.text: Absence of melanocytes on skin biopsy

options.label: E
options.text: Bright blue-white fluorescence on Wood lamp examination

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Perifollicular repigmentation is a feature of vitiligo treatment response, not a diagnostic discriminator between vitiligo and PIH.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: A history of preceding cutaneous inflammation is characteristic of postinflammatory hypopigmentation, but this patient's new symmetrically distributed lesions suggest vitiligo. However, patients can have both conditions simultaneously (vitiligo arising in areas of prior inflammation), so history alone is not the most reliable discriminator.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Absence of melanocytes on biopsy confirms vitiligo, whereas PIH retains melanocytes.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Symmetric distribution is common in vitiligo but can also occur in PIH if the initial inflammation was symmetric. It is not a definitive discriminator.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Both vitiligo and PIH can show hypopigmentation on Wood lamp examination. While vitiligo typically shows bright blue-white fluorescence due to complete lack of pigment, PIH may show less intense hypofluorescence. However, Wood lamp findings can be subjective and overlapping; histology is superior.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of progressive hair loss on the vertex and occiput. She reports significant scalp pruritus, burning, and tenderness over the affected areas. Examination reveals ill-defined patches of erythema with perifollicular scaling and hyperkeratosis. There is marked perifollicular erythema and cast formation, along with scattered areas of scarring alopecia. No mucosal lesions or cutaneous plaques are observed elsewhere on the body.
items.leadIn: Which of the following histopathologic findings would most likely confirm this patient's diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate lichen planopilaris from discoid lupus erythematosus and central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia in scarring alopecia.
items.correctAnswerText: Lymphocytic destruction of the follicular infundibulum and isthmus with a band-like infiltrate sparing the interfollicular epidermis
items.teachingPoint: Lichen planopilaris is a primary lymphocytic scarring alopecia characterized clinically by perifollicular erythema, scaling, and significant pruritus/burning. Histopathology reveals a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate targeting the follicular infundibulum and isthmus with sparing of the interfollicular epidermis. This distinguishes it from discoid lupus erythematosus (which features interface dermatitis, mucin, and thickened basement membranes) and central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (which is often asymptomatic with sparse infiltrates and sebaceous gland loss).
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of progressive vertex/occipital hair loss accompanied by significant pruritus, burning, and tenderness is classic for lichen planopilaris (LPP). LPP is a primary lymphocytic scarring alopecia. Histopathology characteristically shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate targeting the follicular infundibulum and isthmus, leading to perifollicular fibrosis. A key distinguishing feature is the preservation of the interfollicular epidermis, which helps differentiate it from discoid lupus erythematosus.

options.label: A
options.text: Perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate with vacuolar interface dermatitis and thickened basement membrane

options.label: B
options.text: Follicular plugging with hydropic degeneration of the basal layer and mucin deposition in the dermis

options.label: C
options.text: Lymphocytic destruction of the follicular infundibulum and isthmus with a band-like infiltrate sparing the interfollicular epidermis

options.text: Neutrophilic infiltrate centered on the follicular ostia with abscess formation and sinus tract development

options.label: E
options.text: Fibrosis of the follicular stem cell region with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate and loss of sebaceous glands

distractorExplanations.text: This describes the histopathology of discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE). Histologically, DLE features vacuolar interface dermatitis, thickened basement membranes, and periadnexal infiltrates. distractorExplanations.text: This option also describes features of discoid lupus erythematosus, specifically follicular plugging and mucin deposition. The clinical absence of classic DLE plaques and the presence of significant burning/pruritus favor LPP.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. This is the hallmark histopathologic finding of lichen planopilaris.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: This describes folliculitis decalvans, a neutrophilic scarring alopecia. It presents with pustules, crusting, and tufted folliculitis (polytrichia). The absence of pustules and the presence of significant pruritus/burning make this diagnosis unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: This describes central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA). CCCA typically affects women of African descent and presents with vertex hair loss that spreads centrifugally. It is often asymptomatic or associated with mild discomfort, unlike the significant pruritus and burning seen in LPP. Histologically, it shows early perifollicular fibrosis with a sparse infiltrate and loss of sebaceous glands.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of progressive hair loss and scalp pruritus. She reports burning sensations over the vertex and parietal regions where her hair is thinning. Examination reveals patchy, erythematous plaques with perifollicular scaling and hyperkeratotic plugs. There is significant loss of follicular ostia in the affected areas, surrounded by a subtle erythematous halo. A few scattered follicular papules are noted at the periphery of the lesions. Direct immunofluorescence is pending.
items.leadIn: Which of the following histopathologic findings would most strongly support the diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate lichen planopilaris from discoid lupus erythematosus and central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia in scarring alopecia.
items.correctAnswerText: Follicular plugging with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the follicular infundibulum and basket-weave orthokeratosis
items.teachingPoint: Lichen planopilaris is a primary cicatricial alopecia characterized clinically by perifollicular erythema, scaling, and hyperkeratotic plugs. Histopathology typically reveals a lichenoid infiltrate centered on the follicular infundibulum, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, and basket-weave orthokeratosis. Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is a key differential diagnosis; DLE histology typically shows compact hyperkeratosis, vacuolar interface changes with basement membrane thickening, and dermal mucin. Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA) typically shows perifollicular fibrosis with sparse inflammation and lacks prominent follicular plugging.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of perifollicular scaling, hyperkeratotic plugs, loss of follicular ostia, and burning/pruritus is highly characteristic of lichen planopilaris (LPP), a primary cicatricial alopecia. Histopathologically, LPP is characterized by a lichenoid tissue reaction pattern centered on the upper follicle and isthmus, featuring hyperkeratosis (often with prominent follicular plugging), wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, and a dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction of the infundibulum. Basket-weave orthokeratosis is also commonly seen in LPP, distinguishing it from the compact hyperkeratosis often seen in discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE).

options.label: A
options.text: Follicular plugging with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the follicular infundibulum and basket-weave orthokeratosis

options.label: B
options.text: Thinning of the granular layer with hyperkeratosis, dilated follicular ostia, and a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis

options.label: C
options.text: Perifollicular fibrosis with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate and absence of follicular plugging

options.label: D
options.text: Neutrophilic abscesses surrounding the hair shafts with follicular destruction and scarring

options.label: E
options.text: Mucin deposition in the dermis around hair follicles with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Follicular plugging with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the follicular infundibulum and basket-weave orthokeratosis is characteristic of Lichen Planopilaris, not Discoid Lupus Erythematosus. DLE typically shows compact hyperkeratosis, vacuolar interface dermatitis with thickening of the basement membrane, and mucin deposition in the dermis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Perifollicular fibrosis with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate is characteristic of Central Centrifugal Cicatricial Alopecia (CCCA). While CCCA presents with vertex hair loss and follicular dropout, it typically lacks the prominent perifollicular inflammation, scaling, and hyperkeratotic plugs seen in LPP or DLE.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Neutrophilic abscesses surrounding the hair shafts are characteristic of dissecting cellulitis of the scalp or folliculitis decalvans, which present with pustules and crusts rather than the dry, scaly plaques and follicular plugs of LPP.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Mucin deposition in the dermis is a hallmark of Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) and can also be seen in lupus erythematosus tumidus. While DLE is a key differential for LPP, the presence of mucin and compact hyperkeratosis (rather than basket-weave orthokeratosis) favors DLE over LPP.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of severe swelling, erythema, and weeping of the eyelids, ears, and posterior neck following her first use of a new permanent black hair dye at home. She reports intense pruritus and burning that began 24 hours after application. Physical examination reveals diffuse edema with facial puffiness, particularly around the eyes, and erythematous plaques with serous crusting on the hairline and behind the ears. There is no history of atopy or prior skin reactions to cosmetics.
items.leadIn: Which of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis rather than irritant contact dermatitis in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine from irritant dermatitis in a hair-dye reaction.
items.correctAnswerText: A positive patch test to para-phenylenediamine 1% in petrolatum
items.teachingPoint: A positive patch test to para-phenylenediamine is the definitive diagnostic tool for distinguishing allergic contact dermatitis from irritant contact dermatitis in hair dye reactions, as it confirms type IV hypersensitivity sensitization.
items.explanationCorrect: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a common component of permanent hair dyes, is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. A positive patch test to PPD provides objective confirmation of sensitization and is the gold standard for diagnosing ACD. The clinical presentation of facial edema, especially periorbital swelling and involvement of the ears and posterior neck (areas where dye may drip or be applied), is classic for PPD allergy. The delayed onset of symptoms (24-72 hours) further supports a cell-mediated immune response rather than direct tissue toxicity.

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema limited to the scalp with sparing of the face

options.label: B
options.text: Pruritus as the predominant symptom rather than burning or pain

options.label: C
options.text: A positive patch test to para-phenylenediamine 1% in petrolatum

options.label: D
options.text: Onset of symptoms within 4 hours of dye application

options.label: E
options.text: Absence of vesicles or bullae on the affected skin

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Erythema limited to the scalp with sparing of the face is more characteristic of irritant contact dermatitis, which typically occurs at the site of direct chemical exposure without significant spread. Allergic reactions often extend beyond the application site due to systemic absorption or autoeczematization.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: While pruritus is common in both ACD and irritant contact dermatitis, burning or pain is often more prominent in irritant reactions. However, pruritus alone is not diagnostic, as both conditions can cause significant itching.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: A positive patch test to para-phenylenediamine 1% in petrolatum is the most specific and definitive evidence for ACD to PPD. It directly demonstrates delayed-type hypersensitivity, distinguishing it from irritant dermatitis which would not elicit an immune response.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Rapid onset within 4 hours suggests irritant contact dermatitis or a toxic reaction, as allergic reactions typically require sensitization and take 24-72 hours to manifest clinically.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: The absence of vesicles or bullae does not rule out ACD. While severe ACD can present with vesiculation, milder or early cases may only show erythema and edema. Irritant dermatitis can also present without vesicles depending on the irritant strength and exposure duration.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of severe scalp pruritus, erythema, and swelling following the use of a new permanent hair dye. She reports applying the product to her scalp 48 hours ago without gloves or waiting for a patch test. Physical examination reveals marked edema of the scalp, pinnae, and periorbital regions. The erythema extends beyond the hairline onto the forehead and neck. There are no vesicles or bullae, but the skin appears dry and fissured at the hairline. She has no history of eczema or prior adverse reactions to cosmetics.
items.leadIn: Which of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of allergic contact dermatitis rather than irritant contact dermatitis in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine from irritant dermatitis in a hair-dye reaction.
items.correctAnswerText: Delayed onset of symptoms 48 hours after exposure
items.teachingPoint: Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine in hair dyes is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction, typically presenting 24-72 hours after exposure with severe edema and erythema of the scalp, face, and pinnae. The delayed onset helps distinguish it from irritant contact dermatitis, which usually presents within hours of exposure.
items.explanationCorrect: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a common ingredient in permanent hair dyes, is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Symptoms typically manifest 24 to 72 hours after exposure, which aligns with this patient's presentation at 48 hours. The characteristic clinical features of PPD ACD include severe edema, erythema, and scaling affecting the scalp, pinnae, periorbital regions, and face, often extending beyond the area of direct application. The delayed onset is a hallmark distinguishing feature from irritant contact dermatitis, which typically presents immediately or within hours of exposure.

distractorExplanations.text: The absence of vesicles or bullae does not rule out ACD. While acute irritant dermatitis may present with more immediate blistering or erosion, chronic or subacute ACD can present primarily with erythema, edema, and scaling without vesicles.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Failure to use gloves is a risk factor for both irritant and allergic contact dermatitis. While it increases the likelihood of skin injury facilitating sensitization (irritant mechanism), it does not specifically distinguish between the two pathophysiologic processes.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Dryness and fissuring at the hairline are signs of epidermal barrier disruption common in irritant contact dermatitis. While they can occur in ACD, they are more characteristic of the direct cytotoxic effects seen in irritant reactions.

items.stem: A 34-year-old nurse presents with a 6-month history of worsening bilateral hand dermatitis. She reports intense pruritus and fissuring, particularly over the dorsal aspects of her hands and between her fingers. Her symptoms worsen after wearing latex gloves for prolonged periods during surgery but persist despite strict avoidance of latex and use of nitrile gloves. She has been applying over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% ointment twice daily for the past three months with minimal relief. Physical examination reveals erythematous, scaly plaques with multiple linear fissures on the dorsal hands and interdigital spaces. Patch testing to the standard series is negative, but she has a positive reaction to rubber accelerator additives in her nitrile gloves.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate next step for chronic occupational hand dermatitis in a healthcare worker.
items.correctAnswerText: Prescribe a high-potency topical corticosteroid ointment and reinforce strict barrier protection
items.teachingPoint: In chronic occupational hand dermatitis, especially with fissuring and failure of OTC therapy, optimize treatment with high-potency topical corticosteroids ointments and strict allergen avoidance before considering systemic therapies.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient has chronic occupational hand dermatitis, likely allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerators in her nitrile gloves. The most appropriate next step is to optimize topical therapy with a high-potency corticosteroid ointment (e.g., clobetasol) to reduce inflammation and fissuring, combined with strict avoidance of the offending allergen and reinforcement of barrier protection. This approach addresses both the inflammatory component and the ongoing exposure.

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe a high-potency topical corticosteroid ointment and reinforce strict barrier protection

options.label: C
options.text: Refer for photopatch testing to rule out photoallergic contact dermatitis

options.label: D
options.text: Start oral cyclosporine therapy for rapid symptom control

options.label: E
options.text: Switch to vinyl gloves and continue current topical regimen

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic methotrexate is reserved for severe, recalcitrant cases of hand dermatitis that fail optimized topical therapy and strict avoidance. It is not indicated as the next step here.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Photopatch testing is indicated if there is a history of sun-exacerbated dermatitis or exposure to photoallergens. This patient's dermatitis is localized to the hands and linked to glove use, making photoallergy unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Oral cyclosporine is a potent immunosuppressant used for severe, refractory cases. It carries significant side effects and is not appropriate before trying optimized topical therapy.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Switching to vinyl gloves may help if the allergen is in nitrile, but continuing a low-potency OTC steroid is insufficient for chronic fissuring dermatitis. A high-potency prescription steroid is needed.

items.stem: A 34-year-old nurse presents with a 6-month history of recurrent, painful fissures and erythema on her dorsal hands. She works in a busy emergency department where she frequently uses alcohol-based hand sanitizers and latex-free nitrile gloves. Despite consistent use of a thick, fragrance-free emollient multiple times daily and short courses of mid-potency topical corticosteroids prescribed by her primary care physician, her symptoms persist and worsen during work shifts. They are safe for long-term use and do not cause skin thinning, making them ideal for the hands.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of intensely pruritic, erythematous vesicles and bullae on his forearms and hands after accidentally brushing against poison ivy while hiking. He has tried over-the-counter calamine lotion and cool compresses without relief. Physical examination reveals widespread, confluent vesicular dermatitis involving both forearms and extending to the proximal upper arms. He has no systemic symptoms, but the itching is significantly impairing his sleep and ability to work. His medical history is unremarkable, and he takes no regular medications.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic corticosteroid strategy for severe Toxicodendron allergic contact dermatitis.
items.correctAnswerText: Prescribe a 21-day tapering course of oral prednisone starting at 60 mg daily
items.teachingPoint: For severe Toxicodendron allergic contact dermatitis, a prolonged tapering course of systemic corticosteroids (typically 2 to 3 weeks) is required. Short courses (<7-10 days) are associated with a high risk of rebound dermatitis due to the prolonged persistence of urushiol in the skin.
items.explanationCorrect: Severe Toxicodendron (poison ivy/oak/sumac) allergic contact dermatitis often requires a prolonged taper of systemic corticosteries. The standard recommendation is to start at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day (or a fixed dose of 40-60 mg daily) and taper over 2 to 3 weeks (14-21 days). A short course of less than 7-10 days is associated with a high rate of rebound dermatitis because the allergen (urushiol) persists in the stratum corneum and sebaceous glands for weeks. A 21-day taper starting at 60 mg provides adequate duration to prevent rebound while allowing a gradual withdrawal of the anti-inflammatory effect.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with an intensely pruritic eruption that develops on sun-exposed areas within hours of midday outdoor activity during a spring vacation. The rash consists of multiple erythematous papules and plaques with some coalescence, predominantly on the V of her neck and dorsal forearms. The lesions spontaneously resolve within days to weeks after strict sun avoidance, leaving mild hyperpigmentation but no scarring or follicular plugging. She denies new medications, systemic symptoms like joint pain or fever, and has no history of photosensitivity. A punch biopsy shows a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered apoptotic keratinocytes but lacks the interface dermatitis, basement membrane thickening, or mucin deposition typically seen in lupus erythematosus.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate polymorphous light eruption from subacute cutaneous lupus and phototoxic drug reaction.
items.teachingPoint: PMLE is characterized by intensely pruritic papules/plaques on sun-exposed skin appearing hours to days after UV exposure, resolving without scarring. Histology shows superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with apoptotic keratinocytes, lacking the interface changes and mucin of lupus erythematosus. Phototoxic reactions cause exaggerated sunburns, while SCLE features annular/psoriasiform lesions with distinct histologic interface changes.
items.explanationCorrect: Polymorphous light eruption (PMLE) is the most common idiopathic photodermatosis, typically presenting in young women as intensely pruritic papules and plaques on sun-exposed areas within hours to days of UV exposure. The lesions resolve spontaneously without scarring or dyspigmentation (though mild hyperpigmentation can occur). Histology shows a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with apoptotic keratinocytes, distinguishing it from lupus erythematosus. The absence of systemic symptoms, lack of follicular plugging or scarring, and negative medication history further support PMLE over other photodermatoses.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) typically presents with annular or psoriasiform lesions that are less pruritic and more photosensitive, often involving the upper back. Histology would show prominent interface dermatitis with basal vacuolization, basement membrane thickening, and dermal mucin deposition. The patient lacks systemic symptoms (e.g., arthralgias) and the biopsy does not support lupus.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Polymorphous light eruption is the correct diagnosis, as explained above.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Phototoxic drug reactions usually present with exaggerated sunburn-like erythema, edema, and bullae confined strictly to the exposed areas. They are not typically intensely pruritic papules/plaques and resolve more quickly without residual hyperpigmentation in many cases. The patient denies new medications, making this unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Allergic contact dermatitis to sunscreen would present as an eczematous, weeping, or vesicular eruption in areas where the product was applied. It is not strictly limited to sun-exposed skin and would likely involve shaded areas if the product was applied there. The distribution and morphology do not fit.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Porphyria cutanea tarda presents with fragile skin, vesicles, bullae, and erosions on sun-exposed areas (especially dorsal hands), leading to scarring and milia. It is not primarily pruritic papules/plaques, and histology would show a subepidermal blister with festooning of dermal papillae, not the lymphocytic infiltrate seen here.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with a sudden, intensely pruritic and burning rash on her face, neck, and dorsal hands after a 3-day beach vacation. She recently started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection 5 days ago. Examination reveals sharply demarcated, erythematous edema with mild vesiculation on sun-exposed areas, sparing the submental area beneath her chin. She reports applying a new oil-based sunscreen daily but denies using any topical medications or fragrances on the affected areas.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the next best management step for suspected phototoxicity from a known photosensitizing medication.
items.correctAnswerText: Discontinue trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and switch to a non-photosensitizing antibiotic
items.teachingPoint: Drug-induced phototoxicity typically presents as an exaggerated sunburn reaction on sun-exposed skin shortly after starting a photosensitizing medication (e.g., tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, thiazides). The cornerstone of management is immediate discontinuation of the offending systemic agent.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of sharply demarcated, sun-exposed erythema and edema shortly after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is classic for drug-induced phototoxicity. TMP-SMX is a well-known photosensitizing agent, particularly in the sulfonamide component. The immediate and most critical management step is to discontinue the offending systemic medication to prevent further damage and allow resolution. Switching to a non-photosensitizing alternative is necessary for treating the underlying infection.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a severely pruritic, erythematous, and edematous rash on his face and dorsal hands after a weekend hiking trip. He denies prior similar episodes or new topical exposures but reports taking doxycycline for a recent dental procedure. The eruption is sharply demarcated, with some areas showing mild blistering and hyperpigmentation developing. Physical examination reveals a rash confined strictly to sun-exposed areas, sparing the submental fold and the area under his glasses. The patient is otherwise healthy and takes no other medications.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the next best management step for suspected phototoxicity from a known photosensitizing medication.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate photoprotection measures and advise discontinuation of doxycycline
items.teachingPoint: Phototoxicity presents as an exaggerated sunburn reaction strictly limited to sun-exposed areas in patients taking photosensitizing medications (e.g., tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, amiodarone, thiazides). Management requires immediate discontinuation of the offending agent and strict sun protection.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for phototoxicity, a non-immunologic reaction caused by the interaction of a photosensitizing drug (doxycycline) with ultraviolet light. The rash is strictly confined to sun-exposed areas, sparing protected regions (submental fold, under glasses), and presents with acute erythema, edema, and sometimes blistering or subsequent hyperpigmentation. The cornerstone of management is immediate cessation of the offending photosensitizing agent and strict sun protection to prevent further damage and allow the skin to heal. Symptomatic treatment with topical corticosteroids or emollients may be used for comfort, but removing the trigger is paramount.

He also has a history of congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and hypertension. He is currently taking lisinopril, carvedilol, and furosemide. items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the most appropriate medication choice or avoidance principle when treating psoriasis in a patient with demyelinating disease or heart failure risk.
items.teachingPoint: TNF-alpha inhibitors are contraindicated in patients with moderate-to-severe heart failure and demyelinating diseases due to risks of exacerbation. IL-17 inhibitors (e.g., secukinumab, ixekizumab) are effective alternatives for psoriasis that do not carry these specific contraindications.

Unlike TNF-alpha inhibitors, which are associated with worsening heart failure and new-onset demyelinating disease, IL-17 inhibitors do not carry these specific black box warnings or contraindications. Given this patient's history of HFrEF, TNF-alpha inhibitors (such as adalimumab or infliximab) are contraindicated. Apremilast (PDE4 inhibitor) and acitretin (retinoid) are generally considered less effective for moderate-to-severe disease requiring systemic therapy compared to biologics. Methotrexate requires careful monitoring and can be hepatotoxic or myelosuppressive, but the primary concern here is avoiding agents that exacerbate his cardiac condition. Secukinumab offers a robust efficacy profile without the specific cardiac contraindications associated with TNF-alpha blockade.

items.teachingPoint: In patients with psoriasis and pre-existing hepatic risk factors (e.g., alcohol use, elevated transaminases), apremilast is a preferred systemic nonbiologic therapy due to its favorable hepatic safety profile and lack of need for routine liver function monitoring, unlike methotrexate or cyclosporine.
items.explanationCorrect: Apremilast is a phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitor that does not require routine hepatic monitoring and lacks the hepatotoxic potential associated with traditional systemic psoriasis therapies like methotrexate or cyclosporine. In patients with pre-existing hepatic risk factors, such as chronic alcohol use and elevated transaminases, apremilast offers a favorable safety profile regarding liver toxicity, making it the most appropriate initial systemic nonbiologic option among the choices provided.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Methotrexate is contraindicated or requires extreme caution in patients with significant hepatic risk factors, including chronic alcohol use and elevated liver enzymes, due to its potential for dose-dependent hepatotoxicity and fibrosis. Routine hepatic monitoring is required, but the baseline risk makes it a poor initial choice here.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Acitretin is metabolized by the liver and can cause transaminitis. Furthermore, it is highly teratogenic with a long half-life and requires strict pregnancy prevention counseling. While not as strictly contraindicated as methotrexate in mild elevations, it still carries hepatic risks and is less ideal than apremilast given the patient's alcohol history.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. Apremilast is the most appropriate choice due to its lack of significant hepatotoxicity and no requirement for routine hepatic monitoring.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Cyclosporine is primarily nephrotoxic and can cause hypertension, but it also carries risks of hepatotoxicity. More importantly, it is generally reserved for short-term use due to cumulative renal toxicity and malignancy risk. It does not offer a safer hepatic profile compared to apremilast in this context.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Fumarates (e.g., dimethyl fumarate) can cause gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia. While they are generally considered to have a lower risk of hepatotoxicity compared to methotrexate, they can still cause transaminitis and require periodic liver function monitoring. Apremilast remains the safer initial choice for a patient with active hepatic risk factors.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with a history of plaque psoriasis presents to your clinic for management of widespread, erythematous, scaly plaques involving 30% of his body surface area. He has failed topical corticosteroids and calcipotriene. His medical history is significant for obesity (BMI 34 kg/m²) and a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Laboratory evaluation reveals mildly elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels, consistent with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. He denies alcohol use and has no history of hepatitis. Which of the following systemic nonbiologic therapies is the most appropriate initial consideration for this patient?
items.leadIn: Which of the following systemic nonbiologic therapies is the most appropriate initial consideration for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic nonbiologic therapy consideration for psoriasis when hepatic risk factors are present.
items.teachingPoint: In patients with psoriasis and pre-existing hepatic risk factors such as NAFLD, apremilast is a preferred systemic nonbiologic therapy because it does not require routine hepatic monitoring and lacks the hepatotoxicity associated with methotrexate, acitretin, and fumarates.
items.explanationCorrect: Apremilast is a phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitor that does not require routine laboratory monitoring for hepatic, renal, or hematologic toxicity. Given this patient's obesity and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) causing elevated transaminases, avoiding hepatotoxic systemic agents like methotrexate and acitretin is prudent. Apremilast offers a favorable safety profile regarding liver health, making it the most appropriate initial systemic nonbiologic choice in this clinical scenario.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Methotrexate is a first-line systemic agent for moderate-to-severe psoriasis but is hepatotoxic. It can cause hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, particularly in patients with pre-existing liver disease or obesity. Routine monitoring of liver enzymes and periodic biopsy are required, making it a poor choice for this patient with NAFLD.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Acitretin is an oral retinoid that can cause hyperlipidemia and hepatotoxicity. It requires monitoring of liver function tests and lipid panels. Given the patient's NAFLD, acitretin is less favorable than apremilast due to its potential for additional hepatic stress and significant teratogenicity.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that can cause nephrotoxicity and hypertension. While it acts quickly, it is generally reserved for short-term use or severe flares due to long-term toxicity risks. It does not address the hepatic concerns as directly as avoiding hepatotoxins, but its side effect profile is less ideal for initial long-term management in a patient with metabolic syndrome.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Fumarates are systemic immunomodulators used for psoriasis. They can cause gastrointestinal side effects and lymphopenia, requiring periodic blood count monitoring. While they have a lower risk of direct hepatotoxicity compared to methotrexate, apremilast is generally preferred as an initial systemic nonbiologic agent due to its ease of use, lack of required laboratory monitoring, and favorable safety profile in patients with comorbidities like NAFLD.

items.stem: A 34-year-old outdoor landscaper presents with a pruritic, erythematous rash on his face and neck that began 10 days after starting a new topical sunscreen containing octocrylene. The eruption initially appeared as small erythematous papules on sun-exposed areas but has since spread to adjacent sun-protected skin, including the postauricular folds and eyelids. The lesions are mildly edematous and vesicular in some areas. He denies recent systemic medication changes, but reports applying the sunscreen daily for 2 weeks prior to onset. Skin biopsy shows a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils and spongiosis.
items.leadIn: Which of the following findings most strongly supports a diagnosis of photoallergic dermatitis over phototoxicity?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate photoallergic dermatitis from phototoxicity using timing, morphology, and distribution.
items.correctAnswerText: Involvement of skin typically shielded from direct sunlight, such as eyelids and postauricular areas
items.teachingPoint: Photoallergic contact dermatitis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction characterized by pruritus, eczematous morphology (spongiosis with eosinophils), and crucially, spread to adjacent sun-protected skin. Phototoxicity is a non-immunologic reaction with rapid onset, burning/pain rather than itch, and strict confinement to sun-exposed areas.
items.explanationCorrect: Photoallergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It requires prior sensitization and typically manifests 10 to 14 days after exposure, though it can occur sooner upon re-exposure. The key discriminating feature is that the eruption spreads beyond areas of direct sun exposure to involve adjacent sun-protected skin (e.g., eyelids, postauricular folds, V of the neck). Histology typically reveals spongiosis with eosinophils. The vignette describes classic features: delayed onset (10 days), pruritus, spread to protected areas, and eosinophilic spongiotic histology.

options.text: Rapid onset of symptoms within hours of sun exposure

options.label: B
options.text: Involvement of skin typically shielded from direct sunlight, such as eyelids and postauricular areas

options.label: C
options.text: A histologic pattern dominated by necrotic keratinocytes and a sparse inflammatory infiltrate

options.label: D
options.text: A well-demarcated eruption strictly confined to the boundaries of direct solar exposure

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Necrotic keratinocytes and a sparse infiltrate are typical of phototoxic reactions or erythema multiforme, not photoallergic dermatitis. Photoallergy shows spongiosis and eosinophils.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Strict confinement to direct solar exposure boundaries is characteristic of phototoxicity. Photoallergic reactions characteristically spread to adjacent protected skin.

distractorExplanations.text: Onset within 24 hours without prior sensitization suggests phototoxicity. Photoallergy requires a sensitization period (typically days to weeks) before clinical eruption upon re-exposure.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a severe, intensely pruritic rash on his face and neck after returning from a 10-day hiking trip in the tropics. He used a new sunscreen daily and applied fragrant aftershave twice a day. The rash appeared on the third day of exposure, initially as faint erythema that rapidly evolved into confluent edematous plaques with numerous vesicles and oozing. The eruption is strictly confined to the areas exposed to sunlight, with sharp demarcation at the collar line and under his hat. The lesions are disproportionately pruritic compared to typical sunburn.
items.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's eruption?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate photoallergic dermatitis from phototoxicity using timing, morphology, and distribution.
items.correctAnswerText: UV-induced alteration of a topical hapten leading to a T-cell-mediated immune response
items.teachingPoint: Photoallergic contact dermatitis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction characterized by delayed onset (days), intense pruritus, and eczematous morphology (vesicles/oozing) confined to sun-exposed areas. It is distinguished from phototoxicity, which is a direct cytotoxic reaction with rapid onset (hours), pain/burning sensation, and sunburn-like morphology.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation is classic for photoallergic contact dermatitis. Key discriminating features include the intense pruritus (unlike phototoxicity, which is typically painful/burning), delayed onset (day 3 vs. day 1 for phototoxicity), and eczematous morphology with vesicles/oozing. Photoallergy is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction where UV radiation alters a topically applied substance (hapten) into an antigen, triggering a T-cell-mediated immune response. This distinguishes it from phototoxicity, which is a non-immunologic, dose-dependent direct cytotoxic reaction.

options.label: A
options.text: Direct cytotoxic damage to keratinocytes mediated by UV radiation and a chromophore

options.label: B
options.text: UV-induced alteration of a topical hapten leading to a T-cell-mediated immune response

options.label: C
options.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation triggered by solar radiation and a cosmetic antigen

options.label: D
options.text: Complement-mediated vascular injury resulting from immune complex deposition in sun-exposed skin

options.label: E
options.text: Inhibition of DNA repair mechanisms leading to apoptosis of photodamaged basal keratinocytes

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Describes phototoxicity. Phototoxic reactions occur rapidly (hours to 1-2 days), are dose-dependent, resemble severe sunburn (painful/burning rather than pruritic), and lack the eczematous/vesicular morphology seen here.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. Describes photoallergic contact dermatitis, a type IV hypersensitivity reaction requiring prior sensitization and UV-induced haptenization.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Describes a type I hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., solar urticaria). While pruritic, solar urticaria presents with transient wheals that resolve within hours, not persistent eczematous plaques.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Describes conditions like subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) or dermatitis herpetiformis. These are autoimmune/inflammatory conditions with different clinical presentations (e.g., annular SCLE plaques or grouped vesicles in DH) and lack the direct association with a new topical agent triggering an eczematous eruption.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Describes the mechanism of DNA damage leading to skin cancer or severe sunburn. It does not account for the intense pruritus, delayed onset, or eczematous morphology characteristic of photoallergic dermatitis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of an intensely pruritic and painful rash that has progressively worsened. The eruption began on his lower extremities and has since spread to his buttocks, groin, perineum, and face. He reports a 15-pound unintentional weight loss over the past 2 months, along with intermittent diarrhea and worsening control of his long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus. Physical examination reveals erythematous, well-demarcated plaques with superficial blistering and crusting. Notably, there are areas of central clearing with peripheral scaling, creating a geometric or annular configuration. The mucous membranes are also involved, showing erosive cheilitis and glossitis. Laboratory studies reveal normocytic anemia and hypoglycemia.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Recognize a systemic-dermatology overlap syndrome such as necrolytic migratory erythema in the appropriate cutaneous context.
items.teachingPoint: Necrolytic migratory erythema, characterized by erythematous plaques with blistering and crusting in the perineal and acral regions, is a hallmark cutaneous manifestation of glucagonoma syndrome. When accompanied by diabetes mellitus, weight loss, diarrhea, and anemia, a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor should be strongly suspected.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of necrolytic migratory erythema (NME) combined with weight loss, diarrhea, and diabetes mellitus is highly characteristic of a glucagonoma. NME classically affects the perineum, groin, buttocks, and lower extremities, presenting as erythematous plaques that evolve into blisters, erosions, and crusting with central clearing. The associated systemic symptoms (glucose intolerance/diabetes, weight loss, anemia) and mucosal involvement further support this diagnosis. A glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor should be suspected and confirmed with elevated serum glucagon levels and imaging.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Acrodermatitis enteropathica causes a similar rash but is typically associated with zinc deficiency. It usually presents in infancy after weaning from breast milk or as an autosomal recessive disorder. While it can occur in adults with malabsorption, the specific combination of diabetes, weight loss, and the classic NME distribution makes glucagonoma far more likely.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Glucagonoma syndrome

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Pellagra (niacin deficiency) can cause a photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. However, the rash in pellagra is typically photodistributed (e.g., Casal necklace) rather than having the characteristic perineal and acral distribution of NME. Furthermore, pellagra does not typically cause diabetes mellitus or the severe weight loss and anemia seen in glucagonoma.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) presents with widespread erythema and superficial blistering that leads to desquamation. It is caused by exfoliative toxins and typically affects infants and young children or immunocompromised adults. It does not present with the chronic, migratory plaques, diabetes, or weight loss seen in this patient.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause various cutaneous manifestations, including photosensitive rashes and mucosal ulcers. However, SLE typically presents with a malar rash or discoid lesions and is associated with other systemic findings like arthritis, renal disease, and specific autoantibodies. It does not typically present with the characteristic necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes mellitus, or weight loss described here.

judgeRuns.globalComment: The item is well-constructed in terms of clinical presentation, distractor quality, and educational value. However, it contains a fatal medical error: it lists hypoglycemia as a laboratory finding in a patient with a suspected glucagonoma and worsening diabetes. Glucagon is a counter-regulatory hormone that increases blood glucose; therefore, a glucagonoma would present with hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia. This contradiction must be corrected to 'hyperglycemia' for the item to be valid.
fatalFlawReasons: The stem contains a medical contradiction: it describes a patient with worsening type 2 diabetes (implying hyperglycemia) but then lists hypoglycemia as a laboratory finding. Glucagonoma syndrome causes hyperglycemia due to excess glucagon.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of an intensely pruritic, blistering rash that began on his lower extremities and spread to his trunk and perineum. He reports significant unintentional weight loss of 15 kg over the past 6 months and new-onset polyuria and polydipsia. Physical examination reveals confluent erythematous patches with superficial erosions, crusting, and areas of epidermal necrosis on the buttocks and lower abdomen. Laboratory studies demonstrate mild normocytic anemia, elevated fasting blood glucose, and hypoaminoacidemia. A punch biopsy of the rash shows pallor of the upper epidermis with necrotic keratinocytes.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Recognize a systemic-dermatology overlap syndrome such as necrolytic migratory erythema in the appropriate cutaneous context.
items.teachingPoint: Necrolytic migratory erythema is the hallmark cutaneous manifestation of glucagonoma syndrome. Clinicians should suspect a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor in patients presenting with migratory blistering and crusting rashes, particularly when accompanied by weight loss, diabetes mellitus, and hypoaminoacidemia.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of necrolytic migratory erythema (NME), characterized by migratory, blistering, and crusting plaques typically affecting the perineum and lower extremities, combined with weight loss, diabetes mellitus (polyuria/polydipsia), and hypoaminoacidemia is classic for a glucagon-secreting pancreatic tumor (glucagonoma). NME histopathology typically reveals pallor of the upper epidermis with necrotic keratinocytes, consistent with this patient's biopsy results.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Acrodermatitis enteropathica (zinc deficiency) presents with periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia. While it can cause blistering and crusting, the prominent diabetes, weight loss, and hypoaminoacidemia point toward glucagonoma. Zinc deficiency does not typically cause the specific necrolytic histopathology described.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Glucagonoma syndrome is the correct diagnosis. The triad of necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes mellitus, and weight loss is highly specific. Hypoaminoacidemia results from the catabolic effects of excess glucagon.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Pellagra (niacin deficiency) presents with the classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. The rash is typically photosensitive and affects sun-exposed areas (Casal necklace). While pellagra can cause necrolytic changes, the lack of photosensitivity distribution and presence of diabetes/hypoaminoacidemia favor glucagonoma.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Porphyria cutanea tarda presents with fragile skin, vesicles, and bullae on sun-exposed areas (dorsal hands), hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. It is associated with liver disease and HCV, not diabetes or hypoaminoacidemia.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic sclerosis presents with skin thickening (sclerodactyly, mask-like facies), Raynaud phenomenon, and internal organ involvement. It does not cause necrolytic blistering rashes or the metabolic abnormalities seen here.

This is a mandatory requirement under the REMS program to prevent teratogenic exposure.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a rapidly progressive, velvety hyperpigmentation involving the axillae and neck over the past three months. He reports significant unintentional weight loss of 15 pounds and early satiety after meals. Physical examination reveals hyperkeratotic, hyperpigmented plaques in the flexural areas and mucosal involvement with papillary projections on his tongue. He has no personal or family history of insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, or obesity.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

items.correctAnswerText: Initiate a screening colonoscopy and upper endoscopy with biopsy
items.teachingPoint: Malignant acanthosis nigricans is a paraneoplastic syndrome most commonly associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. It should be suspected in patients with rapid-onset acanthosis nigricans, especially those lacking metabolic risk factors, and presenting with mucosal involvement or systemic symptoms like weight loss. Immediate gastrointestinal malignancy screening is required.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient presents with classic features of malignant acanthosis nigricans, including rapid onset in an older adult, significant weight loss, early satiety (suggestive of gastric pathology), and mucosal involvement. While benign acanthosis nigricans is associated with insulin resistance and obesity, malignant cases are strongly linked to internal malignancies, most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma. The presence of mucosal lesions and systemic symptoms significantly increases the suspicion for a paraneoplastic etiology. Therefore, immediate evaluation for an underlying malignancy with upper endoscopy and colonoscopy is the most critical next step.

options.text: Prescribe topical tretinoin and keratolytic agents for symptomatic relief

items.stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a widespread, erythematous rash. The mother reports that the lesions began on the cheeks 4 weeks ago and have since spread to the extensor surfaces of the arms and legs. The infant has been increasingly fussy, especially at night, and frequently rubs the affected areas against the bedding. Physical examination reveals ill-defined, erythematous, scaly patches with overlying excoriations on the cheeks and extensor surfaces. The diaper area is spared, and there are no greasy scales or involvement of the scalp creases.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate infantile atopic dermatitis from seborrheic dermatitis in a young infant with eczematous rash.
items.teachingPoint: Infantile atopic dermatitis typically presents after 2 months of age with pruritic, erythematous, scaly patches on the face (cheeks) and extensor surfaces, characteristically sparing the diaper area. In contrast, seborrheic dermatitis presents with greasy scales in sebaceous-rich areas and often involves the diaper area, while irritant contact dermatitis is confined to the diaper area.
items.explanationCorrect: This infant's presentation is classic for infantile atopic dermatitis (AD). AD typically presents in infants between 2 and 6 months of age. The rash is characteristically distributed on the face (especially cheeks) and extensor surfaces of the extremities, sparing the diaper area. It presents as ill-defined, erythematous, scaly patches and plaques that are intensely pruritic, leading to excoriations and irritability. The sparing of the diaper area is a key distinguishing feature from seborrheic dermatitis and irritant contact dermatitis in this age group.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Seborrheic dermatitis typically presents with greasy, yellowish scales and favors the scalp (cradle cap), nasolabial folds, eyebrows, and intertriginous areas. It is generally non-pruritic or only mildly pruritic, and unlike atopic dermatitis, it frequently involves the diaper area.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Infantile atopic dermatitis

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Irritant contact dermatitis in infants is most commonly caused by prolonged exposure to urine and feces, resulting in a sharply demarcated erythematous rash confined to the diaper area (perianal, gluteal, and genital regions). This patient's rash involves the cheeks and extensor surfaces while sparing the diaper area, making this diagnosis incorrect.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Scabies in infants can involve the face and scalp, unlike in older children and adults. However, it typically presents with papules, vesicles, or burrows and is intensely pruritic. The presence of ill-defined scaly patches on the extensor surfaces and cheeks without mention of burrows or family history of pruritus makes scabies less likely than atopic dermatitis.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Milia are tiny, white, keratin-filled cysts that typically appear on the nose and cheeks of newborns. They are asymptomatic, not erythematous or scaly, and do not cause pruritus or fussiness. This patient's inflammatory, pruritic rash is inconsistent with milia.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a 3-week history of an itchy, scaly patch on his scalp. His mother notes that the area has expanded and several hairs within the lesion have broken off at the surface, leaving small black dots. He recently started playing with a neighbor's kitten. Physical examination reveals a 4-cm erythematous, scaly patch with alopecia and significant posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. KOH preparation of plucked hairs reveals branching septate hyphae.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the best treatment strategy for tinea capitis in a child, including household considerations.
items.correctAnswerText: Oral griseofulvin and washing household bedding with hot water
items.teachingPoint: Tinea capitis requires systemic antifungal therapy (typically oral griseofulvin or terbinafine) because topical agents cannot penetrate the hair shaft. Environmental decontamination of fomites is also essential to prevent reinfection.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient has tinea capitis, a dermatophyte infection of the hair shaft and scalp. Because dermatophytes invade deep into the hair follicle, topical antifungals are ineffective; systemic therapy is required. Griseofulvin remains the first-line oral treatment for tinea capitis caused by Microsporum species (suggested here by the epidemiology of exposure to a kitten) and is highly effective for Trichophyton species as well. Additionally, environmental decontamination of fomites such as bedding, hats, and brushes with hot water is crucial to prevent reinfection. While asymptomatic household members generally do not require treatment, screening and environmental cleaning are recommended.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy with a history of moderate atopic dermatitis presents to the clinic with a sudden onset of widespread vesicles and pustules over his trunk, extremities, and face. He has been afebrile but irritable with decreased oral intake due to painful oral ulcers. His older sibling recently returned from daycare with a similar rash and hand, foot, and mouth lesions. Examination reveals monomorphic 2- to 4-mm vesicles on an erythematous base, with some lesions showing central umbilication. The vesicles are located on the trunk and extremities, sparing the palms and soles.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate eczema coxsackium from eczema herpeticum and impetigo in an atopic child.
items.correctAnswerText: Hand, foot, and mouth disease superimposed on atopic dermatitis (eczema coxsackium)
items.teachingPoint: Eczema coxsackium is a severe manifestation of hand, foot, and mouth disease in children with atopic dermatitis. Differentiation from eczema herpeticum relies on the presence of oral ulcers, a history of enteroviral exposure (e.g., sibling with HFMD), and the absence of systemic toxicity or hemorrhagic crusting typical of HSV infection.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is C. This patient presents with eczema coxsackium, a severe form of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) caused by Coxsackievirus A16 or Enterovirus 71, occurring in children with atopic dermatitis. Key distinguishing features include the history of a sibling with HFMD, oral ulcers causing irritability and decreased intake, and the characteristic widespread monomorphic vesicles on an erythematous base. While classic HFMD involves the palms, soles, and mouth, eczema coxsackium typically presents with widespread truncal and extremity involvement due to autoinoculation or hematogenous spread in the context of compromised skin barrier. The presence of oral ulcers is a crucial clue pointing toward an enteroviral etiology rather than HSV or bacteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Hand, foot, and mouth disease superimposed on atopic dermatitis (eczema coxsackium)

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Eczema herpeticum is caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2 and typically presents with monomorphic punched-out erosions, hemorrhagic crusts, and vesicles on an erythematous base. While the morphology can overlap with eczema coxsackium, the absence of oral ulcers and the lack of a history of contact with HSV (e.g., herpetic gingivostomatitis) make this less likely. Additionally, eczema herpeticum is often accompanied by fever and systemic toxicity, which this patient lacks.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Impetigo presents with honey-colored crusts and flaccid bullae that rupture easily, typically on the face (especially around the nose and mouth) or extremities. It is caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. The widespread monomorphic vesicles, oral ulcers, and contact history with a sibling having HFMD are inconsistent with impetigo.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Varicella zoster virus infection presents with a polymorphic rash featuring lesions in various stages of healing (papules, vesicles, pustules, and crusts) simultaneously. This patient's rash is monomorphic (all lesions are vesicles of the same size and stage), which argues against varicella. Additionally, the patient is afebrile.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Scabies presents with intense pruritus, particularly at night, and characteristic burrows in the web spaces of fingers, wrists, axillae, and genitalia. It does not typically present with widespread monomorphic vesicles, oral ulcers, or a direct contact history of HFMD.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Scabies presents with intense pruritus, particularly at night, and characteristic burrows in the web spaces of fingers, wrists, axillae, and genitalia. It does not typically present with widespread monomorphic vesicles, oral ulcers, or a direct contact history of HFMD.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy with a history of moderate atopic dermatitis presents with a sudden onset of fever and widespread vesicular lesions. Notably, the lesions are concentrated within areas of pre-existing atopic dermatitis, sparing his palms and soles. There is no evidence of crusting or honey-colored exudate.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate eczema coxsackium from eczema herpeticum and impetigo in an atopic child.
items.teachingPoint: Eczema coxsackium is a variant of hand, foot, and mouth disease caused by Coxsackievirus A16 that presents with widespread vesicles predominantly located on areas of pre-existing atopic dermatitis. It should be distinguished from eczema herpeticum by the presence of monomorphic vesicles rather than punched-out erosions and a history of HFMD exposure.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct diagnosis is eczema coxsackium. This condition occurs in children with atopic dermatitis who are infected with Coxsackievirus A16. The clinical presentation mimics classic hand, foot, and mouth disease but is characterized by a more widespread distribution of vesicles that preferentially localize to areas of pre-existing atopic dermatitis. The history of recent exposure to hand, foot, and mouth disease in daycare, combined with the vesicular morphology and distribution, strongly supports this diagnosis. The absence of lesions on the palms and soles helps distinguish it from classic HFMD, though it can still occur.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Eczema herpeticum is caused by Herpes simplex virus and typically presents with monomorphic, punched-out erosions or vesicles that may become hemorrhagic or crusted. It is often accompanied by significant systemic symptoms like fever, but the lesions are usually more uniform and widespread beyond just atopic patches. The history of HFMD exposure and the well-circumscribed nature of the vesicles make this less likely.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Impetigo presents with honey-colored crusts and erosions, typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. The vesicles in this vignette are not described as having honey-colored exudate, and the systemic symptoms (fever) along with the specific vesicular morphology point toward a viral etiology rather than bacterial.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) presents with numerous sterile, non-follicular pustules on an erythematous base, usually following medication exposure. The lesions in this case are vesicles, not pustules, and the history points to a viral exposure rather than a drug reaction.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Eczema coxsackium is the correct answer.

The lesions are described as monomorphic vesicles, whereas varicella is characterized by pleomorphism (lesions in different stages). Additionally, the specific localization to atopic dermatitis sites and the HFMD exposure history favor eczema coxsackium.

items.learningObjective: Identify the appropriate immediate management for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in a child.
items.teachingPoint: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is a toxin-mediated staphylococcal infection characterized by widespread erythema, flaccid bullae, and desquamation with a positive Nikolsky sign. It is distinguished from Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis by the absence of mucosal involvement. Immediate management requires systemic antibiotics effective against Staphylococcus aureus, such as intravenous nafcillin or cefazolin for methicillin-sensitive strains.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), caused by exfoliative toxins from Staphylococcus aureus. The absence of mucosal involvement and the presence of perioral crusting help distinguish it from Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). SSSS is a medical emergency requiring prompt systemic antibiotic therapy targeting methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA). Intravenous nafcillin or cefazolin is the first-line treatment. Supportive care with fluid and electrolyte management is also crucial.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform a skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Intravenous acyclovir is the treatment for severe herpes simplex virus infections, such as eczema herpeticum. While eczema herpeticum can cause vesicles and erosions, it typically presents with punched-out erosions in a patient with atopic dermatitis and does not cause the widespread desquamation or positive Nikolsky sign seen in SSSS.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: A skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence is used to diagnose autoimmune blistering diseases like bullous pemphigoid or linear IgA disease. SSSS is a toxin-mediated condition, not an autoimmune process, so immunofluorescence would be negative. A routine skin biopsy in SSSS shows a split within the granular layer of the epidermis, but this is not required for diagnosis when the clinical picture is classic.

Observation would lead to progression of SSSS, dehydration, and potential sepsis.

distractorExplanations.label: D

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to a widespread, painful rash that began on his face and spread over 24 hours. He was treated with amoxicillin for an acute otitis media 3 days ago but stopped the medication after 24 hours due to perceived lack of improvement. On examination, he is irritable and febrile (38.5°C). There are tender erythematous patches on the face and neck that have progressed to widespread, flaccid bullae and superficial desquamation. Nikolsky sign is positive. There are no mucosal lesions, and his eyes appear normal.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the appropriate immediate management for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in a child.
items.correctAnswerText: Initiate intravenous nafcillin and arrange hospital admission for supportive care
items.teachingPoint: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome presents with widespread erythema, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign without mucosal involvement. It is caused by S. aureus exfoliative toxins and requires prompt hospital admission, intravenous anti-staphylococcal antibiotics, and supportive care.
items.explanationCorrect: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis. It primarily affects infants and young children due to immature renal clearance of toxins and lack of neutralizing antibodies. The clinical presentation of widespread erythema, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and absence of mucosal involvement is classic. Immediate management requires hospital admission for intravenous anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., nafcillin, oxacillin, or cefazolin) and supportive care, including fluid and electrolyte management. Early treatment leads to rapid resolution of the skin lesions.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for worsening atopic dermatitis. His skin is diffusely erythematous, lichenified, and excoriated across the trunk, extremities, and face. He has had severe pruritus disrupting sleep for 6 months. Despite consistent twice-daily emollients and high-potency topical corticosteroids for the past 8 weeks, his disease remains moderate-to-severe. He has no history of recurrent skin infections or significant comorbidities. His growth and development are appropriate for age.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate systemic therapy option for moderate-to-severe pediatric atopic dermatitis after topical failure.
items.teachingPoint: Dupilumab is a first-line systemic biologic therapy for children aged 6 years and older with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis inadequately controlled by topical therapies, offering targeted IL-4/IL-13 inhibition with a favorable safety profile compared to traditional systemic immunosuppressants.
items.explanationCorrect: For pediatric patients (aged 6 years and older) with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis inadequately controlled by topical prescription therapies, dupilumab is a first-line systemic biologic agent. It targets the IL-4 and IL-13 pathways, effectively reducing inflammation and pruritus with a favorable safety profile in children. It is FDA-approved for this specific indication.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for a 3-year history of severe, pruritic eczematous dermatitis predominantly affecting his flexural surfaces. Despite adherence to a regimen of emollients and twice-daily topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment for the past two months, his disease remains poorly controlled with significant sleep disturbance and impairment of daily activities. Skin culture from weeping lesions is negative for bacterial superinfection. He has no history of malignancy, immunodeficiency, or active tuberculosis. His growth parameters are at the 50th percentile for age and sex.
