items.explanationCorrect: For children aged 4 years and older with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis that is refractory to optimized topical therapy, systemic immunomodulators are indicated. Oral cyclosporine is an FDA-approved first-line systemic agent for pediatric patients in this age group who have failed topical treatments. It provides rapid relief of pruritus and inflammation, making it highly suitable for severe cases with significant functional impairment. Close monitoring of renal function and blood pressure is required during therapy.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy with recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB) is evaluated for worsening pain and frequent dressing changes. His mother reports spending up to 4 hours daily applying antimicrobial dressings and managing minor erosions. He has no signs of active infection, but his growth velocity has slowed over the past year despite oral nutritional supplementation. Physical examination shows widespread fragile skin with superficial blisters and healing erosions on the extremities, without deep tissue involvement or malignancy. His current regimen includes daily wound care with nonadherent dressings, acetaminophen for pain, and a multivitamin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

items.correctAnswerText: Refer to a specialized epidermolysis bullosa multidisciplinary clinic
items.teachingPoint: Children with moderate-to-severe epidermolysis bullosa, particularly those with significant wound-care burden or nutritional concerns, should be referred to a specialized multidisciplinary EB clinic for comprehensive management.
items.explanationCorrect: The most appropriate next step is referral to a specialized multidisciplinary clinic. Children with RDEB often face complex challenges including wound care burden, pain management, nutritional deficits, and psychosocial stress. A specialized center provides coordinated care involving dermatology, wound care specialists, nutritionists, pain management, and psychological support to optimize outcomes and reduce caregiver burden. This comprehensive approach is standard of care for moderate-to-severe EB cases.

A specialized multidisciplinary EB center provides comprehensive care, including advanced wound management techniques, nutritional support, physical therapy to prevent contractures, and access to clinical trials for emerging therapies (e.g., integrin beta-6 gene therapy or laminin-332 replacement). This holistic approach is the standard of care for optimizing outcomes in complex EB cases.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever and rapidly spreading skin peeling. items.teachingPoint: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins that cleave desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, causing superficial blistering without mucosal involvement. The absence of mucosal involvement is a key distinguishing feature, as desmoglein 3 (which protects mucosal epithelium) is not targeted by these toxins.

items.teachingPoint: SSSS is distinguished from bullous impetigo by its widespread, hematogenous dissemination of exfoliative toxins causing a positive Nikolsky sign, and from TEN by the sparing of mucous membranes and lack of full-thickness epidermal necrosis. items.explanationCorrect: This patient has staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS). SSSS is caused by exfoliative toxins (ETA and ETB) produced by Staphylococcus aureus, typically at a remote infection site (e.g., nasopharynx or conjunctiva). These toxins circulate hematogenously and cleave desmoglein 1, a cadherin protein in the superficial epidermis (granular layer), causing widespread intraepidermal blistering. Key clinical clues include the patient's young age, history of a resolving infection, widespread tender erythema and flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, but crucially, the complete sparing of mucous membranes.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of chronic, widespread skin scaling that has been present since infancy. His mother reports that the scales are dark brown and finely adherent, most prominent on his lower extremities and extensor surfaces. She notes that the scaling is significantly worse during the winter months but improves somewhat in the summer. Physical examination reveals large, dark, polygonal scales with a dirty appearance on his shins and arms. His face is relatively spared, though mild perioral scaling is noted. He has a history of atopic dermatitis and seasonal allergies, but his parents deny any new medications or systemic symptoms such as fatigue or weight loss. His older brother has similar skin findings, but his younger sister is unaffected.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate X-linked ichthyosis from ichthyosis vulgaris and acquired ichthyosis in a child with generalized scaling.
items.teachingPoint: X-linked ichthyosis is distinguished from ichthyosis vulgaris by the darker, larger scales, relative sparing of the face, involvement of extensor surfaces and neck, and X-linked recessive inheritance (affecting males, carrier mothers). Ichthyosis vulgaris typically features finer white scales, facial involvement, and is associated with atopy.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of dark brown, polygonal scales predominantly affecting the lower extremities and extensor surfaces in a male child is highly characteristic of X-linked ichthyosis (XLI). The absence of facial involvement (or relative sparing compared to the body), the presence of perioral scaling, and the family history (affected older brother) strongly support an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern. The worsening in winter is common to most ichthyoses but does not differentiate them alone.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Ichthyosis vulgaris typically presents with fine, white to gray scales and is almost always associated with atopic diathesis. Crucially, it characteristically involves the face (especially the forehead) and flexural areas are often spared or show accentuated skin markings, whereas XLI spares the face but heavily involves the neck and extensor surfaces with darker scales. The family history of an affected brother also fits XLI better, as ichthyosis vulgaris is autosomal dominant and would typically show affected parents.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Acquired ichthyosis in a child is rare and usually associated with systemic diseases such as lymphoma, sarcoidosis, or HIV. It presents similarly to ichthyosis vulgaris but appears later in life without a childhood history of scaling. The absence of systemic symptoms and the lifelong nature of this patient's condition rule out an acquired etiology.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Atopic dermatitis can cause significant xerosis and scaling, particularly in flexural areas. However, the description of large, dark, polygonal scales on extensor surfaces with relative facial sparing and a specific pattern of inheritance (affected brother, unaffected sister) points toward a genodermatosis rather than simple atopic xerosis. Atopic dermatitis alone does not explain the distinct ichthyotic morphology or the clear genetic pattern.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Lamellar ichthyosis is an autosomal recessive disorder that typically presents at birth with a collodion membrane. Survivors develop large, dark, plate-like scales over the entire body, including the face and flexures. The absence of a collodion membrane history at birth, the relative sparing of the face, and the X-linked family pattern make lamellar ichthyosis unlikely.

Crowded axillary or inguinal freckling (Crowe sign) is a major diagnostic criterion for NF1 and is characteristically absent in Legius syndrome. Therefore, this finding discriminates between the two conditions.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for multiple light brown skin patches present since infancy. Physical examination reveals six café-au-lait macules measuring 5 to 10 mm each, distributed on the trunk and proximal extremities. There is no family history of similar lesions or neurologic disorders. The patient’s growth parameters are normal, and he has no axillary freckling or Lisch nodules. His pediatrician is considering a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) versus Legius syndrome. Which additional cutaneous finding, if present, would most reliably distinguish NF1 from Legius syndrome in this patient?
items.leadIn: Which additional cutaneous finding, if present, would most reliably distinguish NF1 from Legius syndrome in this patient?
items.learningObjective: Identify the discriminating cutaneous clue that separates neurofibromatosis type 1 from Legius syndrome in a child with café-au-lait macules.
items.teachingPoint: Axillary or inguinal freckling is a major diagnostic criterion for NF1 and reliably distinguishes it from Legius syndrome, which presents with café-au-lait macules but lacks freckling, Lisch nodules, and neurofibromas.
items.explanationCorrect: Axillary or inguinal freckling is a major diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and is pathognomonic for NF1 among the conditions causing café-au-lait macules. Legius syndrome, caused by SPRED1 mutations, presents with café-au-lait macules and macrocephaly but lacks axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, and neurofibromas. The presence of axillary freckling reliably confirms NF1 over Legius syndrome.

options.label: E
options.text: Hemangiomas on the face and neck

distractorExplanations.text: Axillary freckling (Crowe sign) is the correct answer. It is a major diagnostic criterion for NF1 and is absent in Legius syndrome, making it the most reliable cutaneous discriminator between these two conditions.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous neurofibromas are also a major criterion for NF1 and would distinguish it from Legius syndrome, but they typically appear later in childhood or adolescence. distractorExplanations.label: C

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermal nevi are seen in various genodermatoses and mosaic conditions but are not characteristic of NF1 or Legius syndrome. They would not aid in distinguishing between these two entities.

distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: A 3-day-old term neonate is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of a widespread rash. The infant was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery without complications and is feeding well. Physical examination reveals multiple 1- to 2-cm erythematous macules and papules scattered across the trunk and extremities. Several lesions have central pustules that rupture easily, leaving a collarette of scale and a faint macular base. The face is spared. The infant appears well, with normal temperature and vital signs.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate erythema toxicum neonatorum from transient neonatal pustular melanosis and neonatal cephalic pustulosis.
items.teachingPoint: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a benign, self-limited rash of early infancy characterized by erythematous macules and papules with central pustules that rupture to leave a collarette of scale, typically sparing the face. It is distinguished from transient neonatal pustular melanosis by the absence of hyperpigmented macules and from neonatal cephalic pustulosis by its widespread distribution beyond the face.
items.explanationCorrect: This infant’s presentation of erythematous macules and papules with central pustules that rupture to leave a collarette of scale, predominantly on the trunk and extremities while sparing the face, is classic for erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN). ETN typically appears within the first few days of life, is benign and self-limited, and shows eosinophils on Gram stain or Wright-Giemsa preparation of the pustule contents.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis presents with fragile pustules that rupture easily, leaving hyperpigmented macules rather than a collarette of scale. It typically involves the face, trunk, and extremities but does not have an erythematous base.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Neonatal cephalic pustulosis is confined to the face (cheeks, forehead, chin) and presents with monomorphic erythematous papules and pustules without the widespread truncal involvement or collarette of scale seen in ETN.

distractorExplanations.label: C

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome presents with diffuse erythema, tenderness, and widespread superficial blistering with positive Nikolsky sign. It is associated with systemic toxicity, unlike the well-appearing infant in this vignette.

distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: A 3-day-old full-term male infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of a new rash. The mother notes that small bumps appeared on his trunk and extremities overnight. On examination, the infant is well-appearing and afebrile. There are scattered 1- to 2-mm pustules on an erythematous base distributed across the trunk and proximal extremities, sparing the palms and soles. Some lesions appear as pustules on a red base, while others show central clearing with a collarette of scale. No lesions are present on the face or scalp.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate erythema toxicum neonatorum from transient neonatal pustular melanosis and neonatal cephalic pustulosis.
items.teachingPoint: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a benign, self-limited rash of the newborn characterized by erythematous macules and papules that evolve into pustules on an erythematous base, often with central clearing as they resolve. It typically appears in the first few days of life and spares the palms, soles, and face.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of well-appearing infant with pustules on an erythematous base distributed across the trunk and extremities is classic for erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN). The presence of lesions with central clearing and a collarette of scale corresponds to the resolving stage of ETN, which is characterized by an evolution from macules/papules to pustules and then to desquamating lesions. ETN is a benign, self-limited condition that typically appears in the first few days of life and resolves spontaneously within a week or two.

items.stem: A 3-week-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging red lesion on his forehead that has grown significantly over the past 10 days. His mother reports that the lesion was barely noticeable at birth but has become raised, bright red, and tender. On examination, there is a 2-cm, well-demarcated, bright red, compressible plaque with a slightly nodular surface located immediately adjacent to the medial canthus of his right eye. The infant’s visual tracking appears intact, but the lesion is physically obstructing the upper eyelid margin. There are no other cutaneous lesions, and his systemic examination is unremarkable.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the most appropriate next step for an infantile hemangioma threatening vision, airway, or feeding.
items.teachingPoint: Oral propranolol is the first-line treatment for infantile hemangiomas that are complicated by threats to vision, airway, or feeding. Prompt recognition and treatment of these high-risk lesions are essential to prevent permanent functional impairment.
items.explanationCorrect: This infant has a rapidly proliferating infantile hemangioma located in a critical anatomical region. Hemangiomas threatening vision (by causing astigmatism, amblyopia, or mechanical ptosis), airway patency, or feeding are considered high-risk and require prompt systemic intervention. Oral propranolol is the first-line therapy for complicated infantile hemangiomas due to its high efficacy, rapid response rate, and favorable safety profile compared to older systemic therapies like corticosteroids. Early initiation is crucial to prevent permanent visual impairment or other functional sequelae.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Observation is appropriate for small, uncomplicated infantile hemangiomas in non-critical locations. However, this lesion is threatening visual function by obstructing the eyelid margin; delaying treatment could result in irreversible amblyopia or astigmatism.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Topical timolol is effective for small, superficial infantile hemangiomas (<5 mm thick) in non-critical locations. It is generally insufficient for larger, thicker, or deep hemangiomas, and it is not appropriate as monotherapy for a lesion threatening vision due to the risk of delayed effective treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Oral propranolol therapy

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Intralesional corticosteroids can be used for localized, small hemangiomas but carry risks of tissue atrophy and ulceration. They are not first-line for larger lesions or those in critical areas where systemic control is needed to prevent rapid progression.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Pulsed dye laser therapy is primarily used for ulcerated hemangiomas to promote healing or for residual telangiectasias after involution. It is not effective as a primary treatment to halt the rapid proliferation of a large, thick hemangioma or to prevent functional complications like amblyopia.

items.explanationCorrect: Infantile hemangiomas in the proliferative phase that threaten vital functions—such as vision (due to ptosis or astigmatism), airway patency, or feeding—are considered high-risk and require prompt systemic treatment. Early intervention is critical to preserve visual development and prevent amblyopia.

items.stem: A 2-week-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging red lesion on his left cheek. The lesion was not present at birth but appeared within the first week of life as a faint pink macule that progressively developed into a raised, bright red nodule over the past 7 days. The parents report no bleeding or ulceration. On examination, there is a well-demarcated, 1.5-cm bright red nodule with a smooth surface and warm to palpation. There are no other cutaneous or systemic abnormalities.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate infantile hemangioma from congenital hemangioma and venous malformation.
items.teachingPoint: Infantile hemangiomas typically are not present at birth and undergo a rapid proliferative phase in the first few months of life, whereas congenital hemangiomas are fully formed at birth and venous malformations are present at birth as soft, compressible lesions without a proliferative phase.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for an infantile hemangioma, which typically appears within the first few weeks of life as a faint pink macule or patch that rapidly proliferates into a raised, bright red nodule during the first 1-3 months. The lesion is warm to palpation due to its high vascularity and well-demarcated borders. The key distinguishing feature is the absence of the lesion at birth followed by rapid postnatal growth.

options.label: E
options.text: Hemangioma of infancy with congenital onset

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Congenital hemangiomas are fully formed at birth and do not exhibit the rapid postnatal proliferative phase seen in infantile hemangiomas. They may be non-involuting (NICH) or rapidly involuting (RICH), but both are present at birth.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Infantile hemangioma is the correct answer. (This field should explain why B is incorrect, but since it's the correct answer, this key will be empty or not used in practice. However, to maintain schema integrity, we provide a placeholder.)

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Venous malformations are present at birth as soft, compressible, blue-purple lesions that do not proliferate. They expand proportionally with the child and may become more prominent with Valsalva or dependent positioning.

distractorExplanations.label: D

The history of absence at birth followed by rapid growth in the first few weeks is classic for this diagnosis.

items.explanationCorrect: Large segmental capillary malformations (port-wine stains) in the V1 distribution are strongly associated with PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa malformations, Hemangiomas, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac defects, and Eye abnormalities). Identifying these structural anomalies is paramount before initiating any other interventions, as they significantly impact prognosis and management.

items.stem: A 2-day-old term male infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of facial lesions noted since birth. The mother reports the patches are present on both upper eyelids and in the midline of the forehead. She notes that the lesions appear more prominent when the infant cries or is bathed in warm water but become less noticeable when calm. There are no other skin lesions, and the physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. The infant is feeding well and has no dysmorphic features or neurologic deficits.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate nevus simplex from capillary malformation (port-wine stain) in infancy.
items.teachingPoint: Nevus simplex (salmon patch) is a benign capillary vascular anomaly characterized by blanching and intensification with crying or temperature changes, typically located on the face or nape of the neck, and often fading in childhood. In contrast, capillary malformations (port-wine stains) are permanent, do not blanch with crying, and may require laser therapy.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient's presentation is classic for nevus simplex (also known as salmon patch or stork bite), a common, benign capillary vascular anomaly. Key distinguishing features include its location on the nape of the neck, glabella, upper eyelids, or philtrum; its blanching and intensifying with crying, fever, or Valsalva maneuvers due to increased blood flow; and its tendency to fade significantly over the first few years of life, particularly on the face. The absence of associated systemic findings further supports this benign diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Capillary malformations (port-wine stains) are present at birth but do not blanch or fade with crying. They typically persist throughout life without treatment and may darken, thicken, or develop nodules over time. Unlike nevus simplex, they are usually unilateral and do not have the characteristic blanching response to temperature or emotional changes.

distractorExplanations.label: B

items.explanationCorrect: Giant congenital melanocytic nevi (GCMN), typically defined as >20 cm in adulthood or covering >9% of body surface area in infancy, carry a significant risk of neurocutaneous melanosis (NCM) and an increased lifetime risk of melanoma. A baseline brain MRI is recommended to screen for NCM, which can be asymptomatic but requires neurologic surveillance. Additionally, these patients require lifelong annual dermatologic examinations to monitor for melanoma and other cutaneous changes.

items.stem: A newborn boy is evaluated for a large, hyperpigmented plaque covering his entire back and extending onto the right flank. The lesion measures approximately 25 cm in its greatest dimension when projected on an adult surface area and contains multiple smaller, hyperpigmented macules scattered across the trunk. The infant is otherwise healthy with a normal neurologic examination and no history of seizures or bulging fontanelles. The parents express significant concern about the risk of malignant transformation and ask for a plan to monitor their child's health.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management and counseling?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate counseling and surveillance plan for a giant congenital melanocytic nevus.
items.correctAnswerText: Order magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine to evaluate for neurocutaneous melanosis.
items.teachingPoint: Infants with giant congenital melanocytic nevi (projected adult size >20 cm) require baseline MRI of the brain and spine to screen for neurocutaneous melanosis, even in the absence of neurologic symptoms.
items.explanationCorrect: Giant congenital melanocytic nevi (GCMN) are defined as lesions projected to be greater than 20 cm in adults. Patients with GCMN are at increased risk for neurocutaneous melanosis (NCM), a condition characterized by the proliferation of benign melanocytes in the central nervous system. Although many infants with GCMN do not have NCM, the risk is significant enough to warrant surveillance. The most appropriate next step in management for an infant with a GCMN is to perform baseline MRI of the brain and spine, typically within the first few months of life, to detect asymptomatic NCM. This allows for early identification and monitoring of potential complications such as hydrocephalus or seizures, even if the infant is currently asymptomatic.

items.stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging, bright red nodule on his upper lip. The lesion appeared at 2 weeks of age and has grown exponentially over the past month. The parents report that the nodule bleeds easily with feeding and has developed a small, painful ulceration in the center. The infant is otherwise healthy and thriving. Physical examination reveals a 1.5 cm deep red, lobulated nodule with central crusting and erosion on the vermilion border of the upper lip. The surrounding skin is unremarkable.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic therapy for this patient?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate first-line therapy for a symptomatic or ulcerated infantile hemangioma requiring treatment.
items.teachingPoint: Oral propranolol is the first-line systemic therapy for infantile hemangiomas requiring treatment, especially those complicated by ulceration, functional impairment, or significant disfigurement.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for an infantile hemangioma in its proliferative phase. While many superficial infantile hemangiomas can be managed with observation or topical therapies, this patient has a deep component and, crucially, presents with ulceration. Ulcerated infantile hemangiomas are painful, prone to infection, and can lead to significant scarring. Oral propranolol is the established first-line systemic therapy for infantile hemangiomas requiring treatment, particularly those that are complicated by ulceration, at risk of functional impairment, or causing significant disfigurement. It promotes rapid involution and ulcer healing.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Intralesional corticosteroids can be used for small, localized hemangiomas but are generally considered second-line to oral propranolol. They carry risks of skin atrophy, hypopigmentation, and systemic absorption, making them less ideal as a first-line agent for an ulcerated lesion on the lip.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Topical timolol maleate is a first-line option for small, superficial infantile hemangiomas. However, it lacks the efficacy required to treat deep components or promote healing in ulcerated lesions as effectively as systemic therapy. Given the size, depth, and complication (ulceration) in this case, topical treatment alone is insufficient.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Oral propranolol

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Topical imiquimod is an immune response modifier primarily used for actinic keratoses and superficial basal cell carcinomas. It has no established role in the treatment of infantile hemangiomas and could potentially worsen irritation or ulceration.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Observation is appropriate for uncomplicated, non-threatening infantile hemangiomas that are not ulcerated. However, this patient's lesion is ulcerated and painful, necessitating active intervention to promote healing, reduce pain, and prevent further complications such as scarring or infection.

The lesion began as a faint pink patch at 2 weeks of age and has progressively grown over the past month. On examination, there is a raised, deep blue-red plaque measuring 3 cm in diameter with overlying central ulceration and crusting. The infant is otherwise healthy, afebrile, and feeding well. He has no history of bleeding disorders or cardiac abnormalities.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate first-line therapy for a symptomatic or ulcerated infantile hemangioma requiring treatment.
items.teachingPoint: Oral propranolol is the first-line systemic treatment for complicated infantile hemangiomas, including those that are ulcerated, functionally impairing, or life-threatening. It has superior efficacy and a better safety profile compared to systemic corticosteroids.
items.explanationCorrect: Oral propranolol is the first-line systemic therapy for infantile hemangiomas (IH) that are complicated, life-threatening, or functionally/visually impairing. This patient has a symptomatic, ulcerated IH on the face. Ulceration causes significant pain and risk of secondary infection, warranting prompt systemic treatment. Propranolol promotes vasoconstriction, inhibits angiogenesis, and accelerates apoptosis of hemangioma endothelial cells. It has largely replaced systemic corticosteroids due to superior efficacy and a more favorable side-effect profile.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Intralesional corticosteroids can be used for small, localized IHs but are generally avoided as first-line for large or ulcerated lesions due to the risk of further tissue atrophy, poor penetration in deep components, and significant pain during injection.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Pulsed dye laser is primarily used for ulcerated hemangiomas to promote healing and reduce pain, or for residual telangiectasias. However, it does not treat the underlying proliferative endothelial cells driving the growth and depth of the lesion. Systemic therapy is required first to halt proliferation.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Oral prednisone was historically the standard of care for complicated IHs but has been largely replaced by propranolol. Propranolol is more effective and associated with fewer adverse effects (e.g., less risk of hypertension, irritability, and growth suppression).

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for a slowly enlarging, firm subcutaneous nodule on the right cheek present since infancy. The lesion is approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, non-tender, and exhibits a characteristic 'teeter-totter' or rock-paper-scissors mobility when palpated. The overlying skin is normal, though mild bluish discoloration is noted in some areas. There are no signs of inflammation or infection. Physical examination reveals no other cutaneous lesions, and the patient's growth and development are normal.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate pilomatricoma from dermoid cyst and epidermoid cyst in a child with a firm subcutaneous facial nodule.
items.teachingPoint: The 'teeter-totter' or rock-paper-scissors sign is a pathognomonic clinical feature of pilomatricoma, resulting from the tumor's firm, calcified nature and its adherence to surrounding tissues, allowing it to pivot on an axis. This sign helps differentiate pilomatricoma from other subcutaneous nodules like epidermoid or dermoid cysts.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a firm, slow-growing subcutaneous nodule with the pathognomonic 'teeter-totter' or rock-paper-scissors sign is highly characteristic of a pilomatricoma (calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe). These benign tumors arise from hair matrix cells and are most common in children and young adults, frequently occurring on the head, neck, or upper extremities. The firmness is due to calcification within the lesion, and the specific mobility pattern helps distinguish it from other subcutaneous masses.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermoid cysts are typically softer, more mobile, and often feature a central punctum. They lack the characteristic rock-paper-scissors mobility and are usually not as firm due to the absence of significant calcification.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Dermoid cysts are congenital lesions often found along embryonic fusion lines (e.g., lateral eyebrow). While they can be firm, they are usually deeper, more mobile, and lack the specific teeter-totter sign. They may contain hair or sebaceous material but do not typically present with the described mobility pattern.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer (Pilomatricoma).

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Infantile hemangiomas are vascular tumors that typically proliferate rapidly in the first few months of life and then involute. They are usually soft, compressible, and have a characteristic bright red or bluish hue, unlike the firm, skin-colored to slightly bluish nodule described here.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Lipomas are soft, doughy, and highly mobile subcutaneous masses composed of adipose tissue. They lack the firmness and calcification associated with pilomatricomas and do not exhibit the rock-paper-scissors mobility.

On palpation, the lesion has a characteristic 'rock-hard' consistency and demonstrates a positive 'teeter-totter' sign, where pressure on one edge causes the opposite side to protrude. The overlying skin is normal in color and texture.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate pilomatricoma from dermoid cyst and epidermoid cyst in a child with a firm subcutaneous facial nodule.
items.teachingPoint: Pilomatricomas are benign hair matrix tumors common in children, characterized by a rock-hard consistency and the pathognomonic 'teeter-totter' sign. Differentiation from other subcutaneous nodules like epidermoid or dermoid cysts relies on these specific palpation findings and the absence of a central punctum.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation is classic for a pilomatricoma (calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe). These benign tumors arise from hair matrix cells and are characterized by a firm, 'rock-hard' consistency due to calcification. The positive 'teeter-totter' sign (or doughnut sign) is a highly specific clinical finding where pressure on one side of the nodule causes the opposite side to bulge out, reflecting its firm, calcified nature within a mobile subcutaneous location. They are common in children and often located on the head, neck, or upper extremities.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermoid cysts typically present as mobile, firm subcutaneous nodules with a central punctum (pore) and may express keratinous material. They lack the rock-hard consistency and teeter-totter sign seen in pilomatricomas.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Dermoid cysts are congenital lesions often found along embryonic fusion lines (e.g., lateral eyebrow). They are usually softer, cystic, and mobile. While they can be present at birth, they do not typically exhibit the extreme firmness or teeter-totter sign characteristic of pilomatricomas.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Pilomatricoma

items.stem: A 3-week-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging, deep-seated violaceous mass on his left thigh. The lesion has been present since birth but has significantly increased in size over the past week, causing mild pain and limiting leg movement. Physical examination reveals a firm, 6-cm indurated plaque with overlying ecchymoses and petechiae. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 25,000/µL (normal: 150,000–450,000/µL), prolonged prothrombin time, and elevated D-dimer levels. The mother is concerned about the diagnosis and asks if this condition will resolve spontaneously like many other vascular birthmarks.
items.leadIn: Which of the following underlying pathologic processes is most likely responsible for this infant's hematologic abnormalities?
items.learningObjective: Recognize which vascular tumor, not infantile hemangioma, is classically associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.
items.correctAnswerText: Consumptive coagulopathy secondary to platelet trapping within a kaposiform hemangioendothelioma
items.teachingPoint: Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (severe thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy) is associated with kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma, NOT infantile hemangiomas. Recognizing this distinction is critical because KMP requires urgent systemic therapy, whereas infantile hemangiomas are typically managed with observation or beta-blockers.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a rapidly enlarging, firm, deep-seated violaceous mass with overlying bruising and severe thrombocytopenia is classic for Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (KMP). KMP is a life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy characterized by platelet trapping and fibrin deposition within the vascular tumor. Crucially, KMP is almost exclusively associated with locally aggressive vascular tumors such as kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) and tufted angioma, NOT infantile hemangiomas. The diagnosis of KMP in the setting of a vascular tumor is a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment with systemic corticosteroids, vincristine, or sirolimus to prevent fatal hemorrhage.

options.label: A
options.text: Benign proliferation of GLUT1-positive endothelial cells

options.label: B
options.text: Consumptive coagulopathy secondary to platelet trapping within a kaposiform hemangioendothelioma

options.label: C
options.text: Congenital absence of endothelial basement membrane leading to venous malformation

options.label: D

options.label: E

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Infantile hemangiomas are benign proliferations of GLUT1-positive endothelial cells. They typically appear after birth, undergo a rapid growth phase, and then involute spontaneously over years. Importantly, infantile hemangiomas do NOT cause Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon or consumptive coagulopathy. Misdiagnosing KMP as an infantile hemangioma can lead to fatal outcomes due to delayed treatment.

distractorExplanations.label: B

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Venous malformations are slow-flow vascular anomalies present at birth that expand with growth but do not involute. distractorExplanations.text: Lymphaticovenous malformations are slow-flow anomalies that may contain phleboliths and cause mild localized coagulopathy, but they do not cause the severe systemic consumptive coagulopathy characteristic of Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.

items.stem: A 3-week-old male infant is evaluated for a rapidly enlarging, violaceous, deep-seated mass on the proximal left thigh. The lesion has been present since birth and has expanded over the past week, causing mild swelling but no functional impairment. Physical examination reveals a firm, indurated plaque with overlying ecchymoses and petechiae. Laboratory studies demonstrate a platelet count of 45,000/µL (normal: 150,000–450,000/µL), a hemoglobin level of 11.2 g/dL, and an elevated d-dimer with normal fibrinogen. The lesion does not exhibit the rapid proliferative phase typical of common vascular tumors and remains stable or slowly progresses rather than involuting spontaneously. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Recognize which vascular tumor, not infantile hemangioma, is classically associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.
items.teachingPoint: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma is a rare, locally aggressive vascular tumor classically associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (severe thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy). Unlike infantile hemangiomas, KHE does not involute spontaneously and requires prompt recognition due to the risk of life-threatening bleeding.
items.explanationCorrect: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare, locally aggressive vascular tumor that typically presents in infancy as a deep-seated, indurated, violaceous mass. It is classically associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (KMP), a life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy characterized by severe thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and elevated d-dimer due to platelet trapping within the tumor. KHE is distinct from infantile hemangioma, which does not cause KMP and typically undergoes spontaneous involution. Early recognition is critical due to the risk of bleeding complications.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Infantile hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor of infancy. It typically appears shortly after birth, undergoes a rapid proliferative phase, and eventually involutes spontaneously. Crucially, infantile hemangiomas do not cause Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon; they are benign and self-limiting.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Congenital hemangiomas (such as RICH or NICH) are fully formed at birth. While they can be large and vascular, they do not cause Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. RICH involutes rapidly within the first year of life, whereas NICH persists without involution.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma is the correct answer. It is locally aggressive, often presents at birth or early infancy as a deep indurated mass, and is strongly associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon due to platelet trapping.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Tufted angioma is a rare vascular tumor that can also be associated with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. However, it typically presents as a slowly progressive erythematous or violaceous plaque with papules, often on the neck or upper trunk. KHE is more commonly associated with severe KMP and deep, indurated masses in extremities or trunk, making it the better fit for this clinical vignette.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Pyogenic granuloma is a common, benign vascular lesion that typically presents as a rapidly growing, friable, red nodule, often on the face or digits. It is usually triggered by minor trauma and does not cause systemic coagulopathy or present as a deep, indurated mass in neonates.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the clinic for evaluation of a changing pigmented lesion on his upper back. He first noticed it about 5 years ago as a small, flat brown spot. Over the past 6 months, he has observed that it is slowly enlarging and becoming slightly raised. He denies any bleeding, crusting, or pruritus. On examination, there is a 12-mm pigmented macule with irregular borders and variegated coloration ranging from light tan to dark brown. The lesion is symmetric, with a central area of darker pigmentation and a peripheral rim of lighter tan. There are no satellite lesions, and the remainder of his skin examination is unremarkable.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate a concerning melanoma from a dysplastic nevus using lesion evolution and morphology.
items.teachingPoint: Dysplastic nevi can clinically mimic melanoma due to asymmetry, irregular borders, and color variegation. However, a long-standing history (years) with slow, gradual evolution over recent months favors a dysplastic nevus over melanoma, which typically demonstrates more rapid growth and change. Careful monitoring or excision with histopathological confirmation is warranted for any changing pigmented lesion.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is Dysplastic nevus. The lesion described exhibits classic features of a dysplastic nevus (atypical mole), including asymmetry in color and structure, irregular borders, and variegated pigmentation. Crucially, the lesion has been present for 5 years with only slow, gradual changes over the last 6 months. Dysplastic nevi are known to undergo slow evolution and can mimic melanoma clinically (the 'ugly duckling' sign is not present here as it's a single lesion, but the slow evolution and lack of rapid growth favor a benign or premalignant process over invasive melanoma). The symmetry and lack of alarming features like rapid growth, ulceration, or diameter >6mm with abrupt changes point away from melanoma.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer, so no explanation needed here.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Lentigo maligna typically occurs on chronically sun-damaged skin (e.g., face, neck) in older patients and presents as a slowly enlarging macule with irregular borders. While the morphology can overlap, the location (upper back) and patient age make this less likely than a dysplastic nevus. Furthermore, lentigo maligna is in situ melanoma, and the slow evolution over 5 years with recent slight changes is more characteristic of a dysplastic nevus.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common type of melanoma and often presents with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, and diameter >6mm. However, melanomas typically demonstrate more rapid evolution over weeks to months rather than years. The lesion's 5-year history with only recent, slow changes and its symmetric appearance favor a dysplastic nevus over an invasive melanoma.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: A compound nevus typically presents as a raised, dome-shaped papule that is uniform in color. It does not usually exhibit the irregular borders and variegated pigmentation seen in this lesion. While compound nevi can be present for years, the morphological features described are more consistent with a dysplastic nevus.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Seborrheic keratosis usually presents as a waxy, 'stuck-on' appearing lesion with a verrucous surface. It is not typically pigmented in the variegated manner described, nor does it usually present as a flat macule with irregular borders. The clinical description does not match the classic appearance of a seborrheic keratosis.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for follow-up of a pigmented lesion on his left upper back. He noticed it gradually enlarging over the past year and recently developed mild pruritus. A punch biopsy was performed, and pathology reports confirm a superficial spreading melanoma with an ulcerated Breslow depth of 1.2 mm, no lymphovascular invasion, and a mitotic rate of 3/mm². The patient is otherwise healthy with no personal or family history of melanoma and no palpable lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Select the next best management step for melanoma after a diagnostic biopsy shows Breslow depth just over 1 mm.
items.correctAnswerText: Wide local excision with 1-2 cm clinical margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy
items.teachingPoint: Melanomas with a Breslow depth >1.0 mm require wide local excision with 1- to 2-cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy for staging.
items.explanationCorrect: For melanomas with a Breslow thickness greater than 1.0 mm, the standard of care involves wide local excision with 1- to 2-cm clinical margins based on the exact depth (typically 1.5 cm for lesions >1.0 to <2.0 mm, though a range of 1-2 cm is accepted for this depth category) and sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). SLNB is recommended for melanomas >1.0 mm in thickness to assess for regional nodal metastasis, which guides prognosis and adjuvant therapy decisions. The patient's 1.2 mm tumor falls squarely into this category.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man presents for follow-up after an excisional biopsy of a changing pigmented lesion on his upper back. The pathologic report reveals a superficial spreading melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1.2 mm, no ulceration, and a mitotic rate of 3/mm². Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended to assess regional nodal status, but the patient declines due to concerns about surgical complications and recovery time. He has no palpable lymphadenopathy on physical examination. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

items.teachingPoint: For melanomas with a Breslow thickness of 1.01 mm to 2.0 mm, wide local excision with a 2-cm clinical margin is the standard of care. Sentinel lymph node biopsy should be offered for staging but does not replace the necessity of definitive local surgical treatment.

This step must be completed regardless of the patient's decision regarding sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB).

items.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, solitary facial papule that has been present for several years. He notes occasional bleeding after minor trauma. On examination, there is a 6-mm, firm, pearly papule on the left nasolabial fold with prominent telangiectasias and a central depression. The lesion lacks pigment, hair follicle openings, or surrounding scaling.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate basal cell carcinoma from trichoepithelioma and intradermal nevus in a pearly facial papule.
items.teachingPoint: Nodular basal cell carcinoma classically presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias and central ulceration on sun-exposed skin. Differentiating it from clinically similar benign lesions like trichoepithelioma and intradermal nevus relies on recognizing these specific vascular and structural features.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient's clinical presentation is classic for nodular basal cell carcinoma. Key features include a pearly appearance, telangiectasias, and central ulceration or depression. The location on the sun-exposed face of an older adult further supports this diagnosis, as basal cell carcinoma is the most common cutaneous malignancy and frequently arises in sun-damaged skin.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Intradermal nevi are typically flesh-colored or lightly pigmented papules that often contain visible hair follicles. They lack the pearly quality, telangiectasias, and central depression seen in this lesion.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Trichoepitheliomas are benign adnexal tumors that can present as pearly papules, often on the nasolabial folds. However, they typically have a smoother surface without prominent telangiectasias or central ulceration and are usually smaller. While clinically similar, the presence of telangiectasias and a central depression strongly favors basal cell carcinoma.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Basal cell carcinoma

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Seborrheic keratoses are common benign lesions that typically present as waxy, stuck-on plaques with a verrucous surface. They often have a greasy appearance and may contain keratin-filled cysts (pseudohorn cysts). They do not exhibit a pearly quality or telangiectasias.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Syringomas are benign eccrine sweat duct tumors that typically present as multiple, small, flesh-colored to yellowish papules on the lower eyelids. They are not typically solitary, pearly, or associated with telangiectasias and central depression.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, ulcerated nodule on his sun-exposed scalp. A shave biopsy is performed. Histopathologic examination reveals a proliferation of highly atypical epithelioid melanocytes extending from the dermoepidermal junction into the underlying dermis. There is a marked inflammatory infiltrate and prominent tumor-associated lymphovascular invasion, but no identifiable junctional melanocytic component. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Correlate melanoma histopathology with the appropriate clinicopathologic diagnosis in a melanocytic lesion.
items.teachingPoint: Nodular melanoma is characterized by a predominantly vertical growth phase with dermal invasion and often lacks an identifiable radial (junctional) growth phase, distinguishing it from other melanoma subtypes that typically exhibit an expansile intraepidermal component.
items.explanationCorrect: The correct answer is nodular melanoma. The clinical presentation of a rapidly enlarging, ulcerated nodule on sun-exposed skin is classic for nodular melanoma. Histologically, nodular melanomas are characterized by a predominantly vertical growth phase with dermal invasion. Crucially, they often lack a significant or identifiable radial (junctional) growth phase, which distinguishes them from other melanoma subtypes that typically present with an expansile intraepidermal component. The presence of marked atypia, inflammation, and lymphovascular invasion further supports a malignant diagnosis.

However, they typically occur in children and young adults, lack the aggressive clinical features of rapid ulceration, and usually show a symmetric architecture with maturation.

distractorExplanations.text: Pigmented basal cell carcinoma can present as a nodular lesion but histologically shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifacts, not melanocytic proliferation. The biopsy specifically describes atypical melanocytes.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man presents for evaluation of a slowly enlarging, indurated lesion on the helix of his right ear. He notes occasional bleeding when shaving nearby areas but no pain or paresthesias. Examination reveals a 1.5-cm erythematous, scaly plaque with focal ulceration and induration at the base. The lesion has been present for approximately 18 months. There is no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy, and the remainder of his physical examination is unremarkable. He has a history of significant cumulative sun exposure and multiple prior actinic keratoses.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Identify the most appropriate management approach for a high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma on the ear or lip.
items.teachingPoint: High-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas located in the H-zone of the face, particularly on the ear or lip, are best managed with Mohs micrographic surgery to ensure complete margin assessment and maximize tissue preservation.
items.explanationCorrect: This patient has a high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) located in the 'H-zone' of the face, specifically on the ear. High-risk features include location (ear, lip), size >6 mm, and clinical features suggesting aggressiveness such as induration and ulceration. Mohs micrographic surgery is the preferred treatment for high-risk cSCCs in cosmetically and functionally sensitive areas like the ear, as it provides complete margin assessment while maximizing tissue preservation. It offers the highest cure rates and is particularly indicated for lesions with perineural involvement risk or recurrent disease, though its use in primary high-risk lesions on the ear is also standard to ensure clear margins and minimize recurrence.

items.explanationCorrect: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumor of the skin that typically presents as a rapidly growing, firm, flesh-colored or erythematous nodule in sun-exposed areas of older adults. Histologically, MCC is characterized by sheets or nests of small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, finely granular 'salt-and-pepper' neuroendocrine chromatin, and numerous mitotic figures. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positivity for cytokeratin 20 (CK20) in a characteristic perinuclear dot-like pattern, along with neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin and chromogranin. This distinguishes it from amelanotic melanoma, which would show S100 and SOX10 positivity, and cutaneous B-cell lymphoma, which would demonstrate CD20+ lymphoid cells.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and prior squamous cell carcinoma presents with a 3-cm, firm, erythematous to violaceous nodule on his left shin that has rapidly enlarged over 4 weeks. The lesion is non-tender, lacks a central keratin plug, and shows no evidence of ulceration. Palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy is noted bilaterally. A punch biopsy reveals a dermal-based proliferation of small, round blue cells with scant cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates strong diffuse positivity for cytokeratin 20 (CK20) with a characteristic perinuclear dot-like pattern, while staining for S100 and SOX10 is negative.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate Merkel cell carcinoma from amelanotic melanoma and cutaneous B-cell lymphoma in a rapidly growing nodule.
items.teachingPoint: Merkel cell carcinoma should be suspected in elderly or immunosuppressed patients presenting with a rapidly growing, firm, erythematous to violaceous nodule. Diagnosis is confirmed by histology showing small round blue cells and immunohistochemistry demonstrating CK20 positivity with a characteristic perinuclear dot-like pattern, alongside negative melanocytic markers (S100, SOX10).
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a rapidly enlarging, firm, erythematous to violaceous nodule in an elderly immunosuppressed patient is highly characteristic of Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC). The histologic description of a dermal proliferation of small, round blue cells is classic for MCC. The definitive diagnostic feature provided is the immunohistochemical profile: strong, diffuse CK20 positivity with a perinuclear dot-like pattern is virtually pathognomonic for MCC. Furthermore, the negative S100 and SOX10 staining effectively rules out melanocytic lesions. The patient's history of CLL also places him at an increased risk for MCC due to chronic immunosuppression.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Amelanotic melanoma can present as a rapidly growing pink or red nodule, but histology would typically show atypical melanocytes rather than small round blue cells. Crucially, amelanotic melanoma would be positive for S100 and SOX10, which are negative in this case.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma can present as a red or purple nodule, but the histology would show a lymphoid infiltrate rather than epithelial small round blue cells. Immunohistochemistry would be positive for B-cell markers (e.g., CD20) and negative for CK20.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Merkel cell carcinoma

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Extramammary Paget disease typically presents as an erythematous, scaly, or eczematous plaque in apocrine-rich areas (e.g., vulva, perianal region), not as a rapidly growing nodule on the shin. Histology would show large pale cells with mucin (Paget cells) that are CK7 positive and CK20 negative.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Basal cell carcinoma usually presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias and grows slowly over months to years, not rapidly over weeks. Histology would show nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifacts, not a diffuse proliferation of small round blue cells.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 1.2-cm, pearly papule with telangiectasias and central ulceration on the left cheek. The lesion has been slowly enlarging over 18 months and is located within the high-risk 'mask area' of the face, near the medial canthus. Dermoscopy reveals arborizing vessels and blue-gray ovoid nests. A shave biopsy confirms nodular basal cell carcinoma with deep infiltration to the reticular dermis and perineural involvement noted at the lateral margin. The patient is medically fit for surgery and desires definitive treatment with maximal cosmetic preservation.

items.teachingPoint: Mohs micrographic surgery is the gold standard for high-risk basal cell carcinoma in tissue-sparing locations, providing complete margin evaluation and maximal tissue preservation to optimize cosmetic and functional outcomes.
items.explanationCorrect: Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice for high-risk basal cell carcinoma in tissue-sparing locations such as the central face, particularly when perineural involvement is suspected. Reconstruction with a full-thickness skin graft is appropriate for the resulting defect to ensure durable coverage and minimize contracture.

MMS provides 100% margin evaluation while sparing surrounding normal tissue, thereby optimizing both oncologic control and cosmetic outcomes in these anatomically complex regions.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man returns to the clinic one week after Mohs micrographic surgery with reconstruction for a basal cell carcinoma on his left cheek. He reports increasing redness, pruritus, and mild swelling around the suture line over the past 48 hours. He has been applying a prescribed topical antibiotic ointment three times daily to the site. On examination, there is well-demarcated erythema and edema involving the immediate periwound area and extending slightly onto the adjacent normal skin. The wound edges are clean without purulence, fluctuance, or foul odor. Mild crusting is present at the suture sites, but there are no signs of systemic illness or spreading cellulitis beyond the immediate surgical field.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Differentiate allergic contact dermatitis to a postoperative topical agent from a true surgical-site infection.
items.teachingPoint: Allergic contact dermatitis to topical antibiotics (e.g., neomycin) should be suspected in postoperative patients presenting with pruritic, well-demarcated erythema and edema around the wound without signs of purulence or systemic infection. Differentiating ACD from surgical site infection is critical to avoid unnecessary antibiotic use and ensure appropriate management by discontinuing the offending topical agent.
items.explanationCorrect: The patient's presentation of pruritus, well-demarcated erythema and edema extending slightly beyond the wound edges, and lack of purulence or systemic signs strongly suggests allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) rather than infection. Neomycin, a common component of topical antibiotic ointments used postoperatively, is a frequent sensitizer. ACD typically presents with intense pruritus and eczematous changes confined to areas of contact, which aligns with the distribution around the suture line and adjacent skin where the ointment was applied. Discontinuation of the offending agent is the primary management.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Staphylococcal wound infection typically presents with increasing pain, warmth, purulent drainage, and often systemic signs like fever. The absence of purulence, fluctuance, foul odor, and the prominent pruritus make this diagnosis unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. See explanation for correct answer.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency characterized by severe pain out of proportion to exam findings, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, and often crepitus or skin necrosis. This patient is well-appearing with localized symptoms, making this diagnosis incorrect.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Herpes simplex virus reactivation would present with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, often preceded by tingling or pain. The absence of vesicles and the presence of pruritus and crusting consistent with topical application make this diagnosis unlikely.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Suture granuloma typically presents as a small, firm, erythematous nodule at the site of an individual suture, often appearing weeks to months later. It does not cause diffuse periwound erythema and edema extending onto adjacent skin.

items.explanationCorrect: This patient’s presentation of intense pruritus, vesicles, and well-demarcated erythema extending beyond the surgical site is classic for allergic contact dermatitis (ACD). Neomycin, a common ingredient in topical antibiotic ointments, is a frequent cause of ACD. The absence of purulence, warmth, induration, and systemic signs (e.g., fever) argues against a true bacterial infection. items.stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a nodular basal cell carcinoma on the nasal tip. The final defect measures 1.5 cm in diameter, involving approximately 25% of the nasal tip but sparing the alar rim. The surrounding skin exhibits moderate rhytides and sebaceous hyperplasia consistent with his age. He is otherwise healthy and has no history of keloid formation. Which of the following reconstruction principles is most appropriate for this defect?
items.leadIn: Which of the following reconstruction principles is most appropriate for this defect?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate reconstruction principle for a nasal ala or tip defect after Mohs surgery.
items.correctAnswerText: Local tissue rearrangement to recruit adjacent lax skin
items.teachingPoint: For nasal tip and ala defects involving up to 50% of the subunit, local tissue rearrangement (flaps) is preferred over skin grafts or secondary intention to optimize aesthetic outcomes, preserve structural support, and match color/texture. Primary closure under tension should be avoided to prevent alar retraction or notching.
items.explanationCorrect: For a 1.5 cm defect on the nasal tip involving approximately 25% of the subunit, local tissue rearrangement (such as a bilobed flap or geometric retrograde triangle flap) is the most appropriate reconstruction principle. The nasal tip and alae are high-tension areas where skin laxity is limited, but adjacent forehead or sidewall skin can often be recruited to cover the defect while preserving aesthetic subunits. This approach provides color and texture match, maintains cartilage support, and avoids the morbidity of distant grafts. Recruitment of adjacent lax skin within the same aesthetic subunit or neighboring high-quality donor site is the cornerstone of nasal reconstruction.

options.label: B

Undermining the wound edges in the subdermal plane and utilizing relaxation incisions at the periphery effectively redistributes tension laterally, allowing for a loose, tension-free primary closure. This principle is fundamental to facial reconstruction and preserves local tissue quality.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man presents for closure of a 2.5-cm elliptical defect on the forehead following Mohs micrographic surgery for basal cell carcinoma. The wound edges are well-approximated, and the underlying subcutaneous tissue is intact. To optimize cosmetic outcome by minimizing tension on the skin surface and aligning the final scar with relaxed skin tension lines, which of the following closure principles should be prioritized during the layered repair?
items.leadIn: Which of the following closure principles is most critical for optimizing cosmetic outcome in this scenario?
items.learningObjective: Identify the wound-closure principle most relevant to minimizing tension and improving scar orientation.
items.correctAnswerText: Tension-relieving deep dermal or subcutaneous sutures
items.teachingPoint: Deep dermal or subcutaneous sutures are the cornerstone of tension-free wound closure. They offload mechanical stress from the epidermis, minimizing scar widening and optimizing alignment with relaxed skin tension lines.
items.explanationCorrect: The most effective method to minimize tension on the skin surface and improve scar orientation is the use of deep dermal or subcutaneous sutures. These deeper layers absorb the mechanical forces generated by skin tension, thereby reducing strain on the epidermal closure. This principle prevents wound dehiscence, widens scars, and causes 'railroad tracking.' By offloading tension to the deeper tissues, the final scar aligns better with relaxed skin tension lines (RSTL) and remains thin.

options.label: A
options.text: Tight approximation of the epidermis with small-gauge sutures

options.label: B
options.text: Deep dermal sutures placed perpendicular to the wound edges

options.label: C
options.text: Epidermal approximation with 4-0 nylon interrupted sutures

options.label: D
options.text: Subcuticular sutures placed parallel to the wound edges

options.label: E
options.text: Tension-relieving deep dermal or subcutaneous sutures

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Tight epidermal approximation with small-gauge sutures places tension directly on the skin surface, increasing the risk of scar widening, ischemia, and 'railroad tracking.' It does not address underlying tension.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Deep dermal sutures should generally be placed parallel to the wound edges (longitudinal) rather than perpendicular. Perpendicular placement can cause puckering or dog-ear deformities and does not effectively distribute tension along the wound axis.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Epidermal sutures alone (e.g., 4-0 nylon) bear the full tension of closure, leading to poor cosmetic outcomes in high-tension areas like the forehead. They are typically used for superficial closure only after deep tension-bearing sutures have been placed.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Subcuticular sutures are excellent for epidermal eversion and cosmetic alignment but should not bear significant tension. They are typically used as a final layer over deep tension-relieving sutures, not as the primary mechanism for offloading tension.

distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-mm, bright red, non-blanching macule on his right cheek that has been present for 2 years. The lesion is a capillary malformation (port-wine stain) that the patient wishes to remove for cosmetic reasons. He has fair skin (Fitzpatrick type II) and no history of keloid formation or recent isotretinoin use. Which of the following laser parameters is most appropriate for this patient's treatment?
items.leadIn: Which of the following laser parameters is most appropriate for this patient's treatment?
items.learningObjective: Choose the most appropriate laser modality for a vascular lesion based on the principle of selective photothermolysis.
items.correctAnswerText: Pulsed dye laser (585-595 nm) with a fluence of 10 J/cm² and a pulse duration of 450 μs
items.teachingPoint: The pulsed dye laser (585-595 nm) is the treatment of choice for superficial vascular lesions such as port-wine stains and telangiectasias. Its efficacy is based on the principle of selective photothermolysis, utilizing a wavelength that targets oxyhemoglobin and a pulse duration matched to the thermal relaxation time of the target vessels.
items.explanationCorrect: The pulsed dye laser (PDL) operating at 585-595 nm is the gold standard for treating vascular lesions like port-wine stains. According to the principle of selective photothermolysis, the laser wavelength must be selectively absorbed by the target chromophore (oxyhemoglobin) while minimizing absorption by surrounding tissue. The PDL's wavelength corresponds to the absorption peak of oxyhemoglobin. Furthermore, the pulse duration (450 μs) is selected to be shorter than or equal to the thermal relaxation time of the targeted blood vessels (typically 10-100 μs for capillaries), allowing for rapid heating and destruction of the vessel wall while sparing adjacent epidermis. The fluence is titrated to achieve purpura, a clinical endpoint indicating effective vessel destruction.

options.label: A
options.text: Long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm) with a fluence of 20 J/cm² and a pulse duration of 10 ms

options.label: B
options.text: Pulsed dye laser (585-595 nm) with a fluence of 10 J/cm² and a pulse duration of 450 μs

options.label: C
options.text: Fractional CO2 laser (10,600 nm) with a fluence of 15 J/cm² and a pulse duration of 1 ms

options.label: D
options.text: Intense pulsed light (IPL) device with a 500-1200 nm filter and a pulse duration of 30 ms

options.label: E
options.text: Ruby laser (694 nm) with a fluence of 8 J/cm² and a pulse duration of 3 ms

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: The Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm) has deeper penetration and lower melanin absorption, making it suitable for deeper vascular lesions (e.g., venous malformations) or hair removal. However, it is less effective for superficial capillary malformations and carries a higher risk of scarring if used at high fluences on the face.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Correct answer. The PDL is the most appropriate choice for superficial vascular lesions based on selective photothermolysis principles.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: The CO2 laser is an ablative laser that vaporizes water-rich tissue. It is used for resurfacing, verrucae, and tumor removal. It lacks selective absorption by hemoglobin and would cause significant nonspecific thermal damage to the lesion and surrounding skin, leading to scarring.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: While IPL can treat vascular lesions, it uses a broad spectrum of light rather than a monochromatic wavelength. PDLs are preferred for port-wine stains due to their specific hemoglobin absorption peak and superior efficacy. IPL is more commonly used for diffuse erythema or photorejuvenation.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: The ruby laser (694 nm) is primarily used for tattoo removal and benign pigmented lesions. While it has some hemoglobin absorption, it is less optimal than PDL for vascular targets and carries a higher risk of epidermal injury and hypopigmentation compared to the PDL.

The lesion consists of dilated capillaries measuring approximately 0.1 to 0.2 mm in diameter. She has fair skin (Fitzpatrick type II) and no history of keloid formation or recent isotretinoin use. items.leadIn: Which of the following laser modalities is most appropriate for this patient's lesion?

items.teachingPoint: The 595-nm pulsed dye laser is the treatment of choice for superficial vascular lesions due to its high absorption by oxyhemoglobin and pulse durations that match the thermal relaxation time of small vessels, minimizing collateral damage.
items.explanationCorrect: The 595-nm pulsed dye laser (PDL) is the gold standard for treating vascular lesions such as port-wine stains, hemangiomas, and telangiectasias. It operates on the principle of selective photothermolysis, targeting oxyhemoglobin with high absorption at this wavelength. The pulse duration is typically shorter than the thermal relaxation time of the target vessels (0.1-0.2 mm), minimizing heat diffusion to surrounding tissue and reducing the risk of scarring or dyspigmentation, especially in Fitzpatrick skin types I-III.
