items.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-year history of intensely pruritic, lichenified papules and plaques on her lower legs. A punch biopsy reveals thickened, eosinophilic, amorphous deposits within the papillary dermis. Special staining with Congo red demonstrates apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Electron microscopy shows randomly arranged, non-branching fibrils with a diameter of 8 to 10 nm. The patient has no history of renal disease, heart failure, or hepatomegaly.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and associated systemic implication?
items.learningObjective: Correlate Congo-red–positive eosinophilic deposits with the most likely cutaneous amyloidosis pattern or systemic implication.
items.correctAnswerText: Primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis with no increased risk of systemic disease
items.teachingPoint: Primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), including lichen and macular types, is characterized by Congo red–positive amyloid deposits in the papillary dermis derived from keratinocyte turnover due to chronic friction. Unlike systemic amyloidosis, PLCA is strictly confined to the skin and carries no risk of visceral involvement.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of intensely pruritic, lichenified papules on the shins is classic for primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), specifically lichen amyloidosis. The histopathologic findings of eosinophilic, amorphous deposits in the papillary dermis that are Congo red–positive and exhibit apple-green birefringence confirm amyloid deposition. The electron microscopy finding of 8–10 nm non-branching fibrils is characteristic of amyloid. Crucially, PLCA is confined to the skin and does not progress to systemic disease; therefore, extensive systemic workup is unnecessary in the absence of other clinical signs.

options.label: A
options.text: Primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis with no increased risk of systemic disease

options.label: B

options.label: C

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. PLCA (including lichen amyloidosis and macular amyloidosis) is confined to the skin. The deposits are derived from keratinocyte breakdown due to chronic scratching (rubbing amyloidosis). There is no increased risk of systemic involvement.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Systemic AL (light chain) amyloidosis can involve the skin, often presenting as waxy papules or purpura (pinch purpura), but it is associated with a plasma cell dyscrasia. While AL amyloid fibrils are Congo red–positive, the clinical context of isolated lichenified shins without systemic symptoms makes PLCA far more likely. Systemic AL requires urgent evaluation, but the vignette points to a localized process.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis is associated with chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or IBD. Cutaneous involvement in AA amyloidosis is extremely rare. The clinical picture of lichenified shins is not characteristic of AA amyloidosis.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Hereditary transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis can present with cutaneous findings, but it is typically associated with prominent peripheral neuropathy and cardiomyopathy. The patient lacks these systemic features, and ATTR amyloidosis is a much rarer cause of isolated shin pruritus.

distractorExplanations.label: E

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a 10-year history of intense pruritus localized to her bilateral shins. Examination reveals hyperpigmented, lichenified plaques with overlying scale and excoriations on the extensor surfaces. A punch biopsy of a representative lesion demonstrates thickened collagen bundles in the upper dermis with amorphous, eosinophilic material deposited along the epidermal-dermal junction and within dermal papillae. The amorphous material stains intensely red-orange with Congo red dye and exhibits apple-green birefringence under polarized light. No significant dermal inflammation or vasculitis is identified.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely systemic implication associated with this patient's cutaneous findings?
items.learningObjective: Correlate Congo-red–positive eosinophilic deposits with the most likely cutaneous amyloidosis pattern or systemic implication.
items.correctAnswerText: No systemic association; localized to the skin
items.teachingPoint: Congo red–positive amyloid in the context of chronic pruritic lichenified plaques (lichen or macular amyloidosis) is keratin-derived and localized to the skin, carrying no risk of systemic organ involvement.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of chronic, intense pruritus on the shins with lichenified plaques is characteristic of macular amyloidosis or lichen amyloidosis. The histologic findings of eosinophilic, Congo red–positive deposits with apple-green birefringence confirm the presence of amyloid. In this specific clinical context (localized cutaneous lichen amyloidosis), the amyloid is derived from keratinocytes due to chronic rubbing and scratching (scrch-and-itch cycle), not from plasma cell dyscrasias. Therefore, it is a form of localized cutaneous amyloidosis with no systemic association or risk for organ involvement.

options.label: A
options.text: Primary amyloidosis (AL) with potential cardiac involvement

options.label: B
options.text: Light-chain deposition disease with renal failure

options.label: C
options.text: No systemic association; localized to the skin

options.label: E
options.text: Serum amyloid A (SAA) secondary to chronic inflammatory arthritis

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Primary amyloidosis (AL) involves immunoglobulin light chains produced by clonal plasma cells. While it can cause cutaneous findings (e.g., purpura, waxy papules), the clinical history of chronic pruritus and lichenification points to a keratin-derived amyloidosis (lichen or macular amyloidosis), which is strictly localized and not associated with systemic AL disease.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Light-chain deposition disease (LCDD) is related to plasma cell dyscrasias but typically presents with non-amyloid deposits (Congo red–negative) or systemic amyloidosis. It does not fit the classic presentation of localized, pruritic lichenified plaques derived from keratin.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: This is the correct answer. Localized cutaneous amyloidosis (lichen or macular) is caused by keratinocyte apoptosis and subsequent deposition of cytokeratin fragments. It has no systemic implications.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy is associated with IgA deposition in the mesangium of the kidneys and is not related to cutaneous amyloidosis. While dermatitis herpetiformis involves IgA, it presents with vesicles and pustules, not Congo red–positive amyloid deposits.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis results from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, IBD) leading to elevated serum amyloid A protein. It typically affects the kidneys and liver and is not associated with localized pruritic lichenified plaques on the shins.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, yellowish papule on his left cheek that has been present for 2 years. An excisional biopsy is performed. Histologic examination reveals a well-circumscribed dermal proliferation of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading. Interspersed within the lobules are numerous mature sebocytes characterized by multivacuolated, foamy cytoplasm. Mitotic figures are rare, and there is no significant cytologic atypia or infiltrative growth pattern. Immunohistochemistry shows strong androgen receptor positivity in the sebaceous component. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.learningObjective: Correlate sebaceous neoplasia on histology with the hereditary cancer syndrome most likely to be relevant clinically.
items.correctAnswerText: Perform microsatellite instability testing and refer for genetic counseling
items.teachingPoint: Sebaceous adenomas are benign adnexal tumors that, particularly when occurring in young patients or multiple lesions are present, should prompt evaluation for Muir-Torre syndrome. This autosomal dominant condition is a variant of Lynch syndrome characterized by sebaceous neoplasms and visceral malignancies (most commonly colorectal and genitourinary). Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), and affected patients require intensive cancer surveillance.
items.explanationCorrect: The histologic description is classic for a sebaceous adenoma, characterized by a predominance of mature sebocytes over basaloid germinative cells. While many sebaceous neoplasms are sporadic, the presence of a sebaceous adenoma (especially in a relatively young patient or if multiple lesions are present) should raise suspicion for Muir-Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer). Muir-Torre syndrome is associated with visceral malignancies, particularly colorectal and genitourinary cancers. The most appropriate next step is to perform immunohistochemical staining or microsatellite instability testing for mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) and refer the patient for genetic counseling to assess the risk of internal malignancies.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.text: Order a dermatologic examination for screening of multiple basal cell carcinomas

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a new, painless, yellowish-orange papule on her right cheek. She notes similar lesions have been appearing intermittently over the past two years. A punch biopsy reveals a lobulated dermal tumor composed of basaloid germinative cells admixed with mature sebocytes exhibiting foamy, multivacuolated cytoplasm. Mitotic figures are rare and necrosis is absent. Given the histologic findings, which of the following hereditary cancer syndromes should be suspected and screened for?
items.leadIn: Given the histologic findings, which of the following hereditary cancer syndromes should be suspected and screened for?
items.learningObjective: Correlate sebaceous neoplasia on histology with the hereditary cancer syndrome most likely to be relevant clinically.
items.teachingPoint: Sebaceous adenomas and other sebaceous neoplasms can be cutaneous markers of Muir-Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome. Patients presenting with these lesions should undergo evaluation for visceral malignancies, particularly colorectal and genitourinary cancers.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a yellowish-orange facial papule and the histologic findings of basaloid germinative cells admixed with mature sebocytes are diagnostic of a sebaceous adenoma. While most sebaceous neoplasms are sporadic, the presence of multiple sebaceous adenomas or a solitary lesion in a young patient should raise suspicion for Muir-Torre syndrome. Muir-Torre syndrome is a phenotypic variant of Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6). Therefore, patients with sebaceous neoplasia should be screened for visceral malignancies associated with Lynch syndrome, particularly colorectal and genitourinary cancers.

options.label: A

distractorExplanations.text: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome is caused by BRCA1/2 mutations. It predisposes to breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancers, but is not associated with sebaceous neoplasms.

distractorExplanations.text: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is the correct answer. Muir-Torre syndrome is a variant of Lynch syndrome characterized by sebaceous neoplasms (adenomas, epitheliomas) and/or keratoacanthomas alongside visceral malignancies.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by NF1 mutations and presents with café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and axillary freckling. It is not associated with sebaceous neoplasms.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Tuberous sclerosis complex presents with facial angiofibromas (which can be erythematous but not typically yellowish-orange or sebaceous on histology), ash-leaf spots, shagreen patches, and renal/cardiac tumors. It is not associated with sebaceous neoplasms.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is associated with hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma. It is not associated with sebaceous neoplasms.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, painful plaque on the scalp that has been present for several years. He reports intermittent throbbing pain and a sensation of pressure, particularly in warm weather or after physical exertion. Physical examination reveals a 4-cm erythematous, scaly plaque with a cobblestone or pebbly surface texture. A biopsy demonstrates two distinct but intermingled histologic patterns: islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction clefts, as well as nests of cuticularized cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and concentric laminated keratin. Additionally, there are multiple well-circumscribed islands of basaloid cells surrounded by thick, hyaline basement membrane material resembling a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern. Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
items.learningObjective: Correlate an adnexal tumor pattern such as cylindroma or trichoepithelioma with the appropriate clinical diagnosis.
items.teachingPoint: Cylindromas are benign adnexal tumors characterized clinically by pebbly, cobblestone plaques (often on the scalp) and histologically by basaloid cell islands surrounded by thick, eosinophilic hyaline basement membrane material that interdigitates to create a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of a painful, pebbly scalp plaque in an adult is highly characteristic of a cylindroma. The histologic description provides the definitive evidence: islands of basaloid cells surrounded by thick, eosinophilic hyaline basement membrane material that interdigitates to form a classic 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern. The presence of cuticularized cells and basaloid islands with retraction clefts can sometimes be seen in mixed adnexal tumors or overlapping lesions, but the thick hyaline rims and jigsaw architecture are pathognomonic for cylindroma. These tumors often arise on the scalp and face and can be solitary or part of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome.

distractorExplanations.label: A
distractorExplanations.text: Multiple familial trichoepithelioma typically presents as multiple small, firm, skin-colored to erythematous papules on the face (especially nasolabial folds), not a solitary painful scalp plaque. Histology shows basaloid islands with horn cysts and papillary mesenchymal bodies, lacking the thick hyaline basement membrane jigsaw pattern.

distractorExplanations.label: B
distractorExplanations.text: Cylindroma is the correct answer, so this field should explain why it's not the distractor. Wait, I need to list distractors A, C, D, E here.

distractorExplanations.label: C
distractorExplanations.text: Basal cell carcinoma can show basaloid islands with peripheral palisading and retraction clefts, which might be suggested by part of the histology. However, BCC does not form thick hyaline basement membrane rings or a jigsaw pattern. Clinically, BCC usually presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias or an ulcerated nodule, not a pebbly plaque.

distractorExplanations.label: D
distractorExplanations.text: Syringoma typically presents as multiple small, firm papules on the lower eyelids. Histologically, it shows ductal structures with a 'tadpole' appearance embedded in a fibrous stroma, lacking the jigsaw pattern of hyaline-rimmed basaloid islands.

distractorExplanations.label: E
distractorExplanations.text: Pilomatricoma presents as a firm, deep-seated nodule, often on the head and neck of children or young adults. Histology is characterized by basaloid cells abruptly transitioning to anucleate 'ghost' or shadow cells, without the hyaline basement membrane rings seen in cylindroma.

He reports a history of similar lesions on his scalp and face that were surgically removed in the past. On examination, there is a 2-cm, firm, erythematous to violaceous nodule with a smooth surface. The lesion is exquisitely tender to palpation. A biopsy reveals multiple dermal nests of basaloid cells surrounded by thick, eosinophilic basement membrane material arranged in a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern.
items.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis?

items.teachingPoint: Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is characterized by multiple cylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, and spiradenomas. Cylindromas classically present as painful scalp nodules with histology showing basaloid islands surrounded by thick basement membrane material in a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern.
items.explanationCorrect: The clinical presentation of multiple adnexal tumors on the scalp and face, combined with the histopathologic finding of basaloid islands surrounded by thick basement membrane material in a 'jigsaw puzzle' pattern, is diagnostic of cylindroma. Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by the development of multiple cylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, and spiradenomas. The combination of these specific tumor types is the hallmark of this syndrome.
